question: What proportion of adults having hip fracture surgery receive intravenous tranexamic acid before the start of surgery?
why: NICE widened TXA to all adults whose surgery breaches the skin (NG24, 2026). One hip fracture audit in the library [1725] reached 85% with protocol and teaching; nobody has audited against the 2026 wording.

standard.source: NICE NG24 rec 1.3.1 and 1.3.3 (2015, updated February 2026)
standard.wording: 1.3.1 Offer tranexamic acid to adults having surgery in an operating theatre if: there is any risk of bleeding and the procedure will breach the skin or mucous membranes. [2026] ... 1.3.3 When using tranexamic acid for adults having surgery, administer it just before the start of surgery. Typically give 1 g by slow intravenous injection. [2026]

pass: TXA given IV between induction and knife-to-skin, recorded on the anaesthetic chart; or a specific contraindication documented.
population: Adults (≥60) having surgery for hip fracture. Exclude patients managed without surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive operated hip fracture patients over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: NHFD extract for case list; anaesthetic chart or anaesthetic e-record for TXA dose and time; theatre system for knife-to-skin time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a default 'Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction' line to the hip fracture anaesthetic e-record or pre-printed chart, with an 'omitted because' box.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive operated hip fractures, same template.
close_loop: Present at the joint anaesthetic and trauma governance meeting. If it works, make the default line permanent and add TXA to the monthly hip fracture dashboard.
evidence: [1725] hip fracture TXA: 70% → 85% (protocol update and teaching; p=0.23)
[2572] HPB: TXA prompt on WHO time-out did not increase pre-operative dosing (checklist prompt alone fails)
[1743] trust-wide e-record monitoring: 78.7% → 86.3% overall, T&O 98.2% (electronic tracking)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the anaesthetic e-record
pass_short: IV tranexamic acid given between induction and knife-to-skin, or contraindication documented

question: What proportion of red cell transfusions for non-bleeding hip fracture patients are given as a single unit followed by reassessment?
why: Back-to-back two-unit transfusions are common on trauma wards. The library has threshold audits [1254][1294] but single-unit practice was only measured once (54.2%) with no loop.

standard.source: NICE NG24 rec 1.6.1 and 1.6.2 (2015, updated February 2026)
standard.wording: 1.6.1 Consider single‑unit red blood cell transfusions for adults (or equivalent volumes calculated based on body weight for children or adults with low body weight) who do not have active bleeding. [2015] 1.6.2 After each single‑unit red blood cell transfusion (or equivalent volumes calculated based on body weight for children or adults with low body weight), clinically reassess and check haemoglobin levels, and give further transfusions if needed. [2015]

pass: One unit prescribed per episode, and a documented Hb check or clinical review before any further unit.
population: Transfusion episodes in adults admitted with hip fracture. Exclude major haemorrhage and active bleeding documented at the time.
sample: 40 consecutive transfusion episodes in hip fracture patients over the last 3–4 months.
data_source: Blood bank issue log (Trust transfusion lab) for episodes; EPMA or transfusion chart for units prescribed; lab system for Hb between units; notes for review.

question: What proportion of older adults admitted with a pelvic fragility fracture receive pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for one month?
why: Pelvic and acetabular fragility fractures are often managed non-operatively outside the hip pathway. NICE gives them the same one-month prophylaxis as hip fractures. No audit in the library; the NHFD adds pelvic fractures from 2026.

standard.source: NICE NG89 rec 1.11.2 (2018, updated 2019)
standard.wording: Offer VTE prophylaxis for a month to people with fragility fractures of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur if the risk of VTE outweighs the risk of bleeding. Choose either: LMWH, starting 6 to12 hours after surgery or fondaparinux sodium, starting 6 hours after surgery, providing there is low risk of bleeding. [2018]

pass: LMWH or fondaparinux prescribed in hospital and on discharge to cover 28 days or more from admission; or a documented reason (bleeding risk, already anticoagulated).
population: Adults ≥60 admitted with a low-energy pelvic ring or acetabular fracture. Exclude high-energy trauma and patients on therapeutic anticoagulation.
sample: 30 consecutive admissions over the last 6–9 months.
data_source: Admissions or coding list (ICD-10 S32.1–S32.8) or NHFD pelvic dataset; EPMA for inpatient doses; discharge prescription (TTO) for days supplied.

[1691] arthroplasty: 90% → 98% (discharge pack and nurse check)

pass_short: LMWH or fondaparinux covering at least 28 days from admission, or reason documented

question: What proportion of hip fracture patients whose surgery is delayed beyond the day after admission receive pre-operative pharmacological VTE prophylaxis?
why: About four in ten patients miss surgery by the day after admission (NHFD KPI 2 national 57%). Delayed patients lie immobile without cover. No audit in the library measures pre-operative prophylaxis in this group.

standard.source: NICE NG89 rec 1.11.3 (2018, updated 2019)
standard.wording: Consider pre‑operative VTE prophylaxis for people with fragility fractures of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur if surgery is delayed beyond the day after admission . Give the last dose no less than 12 hours before surgery for LMWH or 24 hours before

population: Adults ≥60 with hip fracture operated later than the day after admission. Exclude patients on therapeutic anticoagulation.
sample: 40 consecutive delayed patients from the last 3 months of NHFD data.
data_source: NHFD extract (admission and surgery times) to find delayed cases; EPMA administration record for LMWH doses and times.

question: What proportion of hip fracture patients who had delirium in hospital have the delirium diagnosis written in the discharge summary to the GP?
why: About a third of hip fracture patients fail the post-op 4AT (NHFD KPI 5 national 68% pass). Delirium raises later dementia risk, but GPs are rarely told. 4AT screening is heavily audited; the hand-over is not.

standard.source: NICE CG103 rec 1.6.4 (2010, updated 2023)
standard.wording: Ensure that the diagnosis of delirium is documented both in the person's record or notes, and in their primary care health record. [2010]

pass: The discharge summary sent to the GP names delirium (or acute confusional state) as a diagnosis or complication of this admission.
population: Adults with hip fracture who had delirium in hospital (post-op 4AT ≥4 or delirium diagnosed in notes). Exclude deaths in hospital.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible discharges over the last 3–4 months.
data_source: NHFD extract (post-op 4AT score) to identify cases; notes for diagnosis; electronic discharge summary.

question: What proportion of hip fracture patients with delirium still present at discharge have a plan for cognitive follow-up?
why: Delirium that has not cleared by discharge may unmask dementia. NICE asks for follow-up. No audit in the library looks at this step after hip fracture.

standard.source: NICE CG103 rec 1.7.5 (2010, updated 2023)
standard.wording: For people in whom delirium does not resolve: re-evaluate for underlying causes follow up and assess for possible dementia (see the NICE guideline on dementia ). [2010]

population: Adults with hip fracture whose last 4AT before discharge was ≥4, or whose notes say delirium unresolved. Exclude known dementia already under a memory service.
sample: 30 consecutive eligible discharges over the last 6 months.
data_source: NHFD extract and orthogeriatric notes for last 4AT; discharge summary; memory service referral system.

question: What proportion of hip fracture inpatients staying longer than 7 days have their malnutrition screen repeated every week?

standard.source: NICE CG32 rec 1.2.2 (2006, updated 2017)
standard.wording: All hospital inpatients on admission and all outpatients at their first clinic appointment should be screened. Screening should be repeated weekly for inpatients and when there is clinical concern for outpatients.

pass: A MUST (with a recorded weight) on admission and at least every 7 days until discharge.
population: Adults with hip fracture with length of stay >7 days. Exclude end-of-life care.
sample: 40 consecutive discharges over the last 2 months.
data_source: NHFD extract for length of stay; nursing e-record for MUST dates and weights.

standard.source: NICE NG37 rec 1.3.7 (2016); BOAST Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma (June 2026)
standard.wording: When assessing neurovascular status in a person with a limb injury, document for both limbs: which nerves and nerve function have been assessed and when; the findings, including: sensibility; motor function using the Medical Research Council (MRC) grading system; which pulses have been assessed and when; how circulation has been assessed when pulses are not accessible. Document and time each repeated assessment.

pass: Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses documented for both legs with a time, at first ED assessment.
population: Adults (16+) with knee dislocation, tibial plateau fracture or distal femoral fracture. Exclude periprosthetic fractures only if managed in another pathway (record).
sample: 40 consecutive cases over the last 6 months
data_source: ED record, orthopaedic clerking (EPR), PACS for diagnosis list.

effort: ~15 min per 10 patients
pass_short: Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses of both legs documented with a time

sample: 30–40 consecutive cases over the last 12 months
data_source: Theatre system, operation note, post-op ward round entries (EPR).

question: In adults having orthopaedic trauma surgery other than hip fracture, was tranexamic acid given at the start of surgery?
why: NICE broadened its tranexamic acid advice in 2026 to any theatre surgery that breaches the skin with a bleeding risk. Existing audits cover arthroplasty [1680] and hip fracture [1725] only.

standard.source: NICE NG24 recs 1.3.1 and 1.3.3 (updated 2026)
standard.wording: 1.3.1 Offer tranexamic acid to adults having surgery in an operating theatre if: there is any risk of bleeding and the procedure will breach the skin or mucous membranes. 1.3.3 When using tranexamic acid for adults having surgery, administer it just before the start of surgery. Typically give 1 g by slow intravenous injection.

pass: IV tranexamic acid given before or at knife-to-skin, or a documented contraindication.
population: Include adults having open orthopaedic trauma surgery (e.g. ankle, tibia, femoral shaft, humerus, forearm fixation). Exclude hip fracture, arthroplasty, and percutaneous K-wire-only procedures.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible trauma operations over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Anaesthetic chart / e-prescribing (TXA dose and time); theatre system (knife-to-skin time); pre-op notes (contraindications).

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on trust drive

change: Add 'Tranexamic acid given / contraindicated' to the Time Out on the electronic WHO checklist for all trauma cases.
reaudit: Week 13–14: next 40 eligible trauma operations.
close_loop: Present at joint orthopaedic/anaesthetic audit and the transfusion committee. If it worked, keep the Time Out item and update the trauma anaesthetic guideline.
evidence: [1680] primary TKR: TXA use 48.8% → 73.1% (emails, posters)
[1725] hip fracture: TXA 70% → 85.2%; contraindications documented 0% → 7.4% (protocol update plus teaching)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from anaesthetic charts
pass_short: IV tranexamic acid given at or before knife-to-skin, or contraindication documented

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
question: In adults aged 65 or over, or with an eGFR below 60, listed for elective hip or knee replacement, did the pre-operative assessment record their risk of acute kidney injury?
why: Post-operative AKI after arthroplasty is common and often linked to NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors. The single orthopaedic AKI audit in the library looks at care after AKI [1180], not risk assessment before surgery.

standard.source: NICE NG148 rec 1.1.13 (2019, updated 2024)
standard.wording: Assess the risk of acute kidney injury in adults before surgery. Be aware that increased risk is associated with: emergency surgery, especially when the person has sepsis or hypovolaemia; intraperitoneal surgery; chronic kidney disease (adults with an eGFR less than 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 are at particular risk); diabetes; heart failure; age 65 years or over; liver disease; use of drugs that can cause or exacerbate kidney injury in the perioperative period (in particular, NSAIDs after surgery). Use the risk assessment to inform a clinical management plan.

pass: Pre-op record documents AKI risk and a plan for ACE inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics and post-op NSAIDs (hold, continue or avoid).
population: Include adults aged 65+ or with eGFR <60 listed for elective primary hip or knee replacement. Exclude patients on renal replacement therapy.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: Pre-op assessment record; lab system (eGFR); medication list; post-op drug chart (NSAID prescribed); post-op creatinine.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on trust drive

change: Add an AKI risk box with a medicines plan (ACE inhibitor/ARB/diuretic/NSAID) to the pre-op assessment template, auto-shown when age ≥65 or eGFR <60.
reaudit: Week 13–14: next 40 eligible patients.
close_loop: Present to pre-op assessment nurses and arthroplasty team. If it worked, keep the template box and track post-op AKI rate.
evidence: [1180] post-operative femur fracture AKI bundle: 20% → 100% (teaching, reminders and structured AKI proforma)
[1183] hip fracture: post-op proforma prompting holding ACE inhibitors raised appropriate holding 40% → 88%
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from pre-op records and lab system
pass_short: AKI risk and plan for ACE inhibitors, diuretics and NSAIDs documented pre-operatively

question: In adults aged 65 or over admitted with an orthopaedic injury other than hip fracture, was a delirium screen documented within 24 hours of admission?
why: Delirium screening is embedded for hip fracture but not for other older trauma (wrist, humerus, pelvis, ankle). Surgical 4AT audits show low completion [1153].

standard.source: NICE CG103 recs 1.2.1 and 1.3.1 (2010, updated 2023)
standard.wording: 1.2.1 When people first present to hospital or long-term care, assess them for the following risk factors. If any of these risk factors are present, the person is at risk of delirium. Age 65 years or older. ... 1.3.1 At presentation, assess people at risk for recent (within hours or days) changes or fluctuations that may indicate delirium.

pass: A validated delirium screen (e.g. 4AT) documented within 24 hours of the admission time.
population: Include adults aged 65+ admitted under orthopaedics with a non-hip-fracture injury. Exclude hip fractures (covered by NHFD) and patients intubated on arrival.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible admissions over the last 4–6 weeks.
data_source: EPR admission time; clerking and nursing admission documents; e-observations or 4AT form.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on trust drive

change: Add a 4AT field to the orthopaedic admission clerking proforma that is required for all patients aged 65 or over.
reaudit: Week 13–14: next 40 eligible admissions.
close_loop: Present with the orthogeriatric team. If it worked, keep the proforma field and extend orthogeriatric in-reach to non-hip trauma.
evidence: [1153] surgical inpatients: pre-op 4AT 25% → 35% (education only)
[1823] surgical assessment unit: 4AT completion 40% → 64% (care-plan sections plus teaching)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clerking and nursing notes
pass_short: Validated delirium screen such as 4AT within 24 hours of admission

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care

question: In orthopaedic ward patients with suspected infection and a NEWS2 score of 7 or more, were IV antibiotics given within 1 hour of that score?
why: Post-operative sepsis on orthopaedic wards is less common than in medicine and teams are less practised. The library has ward sepsis audits in medicine [2618] but none on orthopaedic wards.

standard.source: NICE NG253 rec 1.8.3 (2025, updated 2026)
standard.wording: Give people aged 16 or over who are at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic treatment, within 1 hour of calculating the person's NEWS2 score on initial assessment in the emergency department or on ward deterioration.

pass: First IV antibiotic dose administered within 60 minutes of the first NEWS2 ≥7 recorded with suspected infection.
population: Include adult orthopaedic inpatients with a NEWS2 of 7 or more and suspected or confirmed infection. Exclude patients on an end-of-life pathway and those already on IV antibiotics for that episode.
sample: All eligible episodes over the last 6–12 months (expect 30–40), found from e-observations NEWS2 ≥7 reports.
data_source: E-observations (NEWS2 time); medical notes (suspected infection, review time); e-prescribing administration record (antibiotic time); lab system (lactate, cultures).

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on trust drive

change: Set e-observations so a NEWS2 ≥7 on an orthopaedic ward pages the on-call doctor with a sepsis screen, and stock a sepsis grab bag with first-dose antibiotics on each orthopaedic ward.
reaudit: Week 13–14 onwards: all eligible episodes in the following 3 months, same template.
close_loop: Present with the sepsis/deteriorating patient team. If it worked, keep the paging rule and grab bags and add orthopaedic wards to the trust sepsis dashboard.
evidence: [2618] ward sepsis protocol audit: proforma used 13.9%, sepsis 6 bundle 55.5% (no re-audit)
[1972] general surgery: system changes (e-prescribing, weekly micro round) beat education for antibiotic standards
effort: ~30 min per 10 episodes from e-obs and prescribing
pass_short: First IV antibiotic within 60 minutes of the first NEWS2 of 7 or more

question: In adults discharged with opioids after orthopaedic surgery, did the discharge letter state the opioid dose, amount supplied and planned duration?
why: Unclear discharge opioid plans lead to repeat prescriptions and long-term use. Orthopaedic opioid audits in the library look at inpatient prescribing [1298], not the discharge letter.

standard.source: Faculty of Pain Medicine / RCoA 'Surgery and Opioids: Best Practice Guidelines 2021', Discharge Planning 3 and 4
standard.wording: The hospital discharge letter should be available in a timely way and provided to all healthcare professionals involved in caring for the patient, including community pharmacists, to avoid an acute prescription of opioids inadvertently becoming a repeat prescription. The hospital discharge letter must explicitly state the recommended opioid dose, amount supplied and planned duration of use. ... Usually 5 days and no more than 7 days of opioids (including Tramadol) should be prescribed.

pass: Discharge letter states opioid dose, amount supplied and planned duration or stop date, and supply is 7 days or less.
population: Include adults discharged on any opioid (including tramadol and codeine) after orthopaedic surgery. Exclude patients on opioids for over 3 months before admission (opioid tolerant) and palliative care.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible discharges over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Electronic discharge summary / TTO; pharmacy dispensing record (quantity supplied).

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on trust drive
Pass criterion: all three items stated and ≤7 days

change: Add a required 'opioid plan' block (dose, quantity, stop date, GP not to add to repeats) to the discharge TTO template when any opioid is prescribed.
reaudit: Week 13–14: next 40 eligible discharges.
close_loop: Present with the acute pain team and pharmacy. If it worked, keep the TTO block and share it with the local GP prescribing group.
evidence: [1298] primary THR: NG180 posters and teaching increased regular D0 oral opioid prescribing by 30% (inpatient step only)
[1207] hip fracture discharge letter proforma: compliance to 95% (template works)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from discharge letters
pass_short: Discharge letter states opioid dose, amount and duration, with supply 7 days or less

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care

question: In orthopaedic inpatients with Parkinson's disease, was every dose of their Parkinson's medicine given within 30 minutes of the prescribed time in the first 72 hours?
why: Missed or late doses around surgery and fasting cause rigidity, falls and aspiration. Existing audits are in elderly care [1890] [1165]; the orthopaedic audit of pre-op medicines [1630] did not isolate Parkinson's drugs.

standard.source: NICE NG71 recs 1.3.2 and 1.3.4 (2017)
standard.wording: 1.3.2 Antiparkinsonian medicines should not be withdrawn abruptly or allowed to fail suddenly due to poor absorption (for example, gastroenteritis, abdominal surgery) to avoid the potential for acute akinesia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome. 1.3.4 In view of the risks of sudden changes in antiparkinsonian medicines, people with Parkinson's disease who are admitted to hospital or care homes should have their medicines: given at the appropriate times, which in some cases may mean allowing self-medication; adjusted by, or adjusted only after discussion with, a specialist in the management of Parkinson's disease.

pass: All Parkinson's medicine doses due in the first 72 hours given within 30 minutes of the prescribed time (local definition of 'appropriate times'), including during nil-by-mouth periods.
population: Include adult orthopaedic inpatients with Parkinson's disease on levodopa or dopamine agonists. Exclude patients on end-of-life care.
sample: All eligible admissions over the last 12 months (expect 30–40), from pharmacy or e-prescribing search for Parkinson's drugs on orthopaedic wards.
data_source: E-prescribing administration record (prescribed and given times); ED record; anaesthetic chart; notes (NBM plan).

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on trust drive
e.g. dispersible or NG levodopa, rotigotine patch

change: Flag Parkinson's drugs as time-critical in e-prescribing (exact-time dosing and alert when a dose is 30 minutes late) and add a Parkinson's NBM plan to the pre-op checklist.
target: ≥90% of patients with all doses on time
reaudit: Week 13–14 onwards: next 3 months of eligible admissions.
close_loop: Present with pharmacy and the Parkinson's nurse specialist. If it worked, keep the alerts and include orthopaedic wards in the trust time-critical medicines audit.
evidence: [1890] older adults: 30% received all PD doses on time (education only; no re-audit)
[1630] pre-op trauma patients: correct medicines 39% → 61% (poster and meetings)
[1165] PD NBM guideline plus education; 75% missed at least one levodopa dose at baseline
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from e-prescribing
pass_short: All Parkinson's doses in first 72 hours given within 30 minutes of due time

question: In adults having elective primary hip or knee replacement, was a urinary catheter avoided unless a clinical indication was documented?
why: Routine catheters add waste, infection and delay mobilisation. The Green Theatre Checklist lists catheterisation as an avoidable intervention. Orthopaedic catheter audits in the library are in hip fracture [1208], not elective arthroplasty.

standard.source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 8
standard.wording: Avoid clinically unnecessary interventions (e.g. antibiotics, urinary catheterisation, histology examinations)

pass: No urinary catheter inserted in theatre, or a catheter with a documented indication (e.g. retention history, long case, critical fluid balance).
population: Include adults having elective primary total hip or knee replacement. Exclude simultaneous bilateral and revision cases.
sample: 40 consecutive elective primary hip or knee replacements over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: Anaesthetic chart and theatre nursing record (catheter inserted and reason); ward notes (removal time, retention, CAUTI).

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on trust drive

change: Remove catheter packs from the default arthroplasty pick list and add 'catheter: indication' to the Team Brief.
reaudit: Week 13–14: next 40 consecutive cases.
close_loop: Present at theatre users' group and the trust green team. If it worked, keep the pick list change and report catheters and waste avoided.
evidence: [1869] ED older adults: catheter indication documented 36% (guideline created; no re-audit)
[1738] WaSTE multicentre arthroplasty audit: ~14 kg waste per case, mostly infectious stream (no re-audit)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from anaesthetic and nursing records
pass_short: No urinary catheter in theatre unless an indication is documented

question: What proportion of new fracture clinic referrals have a named consultant review documented within 24 hours of first presentation?
why: The 2026 BOASt moved the consultant review target to 24 hours. Library audits measured the old 72-hour target only ([1526] 6% → 100%, [1579] closed loop); none has measured 24 hours.

standard.wording: Patients must have their case reviewed by a named consultant within 24 hours of first presentation. This can be performed in person or virtually in a trauma meeting. The outcome of this review should be documented and a copy sent to the patient and GP.

population: Include: patients of any age referred from ED, MIU or GP to the fracture clinic or virtual fracture clinic (VFC). Exclude: patients admitted from ED.
sample: 40 consecutive referrals from the VFC or fracture clinic referral list over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: ED system (arrival time); VFC or trauma meeting list and EPR note (review time, consultant name).

question: When a patient is cancelled from the trauma list, are they offered food or drink within 1 hour of the cancellation?
why: Patients fasted for a trauma list are often cancelled and then left nil by mouth for hours or into the next day, risking dehydration, delirium and acute kidney injury. Cancellations [2170] and pre-operative fasting (ONA-107) are audited; what happens after cancellation is not.

standard.source: Local standard (no national standard identified)
standard.wording: Patients cancelled from a theatre list are offered food or drink within 60 minutes of the decision to cancel.

pass: Documented offer of food or drink within 60 minutes of the recorded cancellation decision, in patients with no clinical reason to stay nil by mouth.
population: Adults fasted for the trauma list and cancelled for that day. Exclude patients kept nil by mouth for a clinical reason (e.g. bowel obstruction, unsafe swallow) and those still possible for a later list the same day.
sample: Every trauma list cancellation over 4 weeks (typically 20–40); extend until 30 cases.
data_source: Theatre cancellation log; coordinator call time; ward nursing notes and fluid/food chart.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Time the coordinator phones the ward

timeline: Wk 1–4 collect; Wk 5 analyse/present; Wk 6 change; Wk 7–12 embed; Wk 13–16 re-audit
change: Add a 'Cancelled: may eat and drink now?' step to the theatre coordinator's cancellation checklist; the coordinator phones the ward with a one-line script and records the time.
reaudit: Weeks 13–16: same template, next 4 weeks of cancellations.
close_loop: Present at the theatre users' group and trauma governance. If it worked, write the step into the trauma list standard operating procedure.
evidence: [2170] same-day theatre list cancellations: cancellation counts only, not what happened to the patient afterwards
pitfalls: No time is recorded when a case is cancelled → agree before week 1 that the coordinator's phone call time is the start time, and put it on the checklist
Staff keep patients fasted 'in case they go later' → record 'later list still possible today' and count only definite cancellations
Ward nurses feel blamed → present it as a theatre-to-ward communication gap; show results by day of week, never by named ward or nurse
The fix fades when the audit team rotates → build it into the coordinator checklist, not a poster
pearls: Recruit the trauma coordinator and one ward sister in week 1; they collect the data and run the fix
Use a one-line script: '[Patient] is cancelled today and may eat and drink now'
Record next-day nil-by-mouth time as well; it is often the larger harm
Pilot on one ward for 2 weeks before rolling out; name the theatre matron as owner afterwards
Bring one patient story (e.g. 30 hours without food) to governance alongside the percentages
effort: ~10 min per 5 cases from the cancellation log and ward charts
pass_short: Food or drink offered within 60 minutes of cancellation

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: On elective orthopaedic lists, what proportion of turnarounds take 15 minutes or less?
why: Turnaround is lost theatre time between cases. The only turnaround audit in the library is a baseline with a mean of 37.7 minutes against a 15-minute target [2768]; no closed-loop turnaround audit exists in orthopaedics.

standard.source: Local standard; 15-minute turnaround target as used in [2792]
standard.wording: Turnaround (patient leaves theatre to start of the next patient's anaesthetic) of 15 minutes or less.

pass: Time from one patient leaving theatre to the start of the next patient's anaesthetic is 15 minutes or less.
population: All turnarounds on elective orthopaedic lists. Exclude the last case of each list (no following case).
sample: Every turnaround on elective orthopaedic lists over 4 weeks (typically 80–150), plus the previous 4 weeks from the theatre system as a baseline.
data_source: Theatre management system timestamps; delay reason recorded by the theatre coordinator.
timeline: Wk 1–4 collect; Wk 5 analyse/present; Wk 6 change; Wk 7–12 embed; Wk 13–16 re-audit
change: Make 'send for next patient' a fixed step on the theatre checklist, triggered at the start of wound closure and time-logged by the coordinator. If the delay data point elsewhere, fix the leading delay reason instead.
target: ≥50% of turnarounds within 15 minutes and median reduced by 10 minutes
reaudit: Weeks 13–16: same template, 4 weeks of lists.
close_loop: Present the weekly median and top three delay reasons at the theatre users' group. If it worked, add turnaround to the monthly theatre dashboard owned by the theatre manager.
evidence: [2768] Northern Ireland: mean turnaround 37.7 min against a 15-min target; cleaning 8.1 min, extubation 5.1 min (baseline only)
[2379] UK emergency theatre: turnover 39 → 11 min after a dedicated theatre registrar separate from on-call
[2366] UK golden patient policy: first-case start times 30 min earlier on average
[1236] UK elective orthopaedics: presenting at governance alone left team-brief start at 08:05 → 08:08
pitfalls: Theatre-system times are entered late or missing → spot-check 10 cases against a stopwatch before week 1; hand-collect week 1 if they differ
'Orthopaedic turnaround is longer because of laminar flow and big trays' → report median by procedure type (joints, hands, trauma), not one overall figure
Staff speed up only while watched → use 4 weeks of past theatre-system data as a hidden baseline
Nurses and ODPs hear 'work faster' → involve the theatre manager from day 1 and frame it as removing waits (porters, beds, trays)
pearls: Record a delay reason for every turnaround; it tells you which fix to use
Find the list that already turns around fastest and copy its routine
Convert minutes to cases: 20 min saved × 3 turnarounds ≈ one extra case a day
Book the porter for the send-for time, not 'when free'
Take one chart to governance: weekly median turnaround with a line where the change went in
effort: ~2 hours to export and clean 4 weeks of theatre-system data
pass_short: Turnaround from patient leaving theatre to next anaesthetic start is 15 minutes or less

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: On elective orthopaedic lists, what percentage of the planned session time is touch time?
why: Touch time utilisation is the national productivity measure, but a single percentage hides where time is lost; the library has no orthopaedic audit of it.

standard.source: GIRFT touchtime utilisation target, as reported in PMC11488670 (CC BY)
standard.wording: The Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) programme has set targets to achieve 85% touchtime utilisation by 2024/25. Touchtime utilisation is a measure of theatre productivity, defined as the time from the start of anaesthesia to the time a patient leaves the theatre for all cases on a defined theatre list as a percentage of total available theatre time.

pass: List touch time (start of anaesthesia to leaving theatre, summed over all cases, within the planned session) is 85% or more of planned session time.
population: All elective orthopaedic lists. Exclude lists cancelled in full.
sample: All elective orthopaedic lists over 4 weeks (one row per list).
data_source: Theatre management system session and case timestamps.

template.note: First anaesthetic start minus session start

timeline: Wk 1–4 collect; Wk 5 analyse/present; Wk 6 change; Wk 7–12 embed; Wk 13–16 re-audit
change: Fix the largest single source of lost time found: usually the first-case start, using a golden patient (first case identified and prepared the day before).
reaudit: Weeks 13–16: same template, 4 weeks of lists.
close_loop: Present lost minutes by cause at the theatre users' group; if it worked, embed the fix in list-planning procedure and track on the theatre dashboard.
evidence: [2366] UK golden patient policy: start times 30 min earlier on average
[1236] UK elective orthopaedics: average team-brief start 08:05 → 08:08 after governance presentation only
pitfalls: The percentage rewards overrunning or under-booked lists → report late start, turnaround and early finish minutes alongside it
Session times in the system differ from real contracted times → confirm planned session length with the theatre manager before week 1
Surgeons dispute the data → share the raw list-by-list sheet with each team before presenting
pearls: Break lost time into late start, turnarounds and early finish; the fix follows the biggest bar
Pair with the turnaround audit and share one data export
Report cases gained, not percentages, to managers
effort: ~2 hours to export and clean 4 weeks of theatre-system data
pass_short: Touch time is 85% or more of planned session time

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: In elective hip and knee replacements, what percentage of theatre waste by weight goes into the orange (infectious) waste stream?
why: Arthroplasty produces about 14 kg of waste per case, most of it sent to the infectious stream for high-temperature treatment, although much is packaging or non-infectious [1738].

standard.source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 14
standard.wording: RECYCLE/use lowest carbon appropriate waste streams: use recycling waste streams for packaging or, if not available, domestic waste stream (prior to patient entering the room); use non-infectious offensive waste streams (yellow/black tiger) unless clear risk of infection (orange); ensure only appropriate contents in sharps bins (sharps/drugs)

pass: Per case: orange-stream waste as a percentage of total theatre waste weight. Local target: orange share halved from cycle 1.
population: Elective primary total hip and knee replacements. Exclude revisions for infection and patients with known transmissible infection.
sample: 20 consecutive cases (about 10 hips, 10 knees).
data_source: Bag weights recorded by the scrub or circulating team at the end of each case; theatre system for procedure details.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4–8 set up with estates; Wk 9–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Place tiger (offensive) and recycling bins in every arthroplasty theatre; open packaging into recycling before the patient enters; keep the orange bin for items with a clear infection risk, as defined in writing with infection prevention.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: same template, next 20 consecutive cases.
close_loop: Present kilograms, cost and carbon per case at theatre users' group and the Trust sustainability group. If it worked, add the bins to the theatre set-up standard and roll out to all orthopaedic theatres.
evidence: [1738] UK multicentre arthroplasty: 14.79 kg per THA and 13.61 kg per TKA; infectious waste 9.88 kg and 8.68 kg; only 5 of 10 trusts had an offensive stream
[2552] UK theatres: recycling 18.4% → 36.7%, falling back to 26.4% the next month (quick guide only)
[2668] UK general surgery: recyclable share 17% → 28% with posters, but total waste per case rose
pitfalls: Infection prevention objects to moving waste out of orange → agree a written rule for what stays orange before week 1 and quote Green Theatre Checklist item 14
The waste contract has no offensive stream → involve the estates waste manager in week 1; the change date depends on the contract
No scales in theatre → borrow a hanging scale from estates or the waste contractor; weigh each bag before it is tied off
Gains fade after the launch [2552] → make the bins part of the fixed theatre layout, not a poster campaign
Total waste rises while the orange share falls [2668] → report total kg per case alongside the percentage
pearls: Recruit the scrub lead and the estates waste manager as co-leads
Open all packaging into recycling before the patient enters, so nothing is contaminated
Photograph a typical orange bag at baseline; it persuades faster than numbers
Convert kg to cost and carbon using the contractor's price per tonne for each stream
Name a green champion for each theatre to keep the bins in place after rotation
effort: ~5 min per case to weigh bags; 1 hour to analyse
pass_short: Orange-stream waste share per case halved from cycle 1

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: On primary knee replacement instrument trays, what proportion of the instruments are used during the operation?
why: Every instrument on a tray is washed and sterilised whether used or not; trays carry instruments that are rarely touched [2671].

standard.source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 9
standard.wording: REVIEW AND RATIONALISE: clarify necessary kit for case and specify what should be available to open only if needed: “Just in time”; take the opportunity to review instrument sets and identify any targets for overage reduction

pass: Per instrument: used in at least 10% of cases. Instruments used in under 10% of cases are candidates for removal to a separate 'open if needed' pack.
population: Primary total knee replacements using the standard tray. Exclude revisions.
sample: 20 consecutive cases.
data_source: Tray list ticked by the scrub practitioner at the end of each case (instrument handed or used = used).
timeline: Wk 1–3 collect; Wk 4 analyse/present; Wk 5–10 agree new tray with surgeons and sterile services; Wk 11–14 embed; Wk 15–17 re-audit
change: Remove instruments used in under 10% of cases from the main tray into a separate 'open if needed' pack, agreed with all knee surgeons and sterile services.
target: ≥80% of tray instruments used per case
reaudit: Weeks 15–17: same template, 20 cases on the new tray; record any 'open if needed' pack openings.
close_loop: Present instruments removed, sterilisation cost and carbon saved at the arthroplasty meeting. If it worked, update the sterile services tray list and review hip trays next.
evidence: [2671] UK laparoscopic cholecystectomy: 7–19 of 63 tray instruments used; new tray with 60% fewer instruments
pitfalls: Surgeons fear a missing instrument mid-case → keep every removed item in a sealed 'open if needed' pack in the theatre
Surgeons use different instruments → count per surgeon and remove only items unused by all
Sterile services cannot change tray lists quickly → involve the sterile services manager from week 1
pearls: Have the scrub practitioner tick the tray list during closure, while it is fresh
Show surgeons the list of never-used instruments with their names on it; agreement follows quickly
Count 'open if needed' pack openings in the re-audit to prove safety
effort: ~3 min per case for the scrub practitioner
pass_short: Instrument used in at least 10% of cases

question: What proportion of hip fracture patients taking warfarin with an INR above 1.5 on arrival receive intravenous vitamin K within 4 hours of arrival?
why: Warfarin reversal is a common, avoidable cause of delay to hip fracture surgery. Published loops [1131][1506] cut delay with an ED vitamin K trigger, but few units measure how fast reversal actually starts.

standard.source: NICE CG124 Hip fracture: management, rec 1.2.2 (2011, last updated January 2023)
standard.wording: Identify and treat correctable comorbidities immediately so that surgery is not delayed by: anaemia anticoagulation volume depletion electrolyte imbalance uncontrolled diabetes uncontrolled heart failure correctable cardiac arrhythmia or ischaemia acute chest infection exacerbation of chronic chest conditions. [2011]

pass: Intravenous vitamin K (any dose) given within 4 hours of arrival at hospital, recorded on the drug chart or ED record. The 4-hour window is the local definition of 'immediately'. A documented reason not to reverse (for example a metallic heart valve plan agreed with haematology) also passes.
population: Adults aged 60 and over with a hip fracture who were taking warfarin on admission and had an INR above 1.5 on the first sample. Exclude patients managed without surgery and those taking a DOAC only.
sample: All eligible patients over the last 18 months (usually 20–40 in a district general hospital); re-audit uses all eligible patients in the following 6 months.
data_source: NHFD extract for the case list; EPR medicines reconciliation or GP record for warfarin; laboratory system for INR; electronic prescribing or ED drug chart for vitamin K time; ED system for arrival time; theatre system for surgery time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'Taking warfarin? Give vitamin K IV now' line to the ED hip fracture pathway order set, so the dose is prescribed by the ED clinician before the INR result returns.
reaudit: After 6 months: all eligible patients in that period, same template.
close_loop: Present at the hip fracture MDT and ED governance meetings. If it works, keep the order-set line permanently and add 'time to vitamin K' to the monthly hip fracture dashboard.
evidence: [1131] hip fracture: median time to theatre 49.7 h → 33.9 h (nurse-led 2 mg IV vitamin K in ED before clotting results)
[1506] hip fracture: mean time to theatre 53.7 h → 37.6 h; anticoagulation breaches 79% → 34% (early-trigger IV vitamin K protocol)
[1452] hip fracture: single 1 mg IV vitamin K on admission shortened INR reversal and pre-operative delay
[1339] hip fracture on warfarin: median 8 h from fracture confirmation to IV vitamin K (baseline only)
pitfalls: Small numbers make percentages jumpy → use all eligible patients over a long window and report counts as well as percentages.
Haematology or cardiology may object for metallic valves → agree a named exception route with haematology before cycle 1 and count a documented plan as a pass.
Arrival time is unclear for transfers → use the time of arrival at your hospital and state this in the method.
The order-set line is ignored at night → ask the ED nurse in charge to prompt it at triage for every suspected hip fracture.
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and the orthogeriatrician as co-leads so the change sits in both pathways.
Pull INR and warfarin status from the laboratory system rather than notes; it is faster and more complete.
Report the time to surgery for these patients alongside the pass rate; the delay saved is the message that keeps the change alive.
Hand the monthly check to the hip fracture nurse so it survives trainee rotation.
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from EPR and laboratory system
pass_short: IV vitamin K within 4 hours of arrival, or reason not to reverse

question: What proportion of hip fracture patients have a pressure ulcer risk assessment recorded within 6 hours of admission?
why: Hip fracture patients lie immobile on trolleys and are among the highest-risk groups for hospital-acquired pressure ulcers. No closed-loop audit of timely risk assessment in hip fracture has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE QS89 Pressure ulcers, quality statement 1 (2015)
standard.wording: People admitted to hospital or a care home with nursing have a pressure ulcer risk assessment within 6 hours of admission.

pass: A completed validated pressure ulcer risk score (for example Waterlow, Braden or PURPOSE-T) timed within 6 hours of the decision to admit, in the ED or ward record.
population: Adults aged 60 and over admitted with a hip fracture. Exclude patients transferred from another hospital's inpatient ward.
sample: 40 consecutive hip fracture admissions over the last 2 months.
data_source: NHFD extract for the case list; ED system for arrival and decision-to-admit times; electronic nursing assessment for the time the risk score was completed; nursing notes for any pressure ulcer during the admission.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make the pressure ulcer risk score a mandatory field in the ED hip fracture nursing pathway document, completed before the patient leaves the ED.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive hip fracture admissions, same template.
close_loop: Present at the hip fracture MDT and the tissue viability group. If it works, keep the mandatory field and report the 6-hour rate on the ward safety board.
evidence: [5876] London teaching hospital: Waterlow recorded 81% → 100% (education, posters, risk-stratification teaching)
[7760] EPR: aSSKINg template built into the record improved first-visit risk tool completion (system change)
[4173] palliative care: incidence did not improve despite many unspecified changes (vague fixes fail)
pitfalls: Decision-to-admit time is missing for some patients → use ED arrival plus 4 hours as a fallback and apply the same rule in both cycles.
Scores are recorded but not timed on paper → use the electronic nursing record, or the time of the next set of observations if the form is untimed, and say so.
ED nurses see this as a ward task → agree with the ED matron that the hip fracture pathway owns it, before cycle 1.
A mandatory field gets ticked without assessment → spot-check 5 records per cycle for a matching skin check.
pearls: Recruit a tissue viability nurse; they own the standard and will champion the change.
Pair the audit with the ward's pressure ulcer incidents so the harm is visible.
Present results to ED nurses at their huddle, not just at the orthopaedic meeting.
Ask the hip fracture nurse to include the 6-hour rate in the monthly NHFD review.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPR
pass_short: Validated pressure ulcer risk score within 6 hours of the decision to admit

question: What proportion of older adults having surgery for a fragility fracture have a consultant-level decision about resuscitation and treatment escalation documented before surgery?
why: Older patients with fragility fractures have a high early mortality, yet escalation decisions are often made in a crisis. Library audits of escalation plans come from general surgery [2673][2694]; none has targeted fragility fracture surgery.

standard.source: BOAST The Care of the Older or Frail Orthopaedic Trauma Patient (May 2019)
standard.wording: Ceilings of treatment, including transfer, escalation and the appropriateness of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), should be discussed jointly by the treating teams. This should be documented and include the patient and those close to them, considering advanced directives, lasting powers of attorney and safeguarding issues. These decisions should be made at consultant level and prior to any surgery.

pass: A treatment escalation plan, ReSPECT form or DNACPR decision (for or against CPR) signed or endorsed by a consultant, dated and timed before the start of anaesthesia.
population: Adults aged 65 and over having surgery for a fragility fracture (hip, femur, pelvis, humerus, wrist or ankle). Exclude day-case wrist fixation.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible operated patients over the last 2 months.
data_source: Theatre system for the case list and anaesthetic start time; EPR alerts or scanned forms for TEP, ReSPECT or DNACPR; ward round entries for consultant endorsement.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'Escalation plan / ReSPECT completed and consultant-endorsed' tick-box to the pre-operative trauma list checklist, checked at the morning trauma meeting.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible operated patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the trauma governance and orthogeriatric meetings. If it works, keep the trauma-meeting checkpoint and add escalation-plan completion to the hip fracture dashboard.
evidence: [2673] major trauma centre surgical patients: completed TEP 58% → 83% (frailty consultant reviews)
[9333] end-of-life inpatients: ceiling of care in notes 41% → 100% (advance care planning proforma)
[2694] general surgery: 6.2% → 5% (email reminder only; fails)
pitfalls: Staff equate escalation planning with DNACPR and avoid it → frame the audit as 'a documented decision either way' and count 'for full escalation' as a pass.
Consultant endorsement is hard to see in notes → accept a ward round entry naming the consultant who agreed the plan.
Out-of-hours surgery leaves no time → the morning trauma meeting check catches most patients the day before.
Email reminders fail → use the list checklist, not messages.
pearls: Recruit an orthogeriatrician and an anaesthetist; both already discuss risk before surgery.
Agree before cycle 1 which forms count (TEP, ReSPECT, DNACPR) and keep that fixed.
Share one anonymised case where an unplanned crash call followed an undocumented decision.
Give the checklist item to the trauma coordinator so it survives rotation.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from EPR and theatre system
pass_short: Consultant-endorsed escalation plan, ReSPECT or DNACPR decision before anaesthesia starts

question: What proportion of adults with an open fracture have tetanus prophylaxis given or withheld in line with UKHSA guidance?
why: Open fractures are tetanus-prone wounds by definition. One ED audit found tetanus assessment documented in under 5% of open fractures [1274]; no closed loop in orthopaedics has been published in the library.

standard.source: UKHSA Guidance on the management of suspected tetanus cases and the assessment and management of tetanus-prone wounds, section 7.2–7.3 and Table 4 (updated 12 August 2026)
standard.wording: Tetanus-prone wounds are likely to foster anaerobic conditions and consideration should be given to the depth of the wound and degree of tissue damage: ... compound fractures ... A reinforcing dose of tetanus-containing vaccine is recommended (see Table 4). ... Table 4: Received adequate priming course of tetanus vaccine but last dose more than 10 years ago ... Immediate treatment: tetanus prone: Immediate reinforcing dose of vaccine ... Not received adequate priming course of tetanus vaccine. Includes uncertain immunisation status and/or born before 1961. ... Immediate reinforcing dose of vaccine One dose of human tetanus immunoglobulin in a different site.

pass: Tetanus immunisation status recorded and the action matches UKHSA Table 4 for that status and wound risk (vaccine, vaccine plus immunoglobulin, or none required), given before or during the first operation.
population: Adults aged 16 and over with an open fracture of any bone. Exclude open hand fractures of the distal phalanx treated in ED only.
sample: All open fractures over the last 12 months (usually 30–50), then all in the next 6 months.
data_source: Theatre system and trauma list for the case list; ED record for immunisation history; drug chart and ED record for vaccine and immunoglobulin; operation note for contamination and delay to debridement.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

options: primed but last dose over 10 years

template.note: Heavy contamination, devitalised tissue or surgery delayed over 6 h

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a tetanus section with the UKHSA Table 4 decision grid to the ED open-fracture proforma, with vaccine and immunoglobulin on the open-fracture order set.
reaudit: After 6 months: all open fractures in that period, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED and trauma governance. If it works, keep the proforma section and add tetanus to the open-fracture BOAST dashboard.
evidence: [1274] ED open fractures: tetanus prophylaxis 48.8%, tetanus assessment documented 4.9% (baseline)
[4170] plastic surgery trauma: 27% needed further tetanus action on arrival (baseline)
[4748] English EDs: 46% would give an unnecessary booster; local guideline followed 'always' in 29%
pitfalls: Immunisation history is often not asked → the proforma must force a status choice, including 'uncertain'.
Immunoglobulin supply worries → confirm with pharmacy where stock is held before cycle 1.
Over-treatment counts as a fail but staff see it as safe → show the UKHSA table and count unnecessary boosters separately.
Small annual numbers → include all open fractures and report counts.
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant; most doses are given in ED.
Check the Summary Care Record for vaccination history when patients cannot recall.
Put the decision grid on the back of the open-fracture photograph consent sheet or proforma.
Ask the orthoplastic coordinator to check tetanus at the first trauma meeting.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from ED record and drug chart
pass_short: Tetanus status recorded and action matching UKHSA guidance given by first operation

question: What proportion of adults with a reduced shoulder dislocation have axillary nerve function documented after reduction?
why: Nerve injury follows up to 28% of shoulder dislocations [1694]. A post-reduction nerve check is needed to show whether a deficit came from the injury or the reduction; no library audit has measured it.

standard.source: BOAST Peripheral Nerve Injury (December 2021), standards 1.1.1–1.1.2
standard.wording: 1. An examination to assess and document all the functions of a peripheral nerve: 1.1. should be carried out and recorded: 1.1.1. at the first opportunity after injury 1.1.2. after any intervention to the limb such as injection, manipulation or application of cast

pass: A post-reduction entry that records axillary nerve sensation (regimental badge area) and deltoid function, timed after the reduction.
population: Adults aged 16 and over with an anterior or posterior glenohumeral dislocation reduced in ED or theatre. Exclude fracture-dislocations needing fixation.
sample: 40 consecutive reduced shoulder dislocations over the last 3 months.
data_source: ED system coding for the case list; ED notes for pre- and post-reduction examination; PACS for reduction time (post-reduction X-ray).

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a post-reduction nerve box (axillary sensation, deltoid contraction) to the ED shoulder reduction procedure note in the EPR.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive reduced dislocations, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED and trauma governance. If it works, make the box mandatory before the procedure note can be saved.
evidence: [1694] trauma unit: nerve injury in 28% of 100 shoulder dislocations (baseline)
[1728] acute fractures: detailed neurological findings 38.8% → 54.2% (single education session; not significant)
[1710] post-reduction orthogonal radiographs adequate in 22.7% (baseline)
pitfalls: Deltoid is hard to test after sedation or in pain → accept a documented isometric contraction and sensation, and note 'unable to assess' separately.
Post-reduction checks are written before the X-ray and not timed → ask for a timed entry.
ED staff see the audit as orthopaedic criticism → co-present with an ED lead.
Education alone gave small gains [1728] → rely on the template.
pearls: Agree the minimum examination (sensation plus deltoid) before cycle 1.
Recruit the ED emergency nurse practitioners; they perform many reductions.
Use the ED code list for 'dislocation of shoulder' to find cases fast.
Keep the procedure-note change after the audit team rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from ED record
pass_short: Axillary nerve sensation and deltoid function recorded after reduction

question: What proportion of adults aged 65 and over who have surgery for a fragility fracture other than hip fracture are seen by a physiotherapist on the day after surgery?
why: Hip fracture patients have NHFD targets for next-day mobilisation, but older patients with other fractures do not. One major trauma centre found full weight-bearing in only 54.5% of non-hip fragility fractures [1286].

standard.source: BOAST The Care of the Older or Frail Orthopaedic Trauma Patient (May 2019)
standard.wording: All surgery in the frail patient should be performed to allow full weight-bearing for activities required for daily living and within 36 hours of admission, in line with current hip fracture care. Patients should be seen by a physiotherapist on postoperative day one with early identification of functional rehabilitation goals as detailed in the rehabilitation BOAST.

pass: A physiotherapy entry dated postoperative day one (the calendar day after surgery), or earlier, that records a functional assessment or goals.
population: Adults aged 65 and over having surgery for a low-energy fracture of the femur (not hip), pelvis, humerus, elbow, tibia or ankle. Exclude day-case surgery and patients on critical care on day one.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible operated patients over the last 3 months.
data_source: Theatre system for the case list and surgery date; therapy notes or therapy activity system for first contact; operation note for weight-bearing instruction.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add all operated patients aged 65 and over (not only hip fractures) to the daily therapy trauma referral list produced from the theatre system.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible operated patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at trauma governance with the therapy lead. If it works, keep the automatic referral list and report day-one rates by weekday.
evidence: [1639] femoral fractures: mobilised by day after surgery 60% → 79% (therapy-led healthcare assistant training)
[1286] major trauma centre: full weight-bearing 98.5% hip vs 54.5% non-hip fragility fractures (baseline)
[1667] hip fractures: 93% seen day 0–1, but 40% had delayed mobilisation (baseline)
pitfalls: Weekend therapy cover is thin → report weekday and weekend rates separately so staffing is the visible issue.
Therapists may say non-hip patients are lower priority → share the BOAST wording with the therapy lead before cycle 1.
Surgery late at night makes 'day one' short → keep the calendar-day definition fixed in both cycles.
Restricted weight-bearing is used as a reason not to see → count these as fails; rehabilitation goals still apply.
pearls: Recruit the trauma therapy lead as co-author.
Pull the case list from the theatre system by age and procedure, not from memory.
Record length of stay; it helps the business case for weekend therapy.
Add the metric to the existing hip fracture therapy report so it continues.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from theatre system and therapy notes
pass_short: Physiotherapy functional assessment or goals recorded by the day after surgery

area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
question: What proportion of adults aged 65 and over with a head injury and suspected neck injury have a CT cervical spine scan within 1 hour of the risk factor being identified?
why: Older people have cervical fractures from low falls, and missed injuries cause cord damage. Library audits [1147][1304] looked at whether the scan was done, not how quickly; NICE set a 1-hour limit in 2023.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.6.2 (May 2023)
standard.wording: For people 16 and over who have sustained a head injury (including people with delayed presentation), do a CT cervical spine scan within 1 hour of the risk factor being identified if any of these high-risk factors apply: ... there is clinical suspicion of a cervical spine injury and any of these factors: age 65 or over ... [2023]

pass: CT cervical spine acquisition time within 60 minutes of the time the risk factor was first documented (triage or first clinician note recording neck pain, tenderness or suspicion of neck injury).
population: Adults aged 65 and over attending ED with a head injury whose notes record suspicion of cervical spine injury (neck pain, midline tenderness or reduced movement). Exclude patients transferred with imaging already done.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 2 months.
data_source: RIS for CT cervical spine scans in patients aged 65 and over; ED record for triage and first clinician times and the risk factor; RIS for acquisition time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
First note of neck pain, tenderness or suspected injury

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults with diabetes admitted with a limb-threatening foot problem have the multidisciplinary foot care service informed within 24 hours of admission?

standard.source: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems, rec 1.4.1 (2015, last updated October 2019)
standard.wording: If a person has a limb-threatening or life-threatening diabetic foot problem, refer them immediately to acute services and inform the multidisciplinary foot care service (according to local protocols and pathways; also see the recommendation on services and protocols commissioners and service providers should ensure are in place), so they can be assessed and an individualised treatment plan put in place. Ulceration with limb ischaemia (see the NICE guideline on peripheral arterial disease). Clinical concern that there is a deep-seated soft tissue or bone infection (with or without ulceration). Gangrene (with or without ulceration). [2015]

sample: All eligible admissions over the last 6 months (usually 30–40).

question: In children under 16 who have a CT cervical spine scan after a head injury, is one of the NICE risk factors for CT documented before the scan?
why: CT of the neck gives children a meaningful thyroid radiation dose, and NICE restricts it to named risk factors. No library audit has checked the indication for paediatric neck CT.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.6.4 (May 2023)
standard.wording: For people under 16 who have sustained a head injury (including those with delayed presentation), only do a CT cervical spine scan if any of these risk factors apply: the GCS score is 12 or less on initial assessment the person has been intubated there are focal peripheral neurological signs there is paraesthesia in the upper or lower limbs a definitive diagnosis of a cervical spine injury is needed urgently (for example, if manipulation of the cervical spine is needed during surgery or anaesthesia) the person is having other body areas scanned for head injury or multisystem trauma, and there is clinical suspicion of a cervical spine injury there is strong clinical suspicion of injury despite normal X‑rays plain X‑rays are technically difficult or inadequate plain X‑rays identify a significant bony injury. question: What proportion of adults aged 65 and over admitted with a fracture are not given an oral or intravenous NSAID during their admission?
why: NSAIDs in older people with fractures cause kidney injury and bleeding, and NICE advises against them. No library audit has measured NSAID use in older fracture inpatients.

standard.source: NICE NG38 Fractures (non-complex): assessment and management, rec 1.1.6 (February 2016)
standard.wording: Do not offer non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to frail or older adults with fractures.

pass: No dose of a systemic NSAID (for example ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, parecoxib or ketorolac) administered during the admission. Topical NSAIDs and low-dose aspirin are not counted.
population: Adults aged 65 and over admitted under trauma and orthopaedics with a fracture of any site. Local definition of 'older' is 65 and over.
sample: 50 consecutive eligible admissions over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: PAS for the case list; electronic prescribing and administration records for NSAID doses; laboratory system for creatinine to flag AKI.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an electronic prescribing alert for systemic NSAIDs in patients aged 65 and over on trauma wards, and remove NSAIDs from the default trauma analgesia order set for this age group.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 50 consecutive eligible admissions, same template.
close_loop: Present at trauma governance and the drugs and therapeutics committee. If it works, keep the alert and order-set change and report NSAID use quarterly.
evidence: [6477] primary care CKD: total NSAIDs −75%, repeat NSAIDs −90% (automated alert on at-risk records)
[2173] renal colic: NSAID first line 38% → 50% (pathway, emails, posters; shows NSAID habits change slowly)
[1916] over-65 rehabilitation: education alone did not reduce inappropriate PPI prescribing (fails)
pitfalls: Anaesthetists give parecoxib or ketorolac in theatre → include theatre doses and involve anaesthetists from the start.
Younger fit 65-year-olds may benefit from NSAIDs → the NICE wording says 'frail or older'; agree the age cut-off before cycle 1 and keep it.
Alert fatigue → target the alert only to trauma wards and patients aged 65 and over.
Prescribed but not given doses → count administration, not prescription, for the pass.
pearls: Recruit a ward pharmacist; they can run the NSAID search in minutes.
Report AKI rates alongside NSAID use to show harm.
Ask the acute pain team to update the trauma analgesia protocol.
Keep the order-set change after the audit ends.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from electronic prescribing
pass_short: No dose of a systemic NSAID given during the admission

question: In adults having primary elective hip or knee replacement, what proportion start physiotherapy or occupational therapy rehabilitation on the day of surgery?
why: Rehabilitation on the day of surgery shortens stay and reduces complications. Library audits [1730][1167] measured the 24-hour limit; few units measure day-of-surgery starts, which NICE asks for where possible.

standard.source: NICE NG157 Joint replacement (primary): hip, knee and shoulder, rec 1.10.1 (June 2020)
standard.wording: A physiotherapist or occupational therapist should offer rehabilitation, on the day of surgery if possible and no more than 24 hours after surgery, to people who have had a primary elective hip, knee or shoulder replacement. Rehabilitation should include: advice on managing activities of daily living and home exercise programmes and mobilisation for people who have had knee or hip replacement or ambulation for people who have had shoulder replacement.

pass: A therapy entry dated the same calendar day as the surgery recording rehabilitation (mobilisation or exercises).
population: Adults having primary elective total or unicompartmental hip or knee replacement. Exclude revisions and patients admitted to critical care.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: Theatre system for the case list and end-of-surgery time; therapy notes or therapy activity system for first rehabilitation; EPR for discharge date.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Schedule a named therapist on the arthroplasty ward until 19:00 on operating days, with patients from the morning list automatically added to the day-0 therapy list.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the arthroplasty and therapy governance meeting. If it works, keep the extended therapy shift and report day-0 rates with length of stay.
evidence: [1591] hip and knee replacement: all patients mobilised on day 0, length of stay 3.6 → 2.0–2.4 days (MDT rapid recovery group with nurse-led mobilisation)
[1730] knee replacement: mobilised within 24 h 66% → 90.5% (MDT presentation, escalation of pain and nausea)
[1167] hip replacement: mobilised within a day 65% → 74% (analgesia advice; small gain)
pitfalls: Afternoon-list patients return too late → report by list session so the fix targets the right cases.
Spinal anaesthesia motor block delays standing → record the reason and discuss spinal dose with anaesthetists.
Therapy staffing costs → pair the audit with length-of-stay data to support the business case.
Rehabilitation 'offered' but refused → count a documented offer as a pass and record refusals.
pearls: Recruit the arthroplasty therapy lead and the ward manager.
Nurse-led first mobilisation can count if the local pathway allows; agree this before cycle 1.
Report the 24-hour rate too, for comparison with NICE's upper limit.
Keep the extended shift in the rota after the audit.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from theatre system and therapy notes
pass_short: Therapy entry recording rehabilitation on the day of surgery

question: In adults aged 65 and over listed for primary elective hip or knee replacement, what proportion have a validated risk stratification score recorded at pre-operative assessment?
why: Older patients deserve an objective estimate of surgical risk to support shared decisions and plan post-operative care. Library audits of risk scores come from emergency laparotomy [2038] and hip fracture ASA grading [1185]; none from elective arthroplasty.

standard.source: NICE NG180 Perioperative care in adults, rec 1.3.1 (August 2020)
standard.wording: Use a validated risk stratification tool to supplement clinical assessment when planning surgery, including dental surgery. Discuss the person's risks and surgical options with them to allow for informed shared decision making.

pass: A named validated risk tool score (for example SORT, NSQIP surgical risk calculator or P-POSSUM) recorded in the pre-assessment record before the day of surgery.
population: Adults aged 65 and over attending pre-operative assessment for primary elective hip or knee replacement.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: Pre-assessment clinic list and electronic pre-assessment record; clinic letters or consent form for any documented risk discussion; theatre system for surgery date.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a SORT calculator field (auto-populated from pre-assessment data) to the electronic pre-assessment record for patients aged 65 and over.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the pre-assessment and arthroplasty governance meeting. If it works, keep the field and extend it to all ages.
evidence: [2038] emergency laparotomy: NELA risk score documented 26%; discussed with patient 14% (baseline)
[1185] hip fracture: ASA underestimated 25.6% → 14.9% (Clinical Frailty Scale added to ASA assessment)
pitfalls: Staff see ASA as a risk tool → agree before cycle 1 that ASA alone does not count.
Nurses may lack time → an auto-populated calculator avoids extra work.
A score without discussion has little value → record discussion as a secondary measure for the next cycle.
Different tools give different numbers → pick one tool locally and keep it fixed.
pearls: Recruit the pre-assessment lead anaesthetist and nurse.
Record the Clinical Frailty Scale alongside to support a later frailty audit.
Use results to plan enhanced care beds for high-risk patients.
Keep the field in the template after the audit team rotates.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from the pre-assessment record
pass_short: Validated risk score such as SORT recorded before the day of surgery

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of adults whose X-ray suggests possible bone sarcoma are given a suspected cancer pathway referral?
why: Bone sarcoma is rare but delay is common because the presenting X-ray is often first reported outside a cancer pathway (routine trauma or GP films); no audit of this referral step exists in the library.

standard.wording: Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for adults if an X-ray suggests the possibility of bone sarcoma. [2015]

population: Inclusion: all adults (16 and over) whose plain X-ray report includes a comment raising the possibility of a bone tumour or sarcoma (e.g. 'cannot exclude', 'suspicious of', 'refer bone tumour service'), from any requesting source (GP, ED, fracture clinic, orthopaedics), over the last 12-24 months. Exclusion: known metastatic bone disease, known primary bone sarcoma already under follow-up.
sample: All eligible X-ray reports over the last 12-24 months (bone sarcoma referrals are rare; expect 5-15 cases per hospital, so pool radiology reporting system data across the trust or across a network if needed).
data_source: Radiology reporting system (text search for sarcoma/tumour/neoplasm terms in X-ray reports), 2-week wait referral log, PAS referral dates, and the bone sarcoma centre's referral inbox or letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-24 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory radiology 'critical result' alert that fires to the reporting radiologist's and requester's inbox whenever a bone tumour/sarcoma-suggestive phrase is used, with a same-day 2-week-wait referral form linked from the alert.
target: 100% (every suggestive report should trigger same-day referral)
reaudit: At 6 months, same case-finding method and time window
close_loop: Present at the radiology-orthopaedic governance meeting and trust cancer performance meeting; if the alert works, add the sarcoma-suggestive phrase list to the radiology reporting template's critical-results dictionary permanently.
pitfalls: Numbers are tiny in a single hospital → pool data across a network or over 24 months, and report as 'x/y' not a percentage alone.
Free-text radiology reports make cases hard to find by search terms → agree the search phrase list with radiology before starting and screen a wider set manually.
Radiologists may already phone the referrer informally without a written referral → count a documented, dated phone call as a pass if a referral follows within 24 hours.
The finding may be an incidental old lesion (e.g. bone island) → have a second radiologist confirm true suspicion before including the case.
pearls: Recruit a musculoskeletal radiologist as co-lead; they can define the search terms and pull the report list.
Agree the definition of 'suggestive of sarcoma' before counting cases, using the regional bone sarcoma service's own referral criteria.
Link the audit to the regional bone sarcoma MDT's own referral log, which may already record delays.
Keep the critical-result alert switched on after the trainee rotates by naming a radiology governance lead as its owner.
effort: ~30 min per case (searching reports plus checking the referral log); expect only 5-15 cases so total effort is low
pass: A suspected cancer pathway (2-week wait) referral to a bone sarcoma service is made and documented on the day the report is authorised, or the same working day.
pass_short: Suspected cancer pathway referral made on the day the report is authorised

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of children and young people whose X-ray suggests possible bone sarcoma get a specialist appointment within 48 hours?
why: NICE sets a tighter 48-hour standard for children than for adults because paediatric bone sarcomas grow faster; no audit of this step exists in the library, and the adult and paediatric pathways are often confused locally.

standard.source: NICE NG12 rec 1.11.2 (2015), with 'very urgent' defined in NG12 Terms used in this guideline
standard.wording: Consider a very urgent referral (for an appointment within 48 hours) for specialist assessment for children and young people if an X-ray suggests the possibility of bone sarcoma. [2015] ... Very urgent: To happen within 48 hours.

population: Inclusion: patients under 25 whose plain X-ray report raises the possibility of bone sarcoma, over the last 24-36 months (rare in children, so a long window is needed). Exclusion: known bone sarcoma already under follow-up.
sample: All eligible cases identified from the last 24-36 months of radiology reports across the network (expect very few cases in a single hospital; escalate to network level if under 5).
data_source: Radiology reporting system, referral log to the paediatric/teenage-and-young-adult bone sarcoma service, clinic letter or MDT record confirming the appointment date.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect (extended window for cases); Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-24 re-audit
change: Create a single 'child/young person: X-ray suggests bone sarcoma' escalation route that bypasses the general 2-week-wait office and goes straight to the on-call paediatric orthopaedic/oncology consultant by phone, logged on a shared tracker.
reaudit: At 12 months, same case-finding method
