Use a simple diagram-based proforma (regimental badge area, deltoid, pulses) rather than free text to speed up completion.
Keep the paired box live by building it into the ED's electronic procedure note template.
effort: ~10 min per case from the ED procedure note
pass: A documented neurological examination (including axillary nerve sensation and deltoid function) and a circulatory examination (distal pulse) are recorded before the reduction attempt.
pass_short: Neurological and circulatory examination documented before reduction

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of new fracture clinic patients who need information in a different language or an accessible format have this recorded as provided?
why: National BOAST standards require accessible-format and language-appropriate information for fracture patients, but no audit in the library checks whether patients with a communication or language need actually receive it, an equity gap not covered by the library's plain-English letter audit [ONA-135].

standard.source: BOASt Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026), standard 7
standard.wording: Information in an accessible format and language should be available and include instructions for casts, splints, slings, and appliances.

population: Inclusion: new fracture clinic patients with a recorded communication or language need (interpreter required, learning disability, visual or hearing impairment) over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: patients with no recorded communication need.
sample: 30 consecutive fracture clinic patients with a recorded communication or language need over the last 3-6 months (identify via PAS communication-needs flags or interpreter bookings).
data_source: PAS communication needs/flag field, interpreter booking system, clinic letter, plaster room record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory check at fracture clinic booking that reads the PAS communication-needs flag and automatically books an interpreter or flags the need for an accessible-format information leaflet before the appointment.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the fracture clinic governance and trust equality/health inequalities meeting; if the automatic booking check works, keep it as the standard fracture clinic booking process.
pitfalls: Communication needs may not be recorded accurately or consistently on PAS → cross-check with ward or ED records where possible and report the recording gap itself as a finding.
An interpreter booked but not attending on the day is a common real-world failure → record actual use, not just booking.
Family members are sometimes used informally as interpreters, which is not equivalent to a professional interpreter → record this separately and do not count it as a pass.
Small numbers of patients with each type of need make percentages unstable → report by need category as well as combined.
pearls: Recruit the trust's interpreting and translation service manager as co-lead.
Use the trust's equality, diversity and inclusion or health inequalities lead to help frame and present the findings.
Pilot the automatic booking check in one fracture clinic before wider rollout.
Keep the check live by embedding it in the booking team's standard operating procedure, not an individual's reminder.
effort: ~15 min per case from PAS, interpreter booking and clinic records
pass: A patient recorded as needing a language interpreter, an easy-read format, or another accessible communication format has this need documented and the corresponding format/interpreter actually used or arranged for their fracture clinic information.
pass_short: Language or accessible format need documented and the format or interpreter provided

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of patients with a first-time lateral patellar dislocation are assessed by a musculoskeletal physiotherapist within 3 weeks of injury?
why: The national FTLPD standard sets a specific early physiotherapy assessment target that is distinct from, and not covered by, the library's existing patellar dislocation audit [ONA-166], which measures only the skyline X-ray view.

standard.source: BOA Standard: Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (FTLPD) (December 2024), standard 8
standard.wording: Assessment by a musculo-skeletal physiotherapist should occur within 3 weeks of injury.

population: Inclusion: all patients (any age) with a first-time lateral patellar dislocation managed non-operatively as the initial plan, over the last 6 months. Exclusion: patients proceeding directly to surgery for an associated injury before physiotherapy would be due.
sample: 30-40 consecutive first-time lateral patellar dislocations over the last 6 months.
data_source: ED/fracture clinic record, physiotherapy referral and appointment system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a direct physiotherapy self-referral or fast-track booking option to the virtual fracture clinic outcome form for first-time patellar dislocation, bypassing the general physiotherapy waiting list.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT and physiotherapy service governance meeting; if the fast-track referral works, keep it as the standard pathway for this diagnosis.
pitfalls: General physiotherapy waiting lists may make the 3-week target unachievable without a dedicated pathway → escalate capacity constraints if the fast-track referral does not resolve the gap.
Patients may be referred but not attend their first appointment → record both referral date and actual attendance date.
Diagnosis coding for 'patellar dislocation' can be inconsistent between ED and fracture clinic systems → cross-check both sources when identifying cases.
A patient who self-refers to a private physiotherapist would still meet the clinical intent but may not appear in hospital data → note this as a data limitation.
pearls: Recruit the musculoskeletal physiotherapy service lead as co-lead, since capacity is the likely rate-limiting step.
Use the same case list as any recurrent patellar instability MRI audit already running, since patients may overlap.
Agree the fast-track referral criteria and capacity with physiotherapy before cycle 1, not after finding a gap.
Keep the fast-track pathway live by adding it to the virtual fracture clinic outcome form permanently.
effort: ~10 min per case from the fracture clinic and physiotherapy systems
pass: The patient is seen by a musculoskeletal physiotherapist within 3 weeks (21 days) of the date of dislocation.
pass_short: Seen by an MSK physiotherapist within 21 days of dislocation

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of patients considered for surgery after a first-time lateral patellar dislocation have this discussed and documented at an age-appropriate MDT?
why: The national FTLPD standard requires MDT or peer-review discussion before surgery is offered, to avoid unnecessary stabilisation procedures; this specific governance step is not covered by the library's existing patellar dislocation audit [ONA-166].

standard.source: BOA Standard: Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (FTLPD) (December 2024), standard 13
standard.wording: Clinicians considering surgery following FTLPD should discuss their plan within an age-appropriate multi-disciplinary team meeting, or alternative forum for peer review, with written documentation of the outcome included in the medical records.

population: Inclusion: all patients considered for surgery (for the dislocation itself or an associated injury) after a first-time lateral patellar dislocation, over the last 12 months. Exclusion: emergency surgery for an acute vascular or open injury.
sample: 20-30 consecutive patients considered for surgery after FTLPD over the last 12 months.
data_source: MDT/peer-review meeting minutes, clinic letter, theatre listing form.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add 'FTLPD surgical plan' as a standing agenda item template in the knee/sports injury or paediatric orthopaedic MDT, with a mandatory outcome-recording field linked to the theatre listing form.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury and paediatric orthopaedic MDT governance meeting; if the standing agenda item works, keep it as a permanent MDT process.
pitfalls: A single-surgeon department may not have a formal MDT and rely on informal peer discussion → the standard allows an 'alternative forum for peer review', so define and document what this looks like locally.
Surgery decided in a busy clinic without a documented discussion is easy to miss from case-finding → cross-check theatre listing forms against MDT minutes systematically.
Skeletally immature patients may go through a different (paediatric) MDT to adults → make sure both age-appropriate forums are captured.
Retrospective documentation of an MDT outcome after the decision was already made in clinic would not meet the spirit of the standard → check the dates are in the correct order.
pearls: Recruit both adult knee/sports injury and paediatric orthopaedic leads, since the standard applies across ages.
Use the recurrent patellar instability assessment standard's own MRI findings as part of the MDT discussion template.
Agree what counts as an acceptable 'alternative forum for peer review' locally before cycle 1.
Keep the agenda item live by giving the MDT coordinator ownership of the standing template.
effort: ~10 min per case from MDT minutes and the listing form
pass: The decision to offer surgery after a first-time lateral patellar dislocation is documented as having been discussed at an age-appropriate MDT or peer-review forum before listing.
pass_short: Surgery decision discussed at an age-appropriate MDT before listing

area: Foot and ankle, hand and wrist, spine
question: What proportion of adults with non-specific low back pain (with or without sciatica) in a non-specialist setting avoid routine spinal imaging?
why: Unnecessary lumbar spine imaging drives further unhelpful investigation and patient anxiety without changing management; the library's spine audits focus heavily on cauda equina and traumatic fracture imaging, with no audit of this very high-volume imaging stewardship standard.

standard.source: NICE NG59 rec 1.1.4 (2016)
standard.wording: Do not routinely offer imaging in a non-specialist setting for people with low back pain with or without sciatica. [2016]

population: Inclusion: adults presenting to primary care or a non-specialist musculoskeletal/orthopaedic triage service with low back pain, with or without sciatica, over the last 3 months. Exclusion: any red-flag feature present (cauda equina symptoms, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer, significant trauma, fever, progressive neurological deficit).
sample: 40 consecutive eligible low back pain presentations over the last 3 months.
data_source: GP or musculoskeletal triage clinical record, radiology request system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory red-flag checklist to the GP and musculoskeletal triage low back pain template that must be completed before an imaging request can be submitted for non-specific low back pain.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the primary care and musculoskeletal interface meeting and radiology demand management meeting; if the checklist reduces unnecessary imaging, embed it in the referral/request system permanently.
pitfalls: Patient expectation and anxiety commonly drive imaging requests → pair the checklist with patient-facing information explaining why imaging is not needed without red flags.
Clinicians may document a red flag loosely to justify imaging they already intended to request → define red flags precisely in the checklist to reduce this.
Imaging requested by a specialist (e.g. after referral) is outside the scope of this non-specialist-setting standard → clearly define the non-specialist population before starting.
This crosses primary and secondary care, so a hospital-only fix will not reach all GP-ordered imaging → involve GP practices or the musculoskeletal triage service directly.
pearls: Recruit a GP with a special interest in musculoskeletal medicine or the musculoskeletal triage lead as co-lead.
Use the existing NICE NG59 red-flag list as a ready-made teaching and checklist resource.
Present imaging cost and reporting turnaround data alongside the guideline evidence to strengthen engagement.
Keep the checklist current by embedding it in the CCG/ICB musculoskeletal referral and imaging request guidance.
effort: ~10 min per case from the clinical record and radiology system
pass: No lumbar spine X-ray, CT or MRI is requested in primary care or a non-specialist musculoskeletal clinic for a patient with non-specific low back pain (with or without sciatica) and no red-flag features.
pass_short: No lumbar spine imaging requested in non-specialist settings without red flags

question: What proportion of patients with a confirmed limb arterial injury from musculoskeletal trauma have revascularisation started within 1 hour of arrival?
why: Revascularisation is a time-critical (NCEPOD 1) emergency with no safe ischaemic time, and knee dislocation is a classic cause; the library's existing audit [ONA-034] measures pulse documentation in the ED but not the time to definitive treatment once an arterial injury is confirmed.

standard.source: BOA/BAPRAS/Vascular Society Standard: Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma (June 2026), standard 10
standard.wording: Revascularisation is an emergency procedure (NCEPOD 1) and should be commenced within one hour of arrival to hospital.

population: Inclusion: patients with a confirmed arterial injury associated with musculoskeletal trauma (including knee dislocation, tibial plateau or distal femoral fracture with vascular compromise) over the last 12-24 months. Exclusion: supracondylar fractures in children (covered by a separate BOAST).
sample: 15-25 consecutive confirmed arterial injury cases over the last 12-24 months (this is a rare, high-harm emergency, so a long window and possibly network-level pooling is needed).
data_source: ED arrival time (trauma call record), theatre start time, operation note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect (extended window); Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-24 re-audit
change: Classify confirmed limb arterial injury as an NCEPOD category 1 emergency on the theatre booking system with immediate simultaneous notification of orthopaedic, vascular or plastic surgery on-call teams, bypassing the standard trauma list queue.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the trauma network governance meeting and submit alongside TARN data; if the emergency booking classification reduces time to revascularisation, keep it as a standing theatre priority category.
pitfalls: Case numbers are small and high-stakes → review every case individually as well as in aggregate, and involve the trauma network mortality and morbidity process.
Time of injury versus time of arrival can be confused → the standard specifies time of arrival to hospital as the start point, so use that consistently.
Transfer from a non-specialist centre adds an unavoidable delay before the clock at the receiving centre starts → record transfer time separately from in-hospital delay.
Competing emergencies (e.g. major haemorrhage) may genuinely delay theatre access → record this as a documented reason, not a hidden delay.
pearls: Recruit vascular and plastic surgery colleagues as co-leads, since the standard requires consultant-led joint care.
Use the trauma network's existing arterial injury or limb trauma governance process as the case-finding route.
Present a timeline (arrival, CT angiogram, theatre start) for each case to show exactly where any delay occurs.
Keep the NCEPOD category 1 classification live by embedding it in the theatre booking system's fixed category list.
effort: ~20 min per case from ED, radiology and theatre records
pass: Surgical revascularisation is commenced within 1 hour of the patient's arrival at hospital.
pass_short: Surgical revascularisation started within 1 hour of arrival

question: What proportion of patients with suspected limb arterial injury have CT angiography performed concurrently with the initial trauma CT, rather than as a delayed second scan?
why: Performing CT angiography at the same time as the trauma CT avoids a second scan and the delay this causes to diagnosis and revascularisation; the library's existing audit [ONA-029] covers CT angiography for cervical spine injury specifically, not limb arterial injury.

standard.source: BOA/BAPRAS/Vascular Society Standard: Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma (June 2026), standard 8
standard.wording: CT angiogram is recommended if arterial injury is suspected and should be performed concurrently with whole-body CT.

population: Inclusion: trauma patients with a suspected limb arterial injury (absent or asymmetric pulse after reduction and splinting) who proceed to CT, over the last 12 months. Exclusion: patients going directly to theatre without CT due to overwhelming clinical urgency.
sample: 20-30 consecutive suspected limb arterial injury CT episodes over the last 12 months.
data_source: Radiology information system (scan protocol and times), trauma CT report.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic CT angiography arterial-phase extension to the trauma CT protocol whenever 'suspected limb arterial injury' is selected on the trauma CT request, so radiographers do not need a separate request.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the trauma radiology governance meeting; if the combined protocol works, keep it as the default trauma CT protocol option.
pitfalls: Radiographers may not always know a limb arterial injury is suspected at the time of the initial scan → make 'suspected arterial injury' a clear, separate tick box on the trauma CT request form.
Renal function may limit additional contrast in some patients → record any documented contrast-related reason for a separate or deferred scan.

A patient stabilised and reduced after the initial scan may develop new concern for arterial injury later → a later, separate CTA is appropriate in this scenario and should be recorded as a valid reason, not a fail.
Protocol changes need radiology and trauma team agreement together → involve both from the outset.
pearls: Recruit a trauma radiologist and radiographer superintendent as co-leads, since the protocol change is theirs to implement.
Use real (anonymised) cases where a second scan delayed revascularisation to illustrate the value of the change.
Combine data collection with the 1-hour revascularisation audit, since the same patients are involved.
Keep the protocol extension live by adding it to the trauma CT protocol library in the radiology system.
effort: ~10 min per case from the radiology system
pass: CT angiography of the affected limb is performed as part of the same CT episode as the initial trauma/whole-body CT, with no separate second scan visit required.
pass_short: CT angiography done in the same CT episode as the initial trauma CT

question: What proportion of adults with a 'possible target' meniscal lesion and symptoms under 3 months are offered a structured non-operative trial before arthroscopic surgery is considered?
why: The BASK meniscal guideline directs a first-line non-operative trial for possible-target lesions with short symptom duration, avoiding premature surgery; no audit in the library checks this specific staging step.

standard.source: BASK Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery: A National Society Treatment Guideline and Consensus Statement (Bone Joint J 2019;101-B:652-659), Meniscal Tear Management Guideline flowchart
standard.wording: Possible Meniscal Target (MRI) & Corresponding Symptoms/Signs, Symptoms < 3 months: Assessment: Further non-surgical treatment is first line. Recommendation: Optimal Non-Operative Treatment & Re-assess (e.g. provide information, physiotherapy, exercise, analgesia, steroid injection).

population: Inclusion: adults with an MRI-reported 'possible target' meniscal lesion and symptom duration under 3 months, discussed in a knee clinic over the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: locked knee, clear 'target' lesion, symptoms of 3 months or more.
sample: 20-30 consecutive eligible knee clinic patients over the last 6-12 months.
data_source: MRI report, knee clinic letter, physiotherapy referral system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'possible target, symptoms <3 months: non-operative trial plan' prompt to the knee clinic letter template that must be completed before a surgical listing option becomes available for this category.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT; if the prompt reduces premature listing, keep it in the standard clinic letter template.
pitfalls: Classifying a lesion as 'target' versus 'possible target' relies on radiologist and surgeon agreement, which can vary → agree the definition locally using the BASK terminology before starting.
Patients may push for early surgery having researched their MRI report → record shared decision-making discussion as part of the non-operative pathway.
Symptom duration can be difficult to pin down precisely → use the patient's best estimate and record it consistently.
This can read as restricting surgeon autonomy → present it as following an agreed national consensus guideline, not local policy.
pearls: Recruit the knee/sports injury lead surgeon to define local application of the BASK terminology.
Reuse the same case list as the MRI confirmation and advanced-OA overuse audits in this batch to reduce duplicate note review.
Share the BASK flowchart directly with the surgical team as the source of authority for the fix.
Keep the clinic letter prompt live by embedding it in the standard knee clinic template.
effort: ~15 min per case from the MRI report and clinic letter
pass: A patient with a 'possible target' meniscal lesion on MRI and symptoms present for less than 3 months has a documented structured non-operative treatment plan (physiotherapy, exercise, analgesia or injection) before any arthroscopic listing.
pass_short: Structured non-operative treatment plan documented before any arthroscopy listing

question: What proportion of shoulder dislocations have two orthogonal radiographic views before reduction is attempted?
why: A single view can miss the direction of dislocation or an associated fracture, but no audit in the library checks pre-reduction imaging adequacy for shoulder dislocation; the existing audit [ONA-156] covers post-reduction nerve function only.

standard.source: BESS/BOA Patient Care Pathway: Traumatic anterior shoulder instability (Shoulder & Elbow 2015;7(3):214-226)
standard.wording: Two views are required to confirm glenohumeral dislocation and the direction of dislocation. An antero-posterior radiograph is obligatory. Ideally, an axial view should also be obtained as the second view.

population: Inclusion: all patients with a suspected or confirmed shoulder dislocation presenting to the emergency department over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: none.
sample: 40 consecutive shoulder dislocation presentations over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: Radiology information system (views requested and performed), ED procedure note.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set the default ED radiology request protocol for 'suspected shoulder dislocation' to always include both an AP and an axial (or modified axial) view as a single combined request.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the ED and radiology governance meeting; if the combined default request improves compliance, keep it as the standard shoulder dislocation imaging protocol.
pitfalls: Severe pain can genuinely prevent a second view being obtained before reduction → the guideline itself allows a modified axial or scapular Y view as an alternative, so record which alternative (if any) was used.
Clinicians experienced in recognising dislocation direction clinically may feel a second view is unnecessary → present the medico-legal and diagnostic value of confirming direction before reduction.
Radiographer availability out of hours can limit view choice → record time of day to see if this explains variation.
Recurrent dislocators with a well-documented pattern may reasonably need less imaging → consider excluding known recurrent dislocations with a typical re-presentation if locally agreed.
pearls: Recruit an ED radiographer lead to help set the default combined request protocol.
Combine data collection with the pre-reduction neurovascular examination audit in this batch, since the same patients and notes are involved.
Use example missed posterior dislocations (single-view AP only) in teaching to illustrate the risk.
Keep the combined request protocol live by adding it to the RIS default request set for this presentation.
effort: ~10 min per case from the radiology and ED systems
pass: An AP view plus an axial (or modified axial/scapular Y) second view are obtained before the reduction attempt, or a documented reason (e.g. pain precluding positioning) explains a single view with an accepted alternative technique.
pass_short: AP and axial (or scapular Y) views before reduction, or reason documented

question: What proportion of ACL reconstruction consent discussions document the graft options, risks and the surgeon's recommendation?
why: The BOA ACL standard requires graft selection (autograft, allograft, synthetic) with its benefits, complications and risks to be discussed and documented at consent; this specific consent element is not covered by any audit in the library.

standard.source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 7b
standard.wording: Graft selection should be discussed including autograft, allograft and synthetic ligaments. This should include the benefits, complications and risks of all and the preferred graft recommendation.

population: Inclusion: all adults consented for primary ACL reconstruction over the last 6 months. Exclusion: revision surgery where graft choice is highly constrained by prior surgery (record separately).
sample: 30-40 consecutive ACL reconstruction consent episodes over the last 6 months.
data_source: Consent form, pre-operative clinic letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a structured 'graft choice discussion' section to the ACL consent form or a paired patient information sheet, with tick boxes for each graft type discussed and a free-text line for the agreed choice.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT; if the structured section improves documentation, keep it as the standard ACL consent form.
pitfalls: Standard hospital consent forms often have very limited space for procedure-specific detail → use a paired information sheet if the consent form itself cannot be extended.
Patients may already have a strong graft preference from research beforehand → document this as part of the discussion, not a substitute for it.
Trainees consenting patients may be less confident discussing all graft options → pair the fix with a short teaching session on graft choice discussion.
A generic 'risks discussed' tick box without naming graft types would not meet the standard → the fix must specifically separate out graft-related discussion.
pearls: Recruit the knee/sports injury lead surgeon to draft the structured wording.
Use the existing National Ligament Registry consent audit in this batch as a combined data collection opportunity, since both relate to the same consent episode.
Give patients a copy of the graft-choice information sheet to take home, improving both consent quality and patient experience.
Keep the structured section live by embedding it in the standard ACL consent bundle.
effort: ~10 min per case from the consent form and clinic letter
pass: The consent form or pre-operative clinic letter documents the graft options considered, their benefits/risks, and the agreed graft choice.
pass_short: Consent documents graft options, benefits and risks, and the agreed choice

question: What proportion of patients referred to secondary care for tennis elbow have a PRTEE (Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation) score recorded before treatment starts?
why: The BESS tennis elbow pathway defines PRTEE as the core outcome measure for this condition, but the library has no audit of outcome measurement for any elbow condition, making it impossible to track whether treatment is working.

standard.source: BESS patient care pathway: Tennis elbow (Shoulder & Elbow 2023;15(4):348-359), Outcome metrics section
standard.wording: The core outcome set for LET defined by Bateman et al. PRTEE; PRTEE pain & function subscale.

population: Inclusion: adults newly referred to secondary care or a musculoskeletal service for tennis elbow (lateral elbow tendinopathy) over the last 6 months. Exclusion: red-flag referrals for an alternative diagnosis.
sample: 30 consecutive new tennis elbow secondary care assessments over the last 6 months.
data_source: Clinic letter, physiotherapy or orthopaedic assessment record, PROM collection system if one exists.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add the PRTEE questionnaire as a mandatory patient self-completed form in the waiting area at every new tennis elbow appointment, with the score entered into the clinic letter template.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the musculoskeletal/upper limb service governance meeting; if the self-completed form works, keep it as standard practice for every new tennis elbow assessment.
pitfalls: A new questionnaire adds to clinic administrative burden → keep it a short, patient-self-completed form to minimise staff time.
Patients with limited literacy or English as a second language may need support completing it → have an accessible-format or interpreter-assisted version available.
A score recorded but never reviewed at follow-up is of limited value → also check whether a repeat PRTEE is planned to track progress.
Digital and paper systems may both be in use locally, risking inconsistent recording → agree a single method before starting.
pearls: Recruit the musculoskeletal physiotherapy service, since they usually run outcome measure collection already for other conditions.
Use the BESS-defined PRTEE as the core outcome set, avoiding the need to develop a local measure.
Feed results back to referrers to demonstrate the value of the pathway.
Keep the form live by adding it to the department's standard new-patient paperwork pack.
effort: ~10 min per case; the PRTEE itself takes the patient under 5 minutes to complete
pass: A PRTEE score (or its pain and function subscales) is recorded at the first secondary care assessment before any new treatment is started.
pass_short: PRTEE score recorded at first secondary care assessment before treatment

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of patients with a first-time lateral patellar dislocation are given patient information about their injury and rehabilitation?
why: The national FTLPD standard requires accessible patient information (leaflet, video or app-based) to be available, but the library's existing patellar dislocation audit [ONA-166] does not check this information-provision step.

standard.source: BOA Standard: Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (FTLPD) (December 2024), standard 15
standard.wording: Appropriate patient information including leaflets, videos or online / app-based content should be available.

population: Inclusion: all patients with a first-time lateral patellar dislocation assessed in ED or fracture clinic over the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: none.
sample: 40 consecutive first-time lateral patellar dislocation presentations over the last 3-6 months.
data_source: ED discharge record, fracture clinic letter, patient information leaflet log if one exists.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a single FTLPD patient information leaflet (with a QR code linking to a rehabilitation video) and add a mandatory 'information given: yes/no, format' field to the ED and fracture clinic discharge template for this diagnosis.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury MDT and fracture clinic governance meeting; if the leaflet and mandatory field work, keep both as standard practice for this diagnosis.
pitfalls: Verbal advice alone is easy to give but hard to verify or standardise → the fix should make written/digital information the default, with verbal advice as a supplement.
Information given in ED may not be repeated or reinforced at fracture clinic follow-up → check both points in the pathway.
A leaflet only in English may not meet the needs of all patients → pair this with the accessible-format/language audit in this batch where relevant.
Staff may forget to document that a leaflet was given even when it was → make documentation as quick as a single tick box.
pearls: Recruit the physiotherapy team to help create rehabilitation video content, since they already produce exercise materials.
Use the BOA standard itself as the justification when presenting the change to ED and fracture clinic staff.
Combine data collection with the physiotherapy-timing audit in this batch, since the same patients are involved.
Keep the leaflet current by giving the knee/sports injury service ownership of periodic review and updates.
effort: ~10 min per case from the ED and fracture clinic records
pass: The patient's record documents that written, video or app-based information about first-time patellar dislocation and its rehabilitation was given or signposted at the first assessment.
pass_short: Written, video or app-based information given at first assessment

question: What proportion of open fractures have definitive soft tissue closure or coverage achieved within 72 hours of injury?
why: Delayed soft tissue coverage is strongly linked to infection risk in open fractures, but no audit in the library measures this specific BOAST timing standard; existing library items cover antibiotic timing and photography, not definitive closure.

standard.source: BOA/BAPRAS Audit Standards for Trauma: Open Fractures (December 2017), standard 14
standard.wording: Definitive soft tissue closure or coverage should be achieved within 72 hours of injury if it cannot be performed at the time of debridement.

population: Inclusion: all patients with an open fracture of a long bone, hindfoot or midfoot managed with a staged (debridement then later closure) approach over the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: cases closed at the time of debridement (already meeting the standard by definition), hand/wrist/forefoot/digit injuries.
sample: 20-30 consecutive staged open fracture cases over the last 6-12 months.
data_source: Operation notes (debridement and closure/coverage procedures), theatre system dates and times.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add open fracture cases awaiting definitive closure to a shared orthoplastic tracker board with an automatic 72-hour countdown flag visible to both orthopaedic and plastic surgery theatre coordinators.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the trauma network open fracture and orthoplastic governance meeting; if the tracker board reduces delay, keep it as the standard joint theatre planning tool.
pitfalls: Combined theatre lists across two specialties (orthopaedics and plastics) can be hard to coordinate → the tracker board should be visible and editable by both teams' coordinators.
A patient may be too physiologically unstable for definitive closure within 72 hours → record this as a valid clinical reason, not a service failure, but still report it.
Transfer between hospitals for orthoplastic care adds a delay outside the receiving centre's control → record transfer time separately from in-hospital delay.
Wound complexity may make a single 72-hour target unrealistic for some injuries → present results stratified by injury severity if possible.
pearls: Recruit a plastic surgery colleague as joint audit lead, since this standard is inherently a shared orthoplastic responsibility.
Use the trust's existing TARN open fracture data as an additional data source and cross-check.
Present timeline data (injury, debridement, closure) for each case to show exactly where delay occurs.
Keep the tracker board live by giving both specialties' theatre coordinators joint ownership.
effort: ~15 min per case from theatre records
pass: Definitive soft tissue closure or coverage (primary closure, split skin graft, or flap) is completed within 72 hours of the recorded time of injury, or was achieved at the time of the initial debridement.
pass_short: Definitive soft tissue closure or coverage within 72 hours of injury

question: What proportion of adults assessed for recurrent patellar instability have the three required radiograph views performed?
why: The BOA/BASK recurrent patellar instability standard specifies three particular radiograph views needed to detect patella alta, degenerative change, loose fragments and trochlear dysplasia; no audit in the library checks radiograph completeness for this indication (the MRI-findings audit in this batch covers a different imaging modality).

standard.source: BOA Specialty Standard: The Assessment of Patients with Recurrent Patellar Instability (August 2020), standard 2
standard.wording: Radiographs should include: antero-posterior (or PA); true lateral at 20-30 degrees flexion; and axial (skyline) views at 20-30 degrees knee flexion.

population: Inclusion: adults with recurrent (two or more) patellar dislocations having plain radiographs as part of assessment, over the last 12 months. Exclusion: first-time dislocation, patients unable to achieve the required positioning due to acute injury.
sample: 30 consecutive recurrent patellar instability radiograph series over the last 12 months.
data_source: Radiology information system (view codes and images), knee clinic letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a single 'recurrent patellar instability' radiograph request protocol in the RIS that automatically includes all three specified views, replacing ad hoc individual view requests.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the knee/sports injury and radiology governance meeting; if the combined protocol improves completeness, keep it as the default request set for this indication.
pitfalls: Standard knee X-ray protocols may default to only AP and lateral, missing the specified flexion angles and the skyline view → the RIS protocol change should specify the exact positioning, not just view names.
Patients with severe instability or pain may struggle with the 20-30 degree flexed positioning → record any positioning difficulty as a valid reason for an incomplete series.
Requesting clinicians may not specify 'recurrent patellar instability' clearly on the request → agree standard request wording with the knee clinic first.
Radiographers may not be aware of the specific flexion angle requirement → include this in the protocol change and staff communication.
pearls: Recruit a radiographer superintendent to help build the combined request protocol correctly.
Reuse the same case list as the MRI-findings audit in this batch, since the two together complete the full BOA standard.
Use example radiograph series (with and without skyline views) in radiographer teaching to reinforce the requirement.
Keep the protocol live by adding it to the RIS standard request-set library.
effort: ~10 min per case from the radiology system
pass: All three specified radiograph views (AP/PA, true lateral at 20-30 degrees flexion, and axial/skyline at 20-30 degrees flexion) are performed and available at the recurrent patellar instability assessment.
pass_short: AP/PA, true lateral and skyline views all done and available

area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
question: What proportion of patients started on empiric antibiotics for suspected fracture-related infection without a prior diagnostic work-up have those antibiotics stopped once this is identified?
why: The BOAST FRI standard explicitly prohibits empiric antibiotics without a diagnostic work-up and requires them to be stopped if already started, but no audit in the library checks whether this specific stewardship rule is followed once a lapse is identified.

standard.source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (September 2019), standard 5A
standard.wording: Empiric antibiotics without a diagnostic work up should not be given and if already commenced should be stopped.

population: Inclusion: adults started on antibiotics for suspected fracture-related infection over the last 6 months where a case-note review shows no diagnostic work-up was documented before the first dose. Exclusion: systemically septic patients (for whom immediate antibiotics are correctly prioritised).
sample: 20-30 consecutive suspected FRI antibiotic starts over the last 6 months, screened for those started before a work-up was documented.
data_source: EPMA/drug chart, microbiology request system, consultant/MDT review notes.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'diagnostic work-up in place before antibiotics: yes/no' field to the EPMA order for suspected FRI antibiotics, with a forced 48-hour review task if the answer is 'no' and the patient is not septic.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthopaedic infection governance and antimicrobial stewardship meeting; if the EPMA field and review task work, keep them as standard antibiotic stewardship for suspected FRI.
pitfalls: Clinicians may feel uncomfortable stopping antibiotics once started, even without evidence of infection → the fix should build in an explicit, supported review point rather than relying on individual decision-making.
A patient who deteriorates after antibiotics are stopped is a genuine safety concern → ensure the review pathway includes a clear escalation route if this happens.
This audit requires identifying a fairly specific subgroup (antibiotics before work-up) → screening a broader group of FRI antibiotic starts will be needed to find eligible cases.
Antimicrobial stewardship and orthopaedic teams may not routinely cross-reference each other's records → involve pharmacy or the antimicrobial stewardship team in case-finding.
pearls: Recruit the antimicrobial stewardship pharmacist as co-lead; they can help identify cases from EPMA data.
Use the same case list as the weekly bone and joint infection MDT audit in this batch to reduce duplicate work.
Present this as supporting good antimicrobial stewardship, aligning with existing trust stewardship priorities and targets.
Keep the EPMA field and review task live by embedding them in the standard FRI antibiotic order set.
effort: ~20 min per case from EPMA, microbiology and review records
pass: Where empiric antibiotics were started for suspected FRI before a diagnostic work-up (blood cultures, imaging, sampling plan) was in place, they are stopped once the absence of a work-up is identified on consultant or MDT review, unless the patient is systemically septic.
pass_short: Empiric antibiotics stopped once lack of work-up is identified, unless septic

question: What proportion of adults admitted with suspected non-variceal upper GI bleeding do not receive a proton pump inhibitor before their endoscopy?
why: PPI is still given almost routinely in upper GI bleeding; one unit recorded PPI in about 98% of bleeds [2744]. Existing audits count PPI use without separating timing [2283]; none has audited against the NICE advice not to give it before endoscopy.

standard.source: NICE CG141 rec 1.4.3 (2012, updated 2016)
standard.wording: Do not offer acid-suppression drugs (proton pump inhibitors or H2-receptor antagonists) before endoscopy to patients with suspected non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

population: Adults (≥16) admitted with suspected upper GI bleeding who had inpatient endoscopy. Exclude suspected variceal bleeding (known cirrhosis or varices on scope) and patients who did not have endoscopy.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible admissions over the last 3 months.
data_source: Endoscopy reporting system for the case list; ED and admission drug charts (EPMA) for PPI doses and times; endoscopy report for start time and findings.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Remove IV PPI from the ED and surgical admission order set for GI bleeding, and add a 'no PPI before endoscopy (NICE 1.4.3)' line to the GI bleed proforma.
target: ≥80% receive no new pre-endoscopy acid suppression
reaudit: Weeks 13–14, next 40 consecutive admissions, same template.
close_loop: Present at the joint surgical–gastroenterology audit meeting and to ED governance. If it works, lock the order-set change and add a PPI line to the GI bleed pathway.
evidence: [2283] UGIB audit: Blatchford use 12.5% → 50% after education alone; endoscopy <24 h fell 91.4% → 53%
[2744] UGIB audit: PPI given in about 98% (timing not separated); no re-audit
[3018] UK national UGIB audit 2022: pre-endoscopy risk stratification missed in 42%
pitfalls: Gastroenterology or ED consultants may still favour pre-scope PPI → agree the standard with both leads before cycle 1 and cite NICE 1.4.3.
Patients on a regular PPI are counted as failures → record them separately and agree the rule in advance.
Variceal and non-variceal cases get mixed up → decide exclusion on the endoscopy findings and cirrhosis history.
The order set change is bypassed by free-text prescribing → check pharmacy intervention logs in cycle 2.
Gains fade when ED rotates → make the order set the default, not the teaching.
pearls: Recruit the endoscopy lead early; they can pull the case list in minutes.
Pair the audit with PPI after endoscopy when stigmata are seen, so the message is 'later, not never'.
Ask pharmacy to flag new IV PPI in suspected bleeds for 4 weeks.
Show the cost of IV PPI infusions alongside the result.
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from EPR and endoscopy system
pass: No PPI or H2-receptor antagonist given (oral or IV) between arrival and the start of endoscopy, on the drug chart. Patients already on a regular oral PPI who simply continue it are recorded separately and do not fail.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: No PPI or H2 antagonist given before endoscopy

question: What proportion of haemodynamically stable adults admitted with upper GI bleeding have endoscopy within 24 hours of admission?
why: Delay to endoscopy lengthens stay and wastes beds. One UK unit fell from 91.4% to 53% after an education-only cycle [2283]; an Irish unit managed 63% [2744]. No closed loop with a system fix has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG141 rec 1.3.2 (2012, updated 2016)
standard.wording: Offer endoscopy within 24 hours of admission to all other patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

population: Adults (≥16) admitted with upper GI bleeding who were stable at presentation. Exclude those needing immediate endoscopy after resuscitation, those with a documented decision not to scope, and in-hospital bleeds.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible admissions over the last 3 months.
data_source: Endoscopy system for the case list and procedure time; ED system for arrival and admission times; notes for reasons for delay.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: A named daily 'bleed slot' on the endoscopy list, booked by the admitting team through an electronic request that timestamps the referral.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14, next 40 consecutive admissions, same template.
close_loop: Present at the endoscopy users group and divisional governance. If it works, keep the protected slot in the job plan and report the monthly rate on the endoscopy dashboard.
evidence: [2283] UGIB audit: endoscopy <24 h 91.4% → 53% after education only
[2744] UGIB audit: 63% within 24 h, mean delay 42.8 h; no re-audit
[3018] UK national UGIB audit 2022: inpatient endoscopy 83%
pitfalls: Admission time is defined differently between cycles → fix one definition in writing before cycle 1.
Weekend admissions dominate breaches and small numbers skew the rate → report weekday and weekend rates separately.
Endoscopy managers object to 'unused' slots → release the slot to the waiting list at a fixed time if no bleed is booked.
Patients scoped late for good reasons are counted as failures → record the reason and report them separately.
pearls: Recruit an endoscopy nurse manager as co-author.
Record the Blatchford score at the same time; low scores may suit outpatient scopes and free up slots.
Keep a live list of bleeds awaiting endoscopy on the ward handover sheet.
Show bed-days lost per delayed case to win management support.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from endoscopy and ED systems
pass: Endoscopy start time is within 24 hours of the admission time (ED decision to admit or ward arrival, whichever is recorded first).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: Endoscopy within 24 hours of admission

question: What proportion of adults treated for a perforated peptic ulcer are tested for H. pylori and, if positive, given eradication therapy?
why: H. pylori eradication prevents recurrent ulcer and re-perforation, yet testing is easily forgotten after emergency repair. No audit of H. pylori testing after perforated ulcer exists in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG184 recs 1.7.1 and 1.9.1 (2014, updated 2019)
standard.wording: 1.7.1 Offer H pylori eradication therapy to people who have tested positive for H pylori and who have peptic ulcer disease. ... 1.9.1 Test for H pylori using a carbon‑13 urea breath test or a stool antigen test, or laboratory-based serology where its performance has been locally validated.

population: Adults (≥18) with a perforated gastric or duodenal ulcer managed operatively or non-operatively. Exclude deaths before a test was possible.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 18 months (expect 20–40 in a DGH); NELA extract helps identify operative cases.
data_source: NELA extract and theatre system for the case list; pathology system for H. pylori tests and results; drug chart and discharge letter for eradication therapy.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add 'H. pylori serology sent / eradication prescribed' to the emergency laparotomy postoperative order set and discharge template.
reaudit: Re-audit all cases in the 12 weeks after the change plus the next consecutive cases to reach 15; same template.
close_loop: Present at the upper GI MDT and emergency surgery governance. If it works, keep the order-set item and share it with NELA leads.
evidence: [2269] Food bolus follow-up: OGD after bolus 20% → 45% (nearest follow-up audit)
[2626] Colorectal MMR testing 97% → 100% with a reporting standard
[2517] NELA frailty: CFS 0% → 92% after a proforma item
pitfalls: Breath and stool tests give false negatives on PPI → use locally validated serology during admission.
Small numbers make percentages jumpy → report counts and extend the window.
Results return after discharge and no one acts → name the consultant team as owner in the discharge letter.
Gastroenterology may own the result → agree who prescribes before cycle 1.
pearls: Ask the lab to add H. pylori serology to a 'perforated ulcer' order panel.
Recruit the upper GI consultant who runs the follow-up clinic.
Check the GP record for eradication if the hospital record is blank.
Track gastric ulcers for a 6–8 week OGD at the same time.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from pathology and letters
pass: An H. pylori test (serology, breath, stool antigen or biopsy) is sent during admission or planned in the discharge letter with a named owner, and, if positive, eradication therapy is prescribed.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: H. pylori test sent or planned with named owner, eradication if positive

question: What proportion of adults given intravenous antibiotics for acute diverticulitis have a documented review of the IV antibiotics within 48 hours or after their CT, whichever is sooner?
why: IV antibiotics are often continued by default, keeping patients in hospital. Existing diverticulitis audits focus on starting antibiotics [2078][2418]; none has measured the 48-hour IV review in NG147.

standard.wording: Review intravenous antibiotics within 48 hours or after scanning if sooner (see recommendation 1.3.5) and consider stepping down to oral antibiotics where possible.

population: Adults (≥18) admitted with acute diverticulitis who received IV antibiotics. Exclude those who went to theatre within 48 hours.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible admissions over the last 4 months.
data_source: Coding or surgical admissions list for cases; EPMA for antibiotic start and switch times; PACS for CT report time; ward round entries.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add a 48-hour 'IV antibiotic review: continue / oral / stop' box to the EPMA antibiotic order that must be completed on the surgical ward round.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14, next 40 admissions, same template.
close_loop: Present at the surgical audit meeting and antimicrobial stewardship committee. If it works, keep the EPMA prompt and add the rate to the stewardship dashboard.
evidence: [3030] IV metronidazole despite oral suitability 81.4% → 34.2% after prescriber education
[2208] Oral metronidazole use 12.5% → 61% in an acute surgical unit
[2418] Diverticulitis antibiotics in ED: local guideline and teaching after 98% blanket prescribing
pitfalls: 'Continue antibiotics' written without mention of route is counted inconsistently → define what counts as a review before cycle 1.
Weekend admissions skew the timing → report weekday and weekend separately.
Microbiology may object to earlier oral switch in abscesses → agree exceptions (abscess ≥3 cm, sepsis) with them first.
The EPMA prompt is clicked through → spot-check 10 cases for a real decision.
pearls: Recruit the antimicrobial pharmacist; they can pull EPMA data fast.
Record length of stay to show the benefit.
Put the NG147 oral options table on the ward round checklist.
Hand the dashboard to the stewardship team so it survives rotation.
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from EPMA and notes
pass: A dated entry in the notes or drug chart by a prescriber stating the IV antibiotic decision (continue with reason, switch to oral, or stop) within 48 hours of the first IV dose, or within 24 hours of the CT report if that is sooner.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: IV antibiotic decision documented within 48 hours, or 24 hours of CT report

question: What proportion of adults admitted with acute pancreatitis are allowed to eat, or have a documented reason for withholding food, within 24 hours of admission?
why: Routine 'nil by mouth' in pancreatitis persists. One DGH found 91% made nil by mouth with a reason recorded in only 20% and did not re-audit [2447]. No closed-loop audit of feeding in pancreatitis appears in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG104 rec 1.2.5 (2018, updated 2020)
standard.wording: Ensure that people with acute pancreatitis are not made 'nil‑by‑mouth' and do not have food withheld unless there is a clear reason for this (for example, vomiting).

population: Adults (≥18) admitted with a new diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. Exclude those admitted directly to critical care.
sample: 40 consecutive admissions over the last 3–4 months.
data_source: Surgical admissions list or coding for cases; clerking and ward round notes; nursing food charts; dietetic referrals.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Replace the default 'NBM' line in the pancreatitis clerking proforma with 'Diet: eat as tolerated unless vomiting / ileus / procedure (state reason)'.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14, next 40 admissions, same template.
close_loop: Present at the surgical audit meeting and to ward nursing leads. If it works, keep the proforma wording and add it to the pancreatitis pathway.
evidence: [2447] Pancreatitis DGH audit: nil by mouth 91%, reason recorded 20%; no re-audit
[2712] BISAP printed on the clerking proforma: 10% → 80% scored
[2524] Electronic tick box: severity scoring 44% → 84%
pitfalls: Nurses keep patients nil by mouth 'just in case' → brief the ward sisters before the change.
Cases waiting for ERCP or cholecystectomy are counted as failures → accept a documented planned procedure as a reason.
Food charts are incomplete → use the ward round entry as the primary source.
Seniors disagree about early feeding → share the NICE rationale at the audit meeting.
pearls: Recruit a ward dietitian as co-lead.
Add a bedside sign option 'eat as tolerated'.
Measure length of stay as a balancing measure.
Get the consultant on-call rota to sign off the proforma change.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from notes and charts
pass: By 24 hours after admission the patient is on oral diet or free fluids progressing to diet, or the notes record a clear reason for withholding food (for example vomiting, ileus, planned procedure).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: Eating within 24 hours of admission, or reason for withholding food documented

question: What proportion of adults with acute pancreatitis not caused by gallstones or alcohol have serum calcium and triglycerides measured during the admission?
why: Up to a third of cases are labelled idiopathic, and only 45% of these had a further screen in one DGH [2401]. Aetiology audits count 'cause identified' but none has measured the specific tests NICE lists.

standard.source: NICE NG104 rec 1.2.2 (2018, updated 2020)
standard.wording: If gallstones and alcohol have been excluded as potential causes of a person's acute pancreatitis, investigate other possible causes such as: metabolic causes (such as hypercalcaemia or hyperlipidaemia) prescription drugs microlithiasis hereditary causes autoimmune pancreatitis ampullary or pancreatic tumours anatomical anomalies (pancreas divisum).

population: Adults (≥18) with acute pancreatitis where ultrasound shows no gallstones and alcohol is not the recorded cause.
sample: 30–40 consecutive eligible cases over the last 12 months.
data_source: Coding or admissions list; ultrasound reports on PACS; pathology results; discharge letter for follow-up plan.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: An electronic 'pancreatitis cause' blood panel (calcium, triglycerides, IgG4) available from the admission order set.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14 onwards, next 30 eligible cases (may need 3 months), same template.
close_loop: Present at the benign upper GI or HPB meeting. If it works, keep the order panel and add it to the pancreatitis pathway.
evidence: [2401] Pancreatitis DGH audit: 45% of idiopathic cases had a further screen; no re-audit
[2857] Aetiology assessment 62% → 100% after teaching and MDT posters
[1968] Renal colic bloods: calcium 58.8% → 76% with a set panel
pitfalls: Triglycerides taken late are falsely low after fasting → take on admission and note timing.
Alcohol history is vague → define 'alcohol excluded' before cycle 1.
Numbers are small → extend the look-back window.
The lab rejects triglyceride requests without a reason → add the indication to the panel.
pearls: Recruit a biochemist to create the panel.
Include IgG4 and drug review in the same prompt.
Check whether GPs were asked to repeat tests after discharge.
Flag idiopathic cases for HPB review at discharge.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from pathology and PACS
pass: Both adjusted calcium and triglycerides are measured during the index admission.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: Adjusted calcium and triglycerides both measured during the admission

question: What proportion of adults who had potentially curative surgery for colorectal cancer have CEA and CT chest, abdomen and pelvis at the planned intervals over the first 3 years?
why: Follow-up gaps are greatest in year 3; one nurse-led service achieved only 46% for the 3-year CT in high-risk patients [2194]. No closed-loop audit of the NG151 follow-up schedule appears in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG151 rec 1.6.1 (2020, updated 2021)
standard.wording: For people who have had potentially curative surgical treatment for non-metastatic colorectal cancer, offer follow-up for detection of local recurrence and distant metastases for the first 3 years. Follow-up should include serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

population: Adults who had potentially curative resection for non-metastatic colorectal cancer 1–3 years ago. Exclude those who chose no follow-up, entered palliative care or died.
sample: 40 patients operated on 3 years ago (full schedule) from the cancer database.
data_source: Colorectal cancer database or NBOCA list; pathology system for CEA dates; PACS for CT dates; clinic letters for the local schedule.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Automatic surveillance tracking: each patient is loaded onto an electronic recall list at the end of treatment, with CEA and CT requests triggered by the cancer nurse team.
reaudit: After 6 months, audit the next 40 patients using the same template, looking at tests due in the preceding 6 months.
close_loop: Present at the colorectal MDT business meeting. If it works, make the recall list part of the Personalised Stratified Follow-Up protocol.
evidence: [2194] Nurse-led CRC follow-up: 1-year CT 85–100%, 3-year CT in high-risk patients 46%; no re-audit
[2604] Gallbladder polyp recall: 41.6% lost to follow-up → 100% returned to surveillance
[3013] Colonoscopy surveillance: 73.5% adherent to intervals
pitfalls: Local schedules differ from NICE → state the local schedule and audit against it.
Scans done at another trust are missed → check image-sharing systems.
Patients who opt out are counted as failures → record choice as an exclusion.
Recall lists depend on one nurse → give a deputy access.
pearls: Recruit the colorectal CNS team; they hold the follow-up list.
Audit the full 3-year cohort, not recent patients.
Report recurrences found by surveillance to show value.
Link to the Personalised Stratified Follow-Up system if the trust has one.
effort: ~30 min per 10 patients from PACS and pathology
pass: Every CEA and CT due by the local schedule was done within 6 weeks of its due date up to the audit date (or 3 years after surgery).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: Every CEA and CT done within 6 weeks of its due date

question: What proportion of adults having sphincter-preserving rectal cancer surgery have documented pre-operative information about low anterior resection syndrome?
why: Most patients get bowel dysfunction after anterior resection, and many say they were not warned. No audit of LARS information exists in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG151 rec 1.6.2 (2020, updated 2021)
standard.wording: Give information on low anterior resection syndrome (LARS) to people who will potentially have sphincter-preserving surgery. Advise them to seek help from primary care if they think they have symptoms of LARS, such as: increased frequency of stool urgency with or without incontinence of stool feeling of incomplete emptying of the bowels fragmentation of stool (passing small amounts little and often) difficulty in differentiating between gas and stool.

population: Adults having anterior resection or other sphincter-preserving rectal cancer surgery. Exclude abdominoperineal resection and Hartmann's without plan for reversal.
sample: 30–40 consecutive cases over the last 12 months.
data_source: Colorectal cancer database or theatre system; surgeon and CNS clinic letters; consent form; stoma nurse notes.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add 'LARS explained and leaflet given' to the colorectal CNS pre-operative checklist and to the anterior resection consent template.
reaudit: Next 30 consecutive anterior resections (about 4–6 months), same template.
close_loop: Present at the colorectal MDT and CNS team meeting. If it works, keep the checklist item and use the LARS score at follow-up.
evidence: [2609] TURBT patient information leaflet: 30% → 80% after a pathway change
[2817] Hernia discharge documentation improved with a standard leaflet
[2390] Pancreatitis information: satisfaction 60% → 92% after written information
pitfalls: Discussion happens but is not written down → accept any written record and agree sources before cycle 1.
Surgeons see it as consent detail, not audit → frame it as a NICE quality item.
Small numbers → extend the window or pool with a neighbour unit.
Leaflet stock runs out → keep an electronic copy linked in the checklist.
pearls: Recruit the colorectal CNS lead; they own the pre-operative visit.
Use the national LARS leaflet so no one has to write one.
Add the LARS score to the first follow-up clinic template.
Ask two patients to comment on the leaflet.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from letters
pass: Clinic letter, CNS record or consent form documents that LARS was discussed or a LARS leaflet given before surgery.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: LARS discussed or leaflet given before surgery, documented

question: What proportion of women under 50 with triple-negative breast cancer are offered BRCA1/2 genetic testing?
why: Testing changes surgery, systemic therapy and family screening, and NICE applies it regardless of family history. No audit of BRCA testing in triple-negative disease exists in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG101 rec 1.3.6 (2018, updated 2025)
standard.wording: Offer genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations to women under 50 years with triple-negative breast cancer, including those with no family history of breast or ovarian cancer (also see the recommendations on genetic testing in the NICE guideline on familial breast cancer).

population: Women under 50 with newly diagnosed invasive triple-negative breast cancer. Exclude those already known to carry a BRCA variant.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 2 years (expect 20–40 in a DGH unit).
data_source: Breast MDT database for receptor status and age; clinic letters; genetics referral log; genetics lab result.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add an automatic 'TNBC <50: BRCA test offered?' field to the breast MDT outcome form, completed at the diagnostic MDT.
reaudit: All eligible cases in the 6 months after the change, same template.
close_loop: Present at the breast MDT business meeting and to the regional genetics service. If it works, keep the MDT field and mainstream consent pack.
evidence: [2704] Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer: CDH1 testing 58% → 87% with mainstream testing
[2626] Colorectal MMR testing 97% → 100% with a reporting standard
[2072] Lynch testing 79% in colorectal cancer; no re-audit
pitfalls: Some units route testing through genetics with long waits → record the date offered, not only the date tested.
Small numbers → use a 2-year window and report counts.
Oncology offers the test and it is missed in surgical records → check oncology letters too.
Eligibility criteria widen over time → state the NICE criterion used in both cycles.
pearls: Recruit a breast CNS trained in mainstream consent.
Check the regional genetics criteria at the same time.
Report the proportion with results before surgery; it drives surgical choice.
Hand the MDT field to the MDT coordinator so it survives rotation.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the MDT database
pass: Clinic letter or MDT outcome records that BRCA testing was offered (mainstream test sent or genetics referral made), or that the patient declined.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: BRCA testing offered (test sent or genetics referral), or declined, documented

question: What proportion of postmenopausal women with node-positive early invasive breast cancer are offered adjuvant bisphosphonates?
why: Adjuvant bisphosphonates improve survival but uptake is patchy between units. Existing breast bone audits look only at DEXA scans [1518][1311]; none has audited adjuvant bisphosphonate use.

standard.source: NICE NG101 rec 1.12.1 (2018, updated 2025)
standard.wording: Offer bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or sodium clodronate) as adjuvant therapy to postmenopausal women with node-positive invasive breast cancer.

population: Postmenopausal women with node-positive early invasive breast cancer treated with curative intent. Exclude metastatic disease.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients from the last 12 months.
data_source: Breast MDT database for nodal status and menopausal status; oncology letters; chemotherapy prescribing system; dental check records.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Local target e.g. with chemotherapy or within 6 months of surgery

change: Add 'Adjuvant bisphosphonate: yes / no (reason)' to the postoperative MDT outcome template.
reaudit: Next 40 eligible patients (about 6 months), same template.
close_loop: Present at the breast MDT business meeting with oncology. If it works, keep the template field and a dental-check prompt.
evidence: [1518] Baseline DEXA in breast cancer: 38% → 100% after a pathway change
[1311] Bone health on aromatase inhibitors: baseline DEXA 61%, calcium and vitamin D 52%
[2478] NABCOP fitness assessment: 0% → 88.2% after adding a template
pitfalls: Menopausal status is not recorded → agree a definition (age, periods, FSH) before cycle 1.
Oncologists may make the decision outside the MDT → include oncology letters.
Dental delays postpone starts → record the dental check as a separate step.
Off-label status worries prescribers → cite the NICE note on off-label use.
pearls: Recruit a breast oncologist as co-lead.
Pair with the DEXA pathway so bone care is one conversation.
Use the MDT coordinator to pull node-positive cases.
Report both 'offered' and 'started'.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from MDT records
pass: MDT outcome or oncology letter records that adjuvant zoledronic acid or sodium clodronate was offered (started or declined), or a documented contraindication (for example dental work pending).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: Adjuvant bisphosphonate offered, started or declined, or contraindication documented

question: What proportion of pre-operative breast MRIs in newly diagnosed breast cancer have a NICE indication recorded on the request?
why: Routine pre-operative MRI adds cost and delay and can lead to more mastectomies without better outcomes. No audit of breast MRI indications appears in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG101 recs 1.2.2 and 1.2.3 (2018, updated 2025)
standard.wording: 1.2.2 Do not routinely use MRI of the breast as part of the preoperative assessment of people with biopsy-proven invasive breast cancer or ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). 1.2.3 Offer MRI of the breast as part of preoperative assessment to people with invasive breast cancer: if the extent of disease is not clear from clinical examination, mammography and ultrasound assessment for planning treatment if accurate mammographic assessment is difficult because of breast density to assess the tumour size if breast-conserving surgery is being considered for invasive lobular cancer.

population: Adults with newly diagnosed invasive breast cancer or DCIS who had a pre-operative breast MRI.
sample: 40 consecutive pre-operative breast MRIs over the last 4 months.
data_source: Radiology information system for MRI requests; MDT outcomes; histology for tumour type.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Make 'MRI indication' a mandatory drop-down on the breast MRI request, listing the NICE and agreed local indications.
reaudit: Next 40 pre-operative breast MRIs, same template.
close_loop: Present at the breast MDT and radiology governance. If it works, keep the mandatory field and review the indication list yearly.
evidence: [2700] Pancreatitis CT with a local imaging policy: unnecessary scans 28% → 4.3%
[2239] Breast clinical biopsy indication: inappropriate biopsies 80% → 15.4%
[2657] Radiology request acceptance 73% → 89% after request quality work
pitfalls: Radiologists and surgeons disagree on local indications → agree the list at the MDT first.
Requests are made verbally at MDT → use the MDT outcome as a second source.
Neoadjuvant cases inflate MRI use → record them as an agreed indication.
The drop-down becomes a tick box → spot-check 10 cases against the MDT discussion.
pearls: Recruit a breast radiologist as co-author.
Record whether MRI changed the plan; it answers the value question.
Track time from MRI request to surgery as a balancing measure.
Re-audit yearly via the radiology system.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from RIS and MDT records
pass: The MRI request or MDT outcome states one NICE indication (unclear extent, dense breasts, lobular cancer for conservation) or another agreed local indication (for example neoadjuvant therapy, occult primary).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: NICE or agreed local MRI indication stated on the request

question: What proportion of people treated for breast cancer have their annual surveillance mammogram within 13 months of the previous one?
why: Missed surveillance mammograms delay detection of recurrence and new primaries. Surveillance audits in the library cover B3 lesions [2867] but none has audited annual mammography after breast cancer.

standard.source: NICE NG101 rec 1.15.1 (2018, updated 2025)
standard.wording: Offer annual mammography for 5 years to all people who have had or are being treated for breast cancer, including DCIS. For women, continue annual mammography past 5 years until they enter the NHS Breast Screening Programme (NHSBSP) in England or the Breast Test Wales Screening Programme (BTWSP) in Wales.

population: Adults treated for breast cancer or DCIS 1–5 years ago with breast tissue remaining or a contralateral breast. Exclude bilateral mastectomy, metastatic disease and death.
sample: 50 patients diagnosed 2–4 years ago, randomly selected from the breast MDT database.
data_source: Breast MDT database for the cohort; PACS or breast imaging system for mammogram dates; clinic letters for planned surveillance.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add each patient to an electronic surveillance recall list in the breast imaging system at the end of treatment, with automatic invitations.
reaudit: After 6 months, check mammograms due in that period for the same cohort plus 20 new patients.
close_loop: Present at the breast MDT business meeting and to the breast imaging manager. If it works, keep the recall list and a monthly overdue report.
evidence: [2604] Gallbladder polyp recall: 41.6% lost to follow-up → 100% returned to surveillance
[2867] B3 lesion surveillance: 64% referred for annual mammograms
[2780] Gallbladder polyp surveillance: 17% of pathways adherent
pitfalls: Patients discharged to GP-led follow-up are missed → include open-access follow-up patients.
Scans done at another site are not visible → check shared PACS.
DNAs are counted as failures → record them and check re-invitation.
Recall lists get switched off after IT upgrades → name an owner.
pearls: Recruit the breast imaging superintendent.
Sample randomly across years to show where gaps happen.
Report any cancers found by surveillance.
Check that patients reaching 5 years are moved to screening.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from PACS
pass: Each surveillance mammogram due in the audit period was done within 13 months of the previous one (or of the end of surgery for the first).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
pass_short: Each surveillance mammogram done within 13 months of the previous one

question: What proportion of adults with an incidental abdominal aortic aneurysm of 3.0 cm or more on imaging are referred to the vascular service within the NICE time frame?
why: Aneurysms found by chance on CT or ultrasound often go unreferred. No audit of incidental AAA referral exists in the library.

standard.wording: Refer people with an AAA that is 5.5 cm or larger to a regional vascular service, to be seen within 2 weeks of diagnosis. Refer people with an AAA that is 3.0 cm to 5.4 cm to a regional vascular service, to be seen within 12 weeks of diagnosis.

population: Adults with a new AAA ≥3.0 cm reported on CT or ultrasound done for another reason. Exclude those already known to vascular, those in the screening programme and those with documented palliative care decisions.
sample: 40 consecutive cases found by a radiology report text search ('aneurysm', 'aortic') over the last 6–12 months.
data_source: Radiology information system text search; vascular referral log; clinic system; GP letters.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Radiology adds a coded 'AAA ≥3 cm' alert that automatically copies the report to the vascular service's referral inbox.
reaudit: Next 40 cases after the alert goes live (about 3–6 months), same template.
close_loop: Present at vascular network governance and radiology discrepancy meeting. If it works, keep the coded alert and audit it yearly.
