question: Do adults recognised as dying in hospital have anticipatory medicines prescribed with an indication and dose range for each drug?
why: End-of-life audits in the library measure documentation of recognition of dying and DNACPR [1829], [1871]; anticipatory prescribing quality is measured only in Parkinson's disease [1902].

standard.source: NICE NG31 rec 1.6.1 (2015)
standard.wording: Use an individualised approach to prescribing anticipatory medicines for people who are likely to need symptom control in the last days of life. Specify the indications for use and the dosage of any medicines prescribed.

pass: Within 24 hours of recognition of dying, as-required medicines are prescribed for pain, agitation, nausea and vomiting, breathlessness and respiratory secretions, each with an indication, dose, route and maximum 24-hour dose, adjusted for renal function where relevant.
population: Adult inpatients who died after being recognised as dying (documented in notes) for 24 hours or more. Exclude: sudden unexpected deaths, deaths within 24 hours of admission.
sample: 40 consecutive deaths over the last 2–3 months (mortuary or bereavement office list).
data_source: Bereavement office list; notes for recognition of dying time; EPMA as-required prescriptions; eGFR from laboratory system.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Build an end-of-life anticipatory medicines order set in EPMA with pre-filled indications, dose ranges, maximum doses and a renal-impairment version, agreed with the palliative care team.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible deaths, same template.
close_loop: Present at the end-of-life care steering group (NACEL lead). If it works, keep the order set and include it in the trust NACEL action plan.
evidence: [1902] Oxford: anti-dopaminergic prescribing in dying Parkinson's patients 47% → 50% after leaflet and EoL guidance (mixed)
[1829] Irish stroke and geriatric services: recognition of dying 92.9–94.1%; risk of dying communicated to family 75% (education only)
[1784] NACEL round two: 71% of category 1 deaths had an individualised end-of-life care plan (national audit)
pitfalls: Recognition of dying time unclear → use the first documented statement that the person is dying.
Order sets used blindly → keep 'individualise and review daily' wording and a palliative contact.
Palliative team concern about standardisation → co-design the order set with them.
Deaths spread over many wards → sample through the bereavement office list, not wards.
pearls: Recruit the hospital palliative care nurse specialist and an EPMA pharmacist.
Link the audit to NACEL so the trust already has a governance route.
Include renal dosing; it is the most common error.
Add the order set to the end-of-life care plan document.
effort: ~25 min per 10 deaths from EPMA and notes
group: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
pass_short: Within 24 hours, as-required medicines for five symptoms prescribed with indication and dose range

area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: Do adults in the last days of life in hospital have their hydration status assessed and documented every day?
why: Hydration audits in the library concern general acute wards [1863]; end-of-life documentation audits do not measure daily hydration assessment [1829], [1871].

standard.source: NICE NG31 rec 1.4.4 (2015)
standard.wording: Assess, preferably daily, the dying person's hydration status, and review the possible need for starting clinically assisted hydration, respecting the person's wishes and preferences.

pass: A hydration assessment (for example oral intake, thirst, mouth, signs of dehydration or overload) and a decision about clinically assisted hydration are documented on every full day between recognition of dying and death.
population: Adult inpatients who died after being recognised as dying for 48 hours or more. Exclude: sudden deaths, deaths within 48 hours of admission.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible deaths over the last 3 months.
data_source: Bereavement office list; medical and nursing notes; end-of-life care plan; fluid charts; EPMA for subcutaneous or IV fluids.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a daily 'Hydration and mouth care' box to the individualised end-of-life care plan, reviewed at the daily ward round.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible deaths, same template.
close_loop: Present at the end-of-life care steering group. If it works, keep the care plan box and include it in the trust NACEL action plan.
evidence: [1863] St Michael's Dun Laoghaire: 38% of patients needed prompting to drink (single cycle)
[1829] Irish stroke and geriatric services: end-of-life documentation audited; education recommended (single cycle)
[1784] NACEL round two: individualised end-of-life care plan in 71% of category 1 deaths (national audit)
pitfalls: Nursing and medical notes in different systems → check both.
'Comfortable' entries counted as assessment → define what counts before cycle 1.
Families distressed by 'withholding fluids' → pair with the discussion field and leaflet.
Deaths with short dying phase → require 48 hours so every day can be judged.
pearls: Recruit the palliative care nurse specialist and ward matrons.
Use NACEL case note review forms to align definitions.
Keep the care plan box short (three lines).
Share one anonymised good example at ward huddles.
effort: ~25 min per 10 deaths from notes
group: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
pass_short: Hydration assessment and assisted hydration decision documented every full day until death

area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: Do older inpatients started on a strong opioid have a regular laxative prescribed at the same time?
why: Opioid–laxative co-prescribing has been audited in surgical patients (34% co-prescribed) [2463]; in older and palliative inpatients only constipation care as a whole has been studied [1787].

standard.source: NICE CG140 rec 1.1.18 (2012, updated 2016)
standard.wording: Prescribe laxative treatment (to be taken regularly at an effective dose) for all patients starting strong opioids.

pass: A regular (not only as-required) laxative prescribed within 24 hours of the first strong opioid prescription, unless contraindicated (for example bowel obstruction, stoma with high output) and documented.
population: Inpatients aged 65+ on care of older people, acute medical or palliative beds starting a strong opioid (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl patch, buprenorphine patch, others). Exclude: already on a regular laxative, bowel obstruction, diarrhoea at start.
sample: 40 consecutive new strong opioid starts over the last 2 months (EPMA report).
data_source: EPMA new strong opioid prescriptions; EPMA laxative prescriptions; bowel chart; notes.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Link a regular laxative prompt to all strong opioid prescriptions in EPMA (opioid order set includes a laxative that must be accepted or declined with a reason).
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 new starts, same template.
close_loop: Present at the medicines safety committee and palliative care group. If it works, keep the EPMA link and extend to all adult wards.
evidence: [2463] Queen Elizabeth Birmingham general surgery: 34% of patients on opioids co-prescribed laxatives (education planned, single cycle)
[1787] Bournville Ward Birmingham: inpatient-developed constipation down 6% after teaching and weekly MDT review (mixed)
[1341] QEHB surgical departments: safe opioid prescribing audited (related topic)
pitfalls: As-required laxatives counted → count only regular prescriptions.
Weak opioids (codeine) included by mistake → list strong opioids before cycle 1.
Alert fatigue → only trigger the prompt when no regular laxative is on the chart.
Patients refuse laxatives → still a pass if prescribed; record refusals.
pearls: Recruit the ward pharmacist; the EPMA report takes minutes.
Suggest a default stimulant laxative in the order set.
Record bowel outcome as a balancing measure.
Share results with surgery too; the same EPMA change helps them.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPMA report
group: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
pass_short: Regular laxative prescribed within 24 hours of first strong opioid, unless contraindicated

area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: When an adult in hospital is recognised as dying, are medicines that no longer give symptom benefit stopped within 24 hours?
why: End-of-life audits in the library measure documentation and anticipatory prescribing in Parkinson's disease [1829], [1902]; stopping non-beneficial medicines at recognition of dying is not measured.

standard.source: NICE NG31 rec 1.5.1 (2015)
standard.wording: When it is recognised that a person may be entering the last days of life, review their current medicines and, after discussion and agreement with the dying person and those important to them (as appropriate), stop any previously prescribed medicines that are not providing symptomatic benefit or that may cause harm.

pass: Within 24 hours of recognition of dying, a documented medicines review, and statins, bisphosphonates, vitamin supplements, oral hypoglycaemics (unless symptomatic), routine VTE prophylaxis and other non-symptomatic medicines are stopped or have a documented reason to continue.
population: Adult inpatients who died after being recognised as dying for 24 hours or more. Exclude: sudden deaths, deaths within 24 hours of admission.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible deaths over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: Bereavement office list; notes for recognition of dying; EPMA active prescriptions at recognition and 24 hours later.

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately
Statins, bisphosphonates, vitamins, VTE prophylaxis etc.
All stopped or justified within 24 hours

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'Medicines review at recognition of dying' checklist to the individualised end-of-life care plan, listing common medicines to stop.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible deaths, same template.
close_loop: Present at the end-of-life care steering group and medicines safety committee. If it works, keep the checklist and add it to the EPMA end-of-life order set.
evidence: [1902] Oxford: prescribing for dying Parkinson's patients re-audited over multiple cycles; anti-dopaminergic prescribing 47% → 50% (mixed)
[1829] Irish stroke and geriatric services: recognition of dying documented in 92.9–94.1% (single cycle)
[3413] Psychiatric wards: EPMA transition raised safe deprescribing compliance from under 34% to 100% (system change)
pitfalls: Disagreement on what is 'non-symptomatic' → agree a list with palliative care before cycle 1.
Anticoagulants for AF debated → count a documented reason as a pass.
Families want medicines continued → the discussion field captures this.
Recognition of dying reversed → exclude patients who stabilised and were discharged.
pearls: Recruit the palliative care consultant and ward pharmacist.
Run the EPMA 'active prescriptions' report at recognition time for quick data.
Count doses given after recognition; it is a striking figure.
Pair with the anticipatory medicines audit to share data collection.
effort: ~20 min per 10 deaths from EPMA and notes
group: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
pass_short: Medication review within 24 hours, non-symptomatic medicines stopped or reason to continue documented

question: What proportion of adults seen by liaison psychiatry after self-harm are given a copy of their care plan before they leave the emergency department or ward?
why: Liaison self-harm audits measure timeliness and assessment content [3686] [3322] [3125]; whether the person leaves with their own copy of the plan has not been measured in a closed loop in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.5.16 (2022)
standard.wording: Give the person a copy of their care plan, and share the plan as soon as possible with relevant healthcare professionals and social care practitioners involved in the person's care.

pass: The liaison record states that a written or printed care plan (including crisis contacts) was given to the person before discharge from the emergency department or ward.
population: Adults (18+) who had a liaison psychiatry psychosocial assessment after self-harm. Exclude people admitted to a mental health bed straight from assessment and people who left before assessment finished.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible assessments over the last 2 months
data_source: Liaison psychiatry electronic record (assessment and outcome entry); emergency department discharge record; GP letter

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive
Plan agreed with the person recorded

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'print patient copy' step and a mandatory 'copy given: yes/no/declined' tick box to the liaison electronic assessment template.
target: ≥90% given a copy or documented as declined
reaudit: Wk 13–14, 40 consecutive assessments, same template
close_loop: Present at the liaison team business meeting and the trust self-harm or suicide prevention group; if it works, make the tick box permanent and add the rate to the liaison monthly dashboard.
evidence: [3125] Newcastle liaison team: 58% → 98% of notes with at least half the NCEPOD elements, discharge plan 2% → 29% (e-template, training and named guardians)
[3523] West London liaison service: driving status recorded 5% → 50% (template prompt and reminders)
[3322] Dorset liaison: carer or parent understanding recorded in 40% of self-harm assessments (single cycle)
pitfalls: Out-of-hours assessors cannot print in the emergency department → allow a copy by text or email, or a handwritten crisis card, to count as a pass.
Notes say 'plan discussed' but not 'copy given' → define the pass wording before cycle 1 and keep it the same in cycle 2.
People who leave soon after assessment skew the rate → record 'left before copy could be given' separately.
Staff see the tick box as more paperwork → show them the NG225 wording and keep the box to one click.
pearls: Recruit the liaison team manager and one band 6 nurse as co-leads; they own the template.
Agree with IT a one-page printable plan built from fields already in the assessment.
Keep a stock of printed crisis cards in the emergency department mental health room.
Hand the monthly count to the team manager so it survives the trainee rotation.
effort: ~20 min per 10 assessments from the liaison record
pass_short: Liaison record states written care plan given before discharge

question: What proportion of liaison psychiatry self-harm assessments give a reason for discharge that does not rest on a 'low/medium/high' risk rating?
why: NG225 (2022) moved away from risk scoring, but liaison notes still often end with a risk category [3686] [3322]; no audit in the library measures whether discharge decisions rest on a risk grade.

standard.source: NICE NG225 Self-harm, rec 1.6.2 (2022)
standard.wording: Do not use risk assessment tools and scales to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged.

pass: The outcome section gives the reason for the disposal in terms of needs, formulation and safety plan, and does not use a risk score or a 'low/medium/high' category as the stated reason.
population: People aged 16+ assessed by liaison psychiatry after self-harm and discharged from the emergency department or ward. Exclude those admitted to a mental health bed.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible discharges over the last 2 months
data_source: Liaison psychiatry electronic assessment (risk and outcome sections)

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive
Any low/medium/high grade or score anywhere in the note
Fail if the stated reason is the grade

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Replace the 'overall risk: low/medium/high' drop-down in the liaison template with a free-text 'risk formulation and safety plan' box and a 'reason for this disposal' box.
target: ≥90% with a needs-based reason and no risk grade used as the reason
reaudit: Wk 13–14, 40 consecutive discharges, same template
close_loop: Present at the liaison and crisis teams' governance meeting; if it works, ask the trust to remove the risk drop-down from all acute mental health assessment templates.
evidence: [3125] Newcastle liaison team: formulation 0% → 8%, risk management 18% → 53% (e-template, training and named guardians)
[3686] Countess of Chester: risk formulation and full psychosocial assessment gaps after overdose (single cycle)
[3322] Dorset liaison: psychiatric formulation 92%, risk summary 98% on a structured template (single cycle)
pitfalls: Some staff and commissioners still expect a risk grade → agree with the clinical director before cycle 1 that the grade is being removed on NG225 grounds.
Recording a grade is not a fail if it is not the reason → audit the reason, not the presence of the word.
The drop-down is part of a trust-wide form → pilot a liaison-only version first.
Judging 'needs-based' is subjective → two auditors score the first 10 cases and agree the rule.
pearls: Bring the trust suicide prevention lead on side; they usually want this change.
Use real anonymised notes to show the difference between a grade and a formulation.
Pair the template change with the safety plan audit so the box is not left empty.
Ask the governance team to keep the monthly score after the audit team moves on.
effort: ~25 min per 10 assessments
pass_short: Discharge reason given as needs, formulation and safety plan, not a risk category

question: What proportion of patients physically restrained on an adult inpatient ward are offered a documented chance to talk about the incident within 72 hours?
why: Restraint work in the library focuses on reduction and seclusion reviews; patient involvement in post-incident reflection was 12% before a QI programme [3240], and no audit measures the patient debrief offer itself.

standard.source: NICE NG10 Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health, health and community settings, rec 1.4.58 (2015)
standard.wording: Ensure that the service user involved has the opportunity to discuss the incident in a supportive environment with a member of staff or an advocate or carer. Offer the service user the opportunity to write their perspective of the event in the notes.

pass: The notes show that, within 72 hours of the restraint, the patient was offered a discussion of the incident with staff, an advocate or a carer (accepted or declined).
population: Restraint incidents on adult acute and PICU wards. One incident per patient (the first in the period). Exclude patients transferred out within 72 hours.
sample: 40 consecutive restraint incidents over the last 3 months
data_source: Incident reporting system (restraint log); nursing and medical notes for 72 hours after each incident

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'patient debrief offered' field with a 72-hour due time to the restraint incident form, which triggers a task for the named nurse.
reaudit: Wk 13–14, 40 consecutive incidents, same template
close_loop: Present at the reducing restrictive practice group and ward managers' meeting; if it works, add the rate to the monthly restrictive practice report to the board.
evidence: [3240] Lincolnshire inpatient wards: patient involvement in post-incident reflection 12% at baseline, rose by 60% (training, restrictive practice hub, root cause analysis)
[3105] Adolescent PICU, London: consultant seclusion review within 24 h under 70% → over 90% (safety huddles, incident reduction meetings)
[3188] Secure learning disability wards: seclusion risk assessment 48% → 89% (education)
pitfalls: Debriefs happen but are not written down → count only what is documented and say so when presenting.
Staff debrief is confused with patient debrief → keep them as separate fields.
Patients who remain very unwell for days → allow 'deferred, reason recorded' but report it separately.
Ward staff feel judged → frame it as a patient-experience measure and share results by ward, not by name.
pearls: Recruit a ward manager, the restrictive practice lead and a peer support worker.
Ask advocacy services to accept debrief referrals directly.
Put the debrief prompt on the safety huddle board for patients restrained in the last 72 hours.
The incident form field keeps the change after the audit team rotates.
effort: ~30 min per 10 incidents
pass_short: Offered a discussion of the incident within 72 hours of restraint

question: Among detained patients who did not understand their rights at the first explanation, what proportion had their rights explained again within 7 days?
why: Mental Health Act audits in the library cover detention paperwork, section 5(2) forms and consent to treatment [3095] [3398] [3049]; follow-up of patients who did not understand their section 132 rights has not been audited.

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 4.28
standard.wording: Those with responsibility for patient care should ensure that patients are reminded from time to time of their rights and the effects of the Act. It may be necessary to give the same information on a number of different occasions or in different formats and to check regularly that the patient has fully understood it. Information given to a patient who is unwell may need to be repeated when their condition has improved.

pass: A further section 132 explanation (with understanding recorded) is documented within 7 days of the first explanation that was recorded as not understood, declined or not possible.
population: Patients newly detained under section 2 or 3 whose first rights record says 'not understood', 'partly understood', 'declined' or 'unable'. Exclude patients discharged or regraded within 7 days.
sample: 40 eligible detentions from the last 4 months (use the Mental Health Act office list to find them)
data_source: Mental Health Act office register; section 132 rights forms; nursing notes

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make the electronic section 132 form create an automatic 'repeat rights due' task at 7 days whenever the outcome is anything other than 'fully understood'.
reaudit: Wk 13–14, 40 eligible detentions, same template
close_loop: Present to the Mental Health Act governance committee and hospital managers; if it works, keep the automated task and add it to the Mental Health Act office monthly report.
evidence: [3049] High-dependency rehabilitation unit: Mental Health Act documentation compliance 77% → 98% (medication management committee, PDSA cycles, nurse self-audit)
[3568] NHS Tayside out-of-hours admissions: Mental Health Act status recorded 82.7% → 75.9%, leave status 1.9% → 65.5% (posters)
[3095] Derby: detention justification poorly documented (single cycle)
pitfalls: Paper rights forms are filed but not scanned → agree with the Mental Health Act office to use their tracker as the source.
Repeat explanations are done but written only in nursing notes → search nursing notes as well as forms.
Small numbers on one ward → pool all adult acute wards.
Nurses see it as an administrative task → show the Code wording and the Care Quality Commission focus on rights.
pearls: The Mental Health Act administrator is the key ally; they already track rights.
Agree what 'understood' means (patient can say it back in their own words) before cycle 1.
Easy-read and translated leaflets should be at the nursing station, not in an office.
Hand the monthly report to the Mental Health Act office manager.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients
pass_short: Rights explained again, with understanding recorded, within 7 days of first explanation

question: What proportion of detained patients recorded as lacking capacity to decide about advocacy are referred to an independent mental health advocate within 7 days?
why: No audit in the library measures access to independent mental health advocates; detained patients who lack capacity cannot ask for one themselves.

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 6.16
standard.wording: If a patient lacks capacity to decide whether or not to obtain help from an IMHA, the hospital manager should ask an IMHA to attend the patient so that the IMHA can explain what they can offer to the patient directly.

pass: An IMHA referral (or IMHA visit) is documented within 7 days of the record that the patient lacked capacity to decide about advocacy or did not understand their rights.
population: Patients detained under section 2 or 3 whose rights or capacity record shows they could not decide about IMHA help. Exclude patients discharged within 7 days.
sample: 30–40 eligible patients from the last 6 months across adult and older adult wards
data_source: Section 132 forms; capacity records; advocacy referral log (from the advocacy provider); nursing notes

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Set up an automatic ('opt-out') IMHA referral: the Mental Health Act office emails the advocacy provider for every patient whose rights form records lack of capacity.
reaudit: Wk 13–14, same sample size, same template
close_loop: Present to the Mental Health Act governance committee and the advocacy provider's contract review; if it works, write the opt-out step into the rights procedure.
evidence: [3049] High-dependency rehabilitation unit: Mental Health Act documentation compliance 77% → 98% (committee, PDSA cycles, self-audit)
[3474] Cygnet Churchill wards: Triangle of Care compliance 68–87% → 100% (carer leads, communication forms, logs)
[3399] Drug and alcohol outreach referrals: completeness improved on all items after an auto-reply referral form
pitfalls: Capacity for advocacy is rarely recorded as such → accept 'did not understand rights' as the trigger and define it before cycle 1.
The advocacy provider keeps its own records → ask them for a referral list for the audit period.
Older adult and learning disability wards may have few cases → pool across wards.
Concern that opt-out referral breaches consent → the Code allows it for patients who lack capacity; confirm with the Mental Health Act lead.
pearls: Invite the advocacy service manager to the planning meeting; they often want this data.
Use the Mental Health Act office as the single point that sends referrals.
Include older adult wards, where lack of capacity is most common.
Add the referral date to the rights tracker so it is checked every month.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients
pass_short: IMHA referral or visit documented within 7 days of lack of capacity record

question: What proportion of section 17 leave authorisations have a documented copy given to the patient?
why: Leave audits in the library look at leave risk discussion and leave status in admission plans [3204] [3568]; whether patients receive a copy of their leave form has not been audited.

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 27.22
standard.wording: Copies of the authorisation should be given to the patient and to any carers, professionals and other people in the community who need to know. A copy should also be kept in the patient's notes.

pass: The leave form or notes record that a copy was given to the patient (or offered and declined).
population: New or changed section 17 leave authorisations on adult acute, rehabilitation and forensic wards. Exclude leave to another hospital for physical care.
sample: 40 consecutive leave authorisations over the last 2 months
data_source: Section 17 leave forms (electronic or scanned); nursing notes

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'copy given to patient: yes/declined' box and a patient signature line to the section 17 form, completed by the nurse who explains the leave.
reaudit: Wk 13–14, 40 consecutive authorisations, same template
close_loop: Present to the Mental Health Act governance committee and ward managers; if it works, make the box a required field on the trust form.
evidence: [3568] NHS Tayside out-of-hours admissions: leave status documented 1.9% → 65.5% (posters)
[3204] Tees, Esk and Wear Valleys: leave risk discussion 73% → 100%
[3049] Rehabilitation unit: Mental Health Act documentation 77% → 98% (PDSA cycles, nurse self-audit)
pitfalls: Copies are given but not recorded → the new box makes it visible; do not count cycle 1 as bad practice without explanation.
Forms are scanned late → check the ward folder as well as the electronic record.
Responsible clinicians change forms often → count each new authorisation as one case.
Staff worry patients will lose the form → offer a copy kept in the patient's room or locker.
pearls: Recruit the Mental Health Act administrator and one ward manager.
Agree that 'offered and declined' counts as a pass.
Ask responsible clinicians to hand the form to the named nurse straight after the ward round.
Add the item to the existing Mental Health Act office spot checks.
effort: ~15 min per 10 forms
pass_short: Copy of leave authorisation given to patient, or offered and declined

question: What proportion of people brought to the section 136 place of safety are seen by both the doctor and the AMHP within 3 hours of arrival?
why: One single-cycle s136 audit used a 4-hour local target (60% met) [3635]; another found slow documentation [3420]; no closed-loop audit uses the Code's 3-hour standard.

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 16.47
standard.wording: Assessment by the doctor and AMHP should begin as soon as possible after the arrival of the individual at the place of safety. In cases where there are no clinical grounds to delay assessment, it is good practice for the doctor and AMHP to attend within three hours; this is in accordance with best practice recommendations made by the Royal College of Psychiatrists.

pass: Both the doctor and the approved mental health professional (AMHP) attended within 3 hours of arrival, or a clinical reason for delay (for example, intoxication) is recorded.
population: All adults detained under section 136 and brought to the health-based place of safety. Exclude people moved to the emergency department for physical care before assessment.
sample: 40 consecutive s136 detentions (usually 1–2 months in a typical suite)
data_source: Section 136 monitoring form; place of safety log; AMHP records

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Send an automatic page to both the section 12 doctor rota and the AMHP hub when the place of safety records arrival, with a 2-hour escalation to the on-call consultant.
target: ≥80% within 3 hours or with a recorded reason
reaudit: Wk 13–14, 40 consecutive detentions, same template
close_loop: Present at the joint s136 multi-agency group (police, AMHP service, trust); if it works, add the 3-hour rate to the s136 quarterly report.
evidence: [3635] Wakefield s136 suite: 60% assessed within 4 hours, 90% within 12 hours (single cycle)
[3420] Doncaster s136 assessments: documentation took over 1 day in 61% (single cycle)
[3526] District general liaison team: one-hour breaches 33% → 45.5% after a proforma change alone (breach coding without extra staffing)
pitfalls: The AMHP service is run by the local authority → involve the AMHP lead from the start; they own half of the target.
Arrival time is recorded differently by police and staff → use the place of safety log time only.
Intoxicated patients inflate breaches → record the clinical reason and report both rates.
Staffing shortages at night → split results by in-hours and out-of-hours to target the fix.
pearls: Get the s136 multi-agency meeting to sign off the audit in advance.
Record the reason for each breach using fixed codes.
Keep the escalation rule simple: 2 hours without a doctor or AMHP means a call to the consultant.
Hand the monthly rate to the place of safety manager.
effort: ~15 min per 10 detentions

question: What proportion of adults with anorexia nervosa who have been underweight for 2 years have had a bone density scan considered?
why: Eating disorder audits in the library cover referral data and physical risk recording [3229] [3306]; bone health in anorexia nervosa has not been audited.

standard.source: NICE NG69 Eating disorders: recognition and treatment, rec 1.10.15 (2017, updated 2020)
standard.wording: Consider a bone mineral density scan: after 1 year of underweight in children and young people, or earlier if they have bone pain or recurrent fractures; after 2 years of underweight in adults, or earlier if they have bone pain or recurrent fractures.

pass: A bone density (DXA) scan has been done or requested, or the notes record a decision not to scan with a reason.
population: Adults on the eating disorder service caseload with anorexia nervosa and 2 years or more of underweight. For CAMHS, use 1 year.
sample: 30–40 eligible patients from the caseload
data_source: Eating disorder service record; radiology system; GP letters

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'bone health: DXA due/done/decided against' line to the eating disorder annual review template.
reaudit: Wk 13–14, same caseload, same template
close_loop: Present at the eating disorder service governance meeting; if it works, keep the template line and share with the GP shared-care guide.
evidence: [3229] West Glasgow CAMHS: height and weight on referrals 73.1% → 82.1% (screening and weekly physical health clinic)
[3306] South Lanarkshire CAMHS: weight change recording 40% → 80%
[3534] Prospect Park memory clinic: complete bloods in proforma referrals 80% (proforma)
pitfalls: Duration of underweight hard to find → accept the date of first recorded low BMI.
DXA requested by GP or endocrinology → search radiology and GP letters.
'Consider' is soft wording → the pass counts a reasoned decision either way.
Few patients in adult services → include CAMHS with the 1-year rule.
pearls: Recruit the service's physical health lead or dietitian.
Agree the underweight definition before cycle 1.
Explain results to patients as NG69 advises.
Keep the template line to maintain the change.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients
pass_short: Bone density scan done or requested, or decision not to scan with reason

question: What proportion of people newly diagnosed with dementia by the memory service have a named care coordinator recorded in the diagnosis letter?
why: Memory service audits in the library cover diagnosis recording, referral bloods and post-diagnosis information [3367] [3534] [3279]; a named coordinator after diagnosis has not been audited.

standard.source: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support, rec 1.3.1 (2018)
standard.wording: Provide people living with dementia with a single named health or social care professional who is responsible for coordinating their care.

pass: The diagnosis letter (to the person and GP) names one professional, with contact details, who coordinates care.
population: People newly diagnosed with dementia by the memory service. Exclude people discharged to a care home with an existing coordinator.
sample: 40 consecutive new diagnoses over the last 3 months
data_source: Memory service record; diagnosis letters to the person and GP

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a required 'your named care coordinator' box with name and phone number to the diagnosis letter template.
reaudit: Wk 13–14, 40 consecutive diagnoses, same template
close_loop: Present at the older adult services governance meeting; if it works, keep the letter box and share with local dementia adviser services.
evidence: [3274] Betsi Cadwaladr letters: care coordinator details 8.3% → 54.3% (template with headings and teaching)
[3279] Tees older adult teams: carer's assessment offered 26% → 18% (action plans without a template change)
[3534] Prospect Park memory clinic: complete bloods 11.9% → 80% in proforma referrals (proforma)
pitfalls: Services discharge to GP after diagnosis → the GP or dementia adviser can be the named person; agree this before cycle 1.
Letters have a team phone number only → a team number without a name is a fail.
Dementia adviser services run by charities → include them as coordinators.
Letter templates owned by admin staff → involve the admin lead.
pearls: Recruit the memory service lead nurse.
Check both the patient and GP letters.
Use the dementia adviser service as the default coordinator where available.
Make the box mandatory in the template.
effort: ~10 min per 10 letters
pass_short: Diagnosis letter names one care coordinator with contact details

question: What proportion of people with bipolar disorder discharged from secondary care to their GP have a crisis plan with early warning signs in the discharge letter?
why: Bipolar audits in the library focus on lithium and valproate monitoring; the content of discharge-to-GP plans has only been examined for relapse signatures in older adults on depots (39.7%) [3430].

standard.source: NICE CG185 Bipolar disorder: assessment and management, rec 1.9.4 (2014, updated 2025)
standard.wording: When making transfer arrangements for a return to primary care, agree a care plan with the person, which includes: ... a crisis plan indicating early warning symptoms and triggers of both mania and depression relapse and preferred response during relapse, including liaison and referral pathways ... Give the person and their GP a copy of the plan, and encourage the person to share it with their carers.

pass: The discharge letter or attached plan lists early warning signs and triggers for both mania and depression, and says how to re-refer.
population: Adults with bipolar disorder discharged from community mental health teams to GP care. Exclude deaths and moves out of area.
sample: 30–40 consecutive discharges over the last 6 months
data_source: Discharge letters; care plans; electronic record

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a bipolar crisis plan section (mania signs, depression signs, triggers, how to re-refer) to the community discharge letter template.
reaudit: Wk 13–14, 30–40 discharges, same template
close_loop: Present at the community teams' governance meeting and to the local GP forum; if it works, keep the template section.
evidence: [3430] Black Country older adult depot audit: crisis plan in care plan 89.7%, relapse signature 39.7%
[3274] Betsi Cadwaladr GP letters: follow-up plan 80.2% → 98.6% (template with headings)
[3168] Mid Essex ECT: key items 0–5% → 100% (discharge summary template)
pitfalls: Plans exist in care plans but not in letters → the pass is in the letter sent to the GP.
Warning signs written for one pole only → require both.
Few discharges → pool teams over 6 months.
Template changes need IT time → start with a Word template if needed.
pearls: Recruit a consultant and a care coordinator from one team.
Ask a GP for feedback on the new section.
Reuse the relapse signature from the care plan.
Keep the section in the letter template.
effort: ~15 min per 10 letters
pass_short: Discharge letter lists early warning signs for mania and depression and how to re-refer

question: What proportion of people in out-of-area rehabilitation placements have had placement reviews at 3 months and then every 6 months?
why: Rehabilitation audits in the library focus on medicines management and physical health [3049] [3621]; reviews of out-of-area placements have not been audited.

standard.source: NICE NG181 Rehabilitation for adults with complex psychosis, rec 1.5.13 (2020)
standard.wording: A designated care manager (or 'out-of-area placement review officer') based within the community mental health rehabilitation team, should review the person's placement after the first 3 months and then every 6 months, to ensure it still meets their needs.

pass: Documented placement reviews at 3 months (±4 weeks) after placement and then at intervals of no more than 6 months.
population: Adults with complex psychosis in out-of-area rehabilitation placements funded by the trust or commissioner for at least 3 months.
sample: All current out-of-area placements (usually 20–40)
data_source: Placement tracker; community rehabilitation team record; review reports

template.note: Local code only; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse and present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Set up a shared out-of-area placement tracker with review due dates that flags overdue reviews to the rehabilitation team manager each month.
reaudit: Wk 13–14 (or 6 months), same cohort, same template
close_loop: Present to the rehabilitation service and commissioners; if it works, keep the tracker as the placement review register.
evidence: [3657] Pennine Care community team: high-dose antipsychotic compliance 60.6% → 77% (register with scheduled reviews)
[3049] High-dependency rehabilitation unit: Mental Health Act compliance 77% → 98% (PDSA cycles)
[3474] Rehabilitation and acute wards: Triangle of Care compliance 87% → 100% (carer leads and logs)
pitfalls: Placements managed by commissioners → agree data sharing before cycle 1.
Reviews done by phone and not written → ask for review reports.
Small numbers → include all current placements.
No designated reviewer → name one as part of the change.
pearls: Recruit the rehabilitation consultant and the placement commissioner.
Use the tracker to show time spent out of area.
Share results with families.
Keep the tracker with the team manager.
effort: ~20 min per 10 placements
pass_short: Placement reviews at 3 months, then at least every 6 months

question: What proportion of infants younger than 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher seen by the paediatric team have all four NICE first-line investigations (full blood count, blood culture, CRP and urine test)?
why: Febrile young infants are high risk, and missed urine samples are the commonest gap in the screen. The library holds only a registry entry on consultant sign-off for febrile infants [451] and one ED sepsis audit [3007]; no closed-loop audit of the NG143 under-3-month screen has been published.

standard.source: NICE NG143 rec 1.5.3 (2019, updated 2021)
standard.wording: Perform the following investigations in infants younger than 3 months with fever: full blood count blood culture C-reactive protein urine testing for urinary tract infection (see the sections on urine collection, preservation and testing in the NICE guideline on urinary tract infection in under 16s) chest X-ray only if respiratory signs are present stool culture, if diarrhoea is present. [2013]

pass: FBC, blood culture, CRP and a urine sample sent for testing, all documented within the index attendance (before discharge or within 4 hours of paediatric review).
population: Infants aged 0–89 days with a recorded temperature ≥38°C at triage or on the ward, assessed by paediatrics. Exclude transfers already fully investigated elsewhere.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible infants over the last 6 months (use ED/PAU coding for fever plus age filter).
data_source: ED/PAU attendance record for age and temperature; pathology system for FBC, CRP, blood culture and urine sample time stamps; clerking notes for reasons for omission.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Pass criterion; note method in next field

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'febrile infant under 3 months' order set to the EPR (FBC, CRP, blood culture, urine MC&S in one click) and a matching sticker for the PAU clerking proforma.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible infants, same template.
close_loop: Present at the paediatric audit meeting and ED–paediatric interface meeting. If compliance rises, make the order set default for any ED triage entry of age <90 days with temperature ≥38°C.
evidence: [3007] paediatric severe sepsis in ED: blood cultures, lactate and timing gaps at baseline (no second cycle reported)
[1517] arthroplasty analgesia: electronic order set 0% → 58% full protocol compliance (order set works)
[3242] psychiatry admissions: checklist of required investigations 53% → 94% ECG, bloods to 100% (checklist works)
pitfalls: Urine not obtained before antibiotics in sick infants → record 'attempted, not obtained' separately so the team is not penalised for correct treatment-first care.
Parent-reported fever without a measured temperature → decide before cycle 1 whether to include (NG143 treats parental report as valid); keep the same rule in cycle 2.
Tests sent but sample rejected or clotted → count as sent, and report rejection rate as a secondary finding.
Order set bypassed by locum staff → build it into the triage prompt, not just the paediatric menu.
pearls: Recruit an ED paediatric nurse lead; most omissions happen before the paediatrician arrives.
Agree with the lab that urine from under-3-month infants is always cultured, not just dipped.
Run a weekly list from ED triage of age <90 days to capture cases as they happen.
Hand the order set and audit spreadsheet to the next rotation's audit lead at changeover.
effort: ~25 min per 10 infants from EPR and pathology
pass_short: FBC, blood culture, CRP and urine test all sent during the attendance

question: What proportion of children under 5 with fever and at least one amber feature who are discharged without a diagnosis receive a documented safety net?
why: Discharged children with amber features are the group NICE flags for re-presentation risk. Safety-netting advice is the weakest item in discharge audits elsewhere (14–45% [2860][2817]); no paediatric fever safety-net audit has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG143 rec 1.5.25 (2019, updated 2021)
standard.wording: If it is decided that a child does not need to be admitted to hospital, but no diagnosis has been reached, provide a safety net for parents and carers if any 'red' or 'amber' features are present. The safety net should be 1 or more of the following: providing the parent or carer with verbal and/or written information on warning symptoms and how further healthcare can be accessed (see the recommendation on advising parents or carers in the section on advice for home care) arranging further follow-up at a specified time and place liaising with other healthcare professionals, including out-of-hours providers, to ensure direct access for the child if further assessment is required. [2007]

pass: Notes record at least one of: written fever leaflet given (named), verbal warning symptoms listed, a specified review time and place, or open access arranged.
population: Children aged 3 months to 5 years discharged from ED or PAU with fever, at least one amber traffic-light feature recorded, and no definitive diagnosis. Exclude admissions.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible discharges over the last 3 months.
data_source: ED/PAU record (triage observations, traffic-light features), discharge section of clinical notes, discharge letter.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Pass criterion: any of the four

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'safety net given' field with the four NICE options to the ED/PAU discharge screen, linked to printing the Trust fever leaflet.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible discharges, same template.
close_loop: Present at the ED–paediatric governance meeting. If it works, keep the mandatory field and add the leaflet to the PAU discharge pack.
evidence: [2860] colorectal discharge summaries: proforma raised safety-netting 14% → 32% (template helps, not enough alone)
[2643] paediatric post-tonsillectomy discharge: one-click inserts 'go to ED if bleed' 21% → 93% (template snippets work)
[2817] hernia discharge leaflet: safety-netting 45% at baseline; standard leaflet cut GP and ED re-attendance
pitfalls: Amber features not recorded at all → report traffic-light completion as a secondary measure; do not guess features.
Verbal advice given but not written down → the fix makes the record quick; accept a tick plus leaflet name as evidence.
Staff see a mandatory field as box-ticking → pair it with the printed leaflet so the tick produces something for the family.
Seasonal case mix changes between cycles → compare like-for-like months where possible.
pearls: Recruit the ED paediatric consultant and the PAU nurse lead before cycle 1.
Use the Trust or regional fever leaflet already approved; do not write a new one.
Check re-attendance within 7 days as a balancing measure.
Include translated leaflet versions to cover families with limited English.
effort: ~20 min per 10 children from ED record
pass_short: At least one safety-netting measure documented in the notes

question: What proportion of infants aged 6 weeks and over with bronchiolitis and no underlying condition are started on supplemental oxygen only when saturations are persistently below 90%?
why: NICE lowered the oxygen threshold from 92% to 90% in 2021 to cut oxygen use and length of stay. Oxygen prescribing is poor in children's wards [2952][524]; no audit of the 2021 bronchiolitis threshold has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG9 rec 1.4.4 (2015, updated 2021)
standard.wording: Give oxygen supplementation to babies and children with bronchiolitis if their oxygen saturation is: persistently less than 90%, for children aged 6 weeks and over persistently less than 92%, for babies under 6 weeks or children of any age with underlying health conditions. [2021]

pass: Oxygen started only after documented saturations persistently <90% in air (for this group); or no oxygen given where saturations stayed ≥90%.
population: Infants and children aged 6 weeks to 2 years admitted with bronchiolitis. Exclude those under 6 weeks, those with chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease, neuromuscular disease or immunodeficiency, and those needing CPAP or high-flow at arrival.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible admissions during the current bronchiolitis season.
data_source: Observation chart or PEWS record (SpO2 trend), drug chart/oxygen prescription, nursing notes.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Pass criterion: persistently <90% before start, or no oxygen when ≥90%

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Print the NG9 thresholds (90% / 92%) in the oxygen section of the paediatric drug chart or EPR oxygen order, with target range pre-set to 90–94% for this group.
reaudit: Wk 13–14 (same season, or first 40 admissions of next season), same template.
close_loop: Present at the paediatric audit meeting and nursing forum. If it works, fix the target range into the bronchiolitis admission order set.
evidence: [2952] children's hospital oxygen prescribing: 0/14 prescribed → 4/18 after chart with an oxygen section (chart change alone modest)
[524] oxygen prescription for children on the ward (re-audit) registered in the library
[452] high-flow oxygen weaning with stickers: prompt-based weaning in paediatric wards
pitfalls: Saturations recorded only after oxygen started → use the triage and first ward readings; mark 'unknown' rather than guess.
Night-time dips and probe artefact → define 'persistent' before cycle 1 (for example 2 readings 15 minutes apart).
Nurses worry about lower targets → share the NICE 2021 rationale and the trial data on readmission.
Small numbers outside winter → collect over the season peak.
pearls: Recruit the ward sister and a respiratory nurse; nurses start and wean oxygen.
Record length of stay and readmission within 7 days as balancing measures.
Agree the 'underlying condition' exclusion list at the start.
Keep the chart change in the winter surge plan so it survives rotation.
effort: ~20 min per 10 infants from observation charts
pass_short: Oxygen only started when saturations persistently below 90% in air

question: What proportion of infants admitted with bronchiolitis receive none of the treatments NICE advises against (antibiotics, salbutamol, nebulised adrenaline, hypertonic saline, ipratropium, montelukast or steroids)?
why: Bronchodilators and antibiotics are still given in bronchiolitis despite no benefit. The library has paediatric antibiotic-guideline audits [2970][2950] but no audit of low-value drug use in bronchiolitis.

standard.source: NICE NG9 rec 1.4.3 (2015, updated 2021)
standard.wording: Do not use any of the following to treat bronchiolitis in babies or children: antibiotics hypertonic saline adrenaline (nebulised) salbutamol montelukast ipratropium bromide systemic or inhaled corticosteroids a combination of systemic corticosteroids and nebulised adrenaline. [2015]

pass: No listed drug given for bronchiolitis during the admission; antibiotics given for a documented separate indication (for example proven UTI, pneumonia with focal signs) count as a pass.
population: Children under 2 years admitted with a primary diagnosis of bronchiolitis. Exclude PICU transfers and those with a documented alternative diagnosis (viral-induced wheeze, pneumonia).
sample: 40 consecutive admissions this bronchiolitis season.
data_source: Drug chart / EPMA administration records; admission and ward-round notes for indication.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a bronchiolitis admission order set in EPMA that contains only supportive care, with a pop-up alert if salbutamol, adrenaline nebs or steroids are prescribed for a patient with bronchiolitis coded.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 admissions in the same season, same template.
close_loop: Present at the paediatric audit and antimicrobial stewardship meetings. If it works, keep the order set and report monthly with the winter dashboard.
evidence: [2970] tertiary paediatric start-smart: weekly feedback and handover discussion raised guideline compliance median 30% → 100%
[2835] pre-operative tests: digital decision aid cut unnecessary tests by 20–75% (decision support reduces low-value care)
[2950] paediatric empiric anti-infective guideline adherence 98% (antibiotic choice audited, not bronchiolitis use)
pitfalls: Trial of salbutamol in older infants with wheeze → agree before cycle 1 whether a documented single trial in over-12-month infants counts as a fail; keep the rule fixed.
Diagnosis coded as bronchiolitis but clinically viral wheeze → exclude only if the notes state the alternative diagnosis.
ED doses before admission → include ED drug records, as that is where most doses are given.
Pop-up fatigue → alert only on the listed drugs, not all nebulisers.
pearls: Include the ED team; most salbutamol is given before the ward.
Share each case of a listed drug with the prescriber anonymously in feedback.
Pair with a parent leaflet explaining why inhalers are not used.
Report results with the winter pressures data so managers see the length-of-stay link.
effort: ~15 min per 10 children from EPMA
pass_short: No listed drug given for bronchiolitis, unless antibiotics for a separate documented indication

question: What proportion of children and young people treated for diabetic ketoacidosis have their intravenous insulin infusion started 1 to 2 hours after intravenous fluids began?
why: Starting insulin too early is linked with cerebral oedema; NICE sets a 1–2 hour gap and no insulin bolus. The only DKA entry in the library tests junior doctor knowledge [2184]; no audit of actual DKA fluid and insulin timing in children has been published.

standard.source: NICE NG18 rec 1.4.36 and 1.4.37 (2015, updated 2023)
standard.wording: Start an intravenous insulin infusion 1 to 2 hours after beginning intravenous fluid therapy in children and young people with DKA. If a child or young person with DKA is using an insulin pump, disconnect the pump when starting intravenous insulin therapy. [2015] ... When treating DKA with intravenous insulin in children and young people, use a soluble insulin infusion at a dosage between 0.05 units/kg/hour and 0.1 units/kg/hour. Do not give bolus doses of intravenous insulin. [2015]

pass: Insulin infusion start time is 60–120 minutes after the first IV fluid start time, at 0.05–0.1 units/kg/hour, with no IV insulin bolus.
population: Children and young people under 18 treated with IV fluids and IV insulin for DKA (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L with ketones). Exclude those transferred in after insulin was started elsewhere.
sample: All eligible episodes over the last 24 months (typically 20–40 in a district general hospital).
data_source: DKA integrated care pathway/fluid chart for fluid start time; EPMA or infusion chart for insulin start time and rate; blood gas record for severity.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Pass criterion: 60–120 min, 0.05–0.1 units/kg/hr, no bolus

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect (24-month retrospective); Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–24 embed; Wk 25–26 re-audit all episodes since the change
change: Build the BSPED DKA calculator output into a pre-printed or EPR DKA pathway with a timed box: 'IV fluids started at __ : __ ; insulin not before __ : __ (60 min) and by __ : __ (120 min)'.
reaudit: Wk 25–26: all DKA episodes since the change (minimum 10), same template; extend to 12 months if fewer.
close_loop: Present at the paediatric diabetes MDT and paediatric governance. If it works, keep the timed box in the pathway and add DKA timing to the NPDA local dashboard.
evidence: [2184] junior doctor DKA knowledge: correct initial fluid choice 55.5%, cerebral oedema management 33.3%; teaching sessions in cycle 2
[3542] psychiatry MDT notes: co-designed structured template 0–15% → 100% completion (template works)
[1517] arthroplasty analgesia: electronic order set 0% → 58% protocol compliance
pitfalls: Small numbers → use 24 months retrospectively and report counts, not only percentages.
Fluid start time missing (ED bolus not timed) → take the first recorded IV fluid time from ED notes; mark 'unknown' if absent.
ED and ward teams blame each other → include both in the feedback and the change.
Pump users not disconnected → record as a secondary item, not a pass criterion.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric diabetes nurse specialist as co-lead; they see every DKA case.
Use the BSPED calculator print-out as the data sheet; it already has times.
Case-review any episode with cerebral oedema alongside the audit.
Leave a simple case log so the next trainee can re-audit without searching coding.
effort: ~30 min per case from pathway and EPMA
pass_short: Insulin infusion started 60 to 120 minutes after IV fluids, no bolus

question: What proportion of children and young people recovering from diabetic ketoacidosis receive their first subcutaneous insulin dose at least 30 minutes before the intravenous insulin is stopped?
why: Stopping IV insulin before subcutaneous insulin is working causes rebound ketosis and longer stays. No audit of the DKA transition step in children has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG18 rec 1.4.44 and 1.4.45 (2015, updated 2023)
standard.wording: Start subcutaneous insulin in a child or young person with DKA at least 30 minutes before stopping intravenous insulin. [2015] ... For a child or young person with DKA who is using an insulin pump, restart the pump at least 60 minutes before stopping intravenous insulin. Change the insulin cartridge and infusion set and insert the cannula into a new subcutaneous site. [2015]

pass: Subcutaneous injection given ≥30 minutes (or pump restarted ≥60 minutes) before the IV insulin stop time.
population: Children and young people under 18 treated with IV insulin for DKA who transferred to subcutaneous insulin or pump in hospital. Exclude transfers out before transition.
sample: All eligible episodes over the last 24 months.
data_source: EPMA/insulin infusion chart (stop time), subcutaneous insulin administration record, pump documentation in nursing notes.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Pass criterion: ≥30 min injections, ≥60 min pump

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect (24-month retrospective); Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–24 embed; Wk 25–26 re-audit all episodes since the change
change: Add a 'transition to subcutaneous insulin' step to the DKA pathway with fields for SC dose time and a 'stop IV insulin at (SC time + 30 min)' box signed by the nurse.
reaudit: Wk 25–26: all episodes since the change, same template.
close_loop: Present at the paediatric diabetes MDT. If it works, keep the pathway step and add it to nurse induction for the children's ward.
evidence: [2184] junior doctor DKA knowledge gaps in initial management (knowledge audit only)
[3362] lithium clinic proforma: safety-netting and monitoring items rose to 92–100% (proforma works)
[3242] admission checklist: ECG 59% → 94% (checklist of timed steps works)
pitfalls: Stop time of IV insulin not recorded → use the infusion chart end time; mark unknown if missing.
Transition timed with a meal and done out of hours by agency staff → include the step in the nursing section, not only medical notes.
Pump users managed by family → record the time the family restarted the pump.
Small numbers → report counts and each failure as a case story.
pearls: The diabetes nurse specialist is the natural co-lead.
Link to the fluid–insulin timing audit so one data pass covers both.
Ask the ward pharmacist to check overlap on the EPMA at the ward round.
Store the case list in the diabetes team folder for the next cycle.
effort: ~20 min per case
pass_short: Subcutaneous insulin given at least 30 minutes before IV insulin stopped

question: What proportion of babies started on antibiotics for suspected neonatal infection receive the first dose within 1 hour of the decision to treat?
why: Delay to first antibiotic is a common safety finding on postnatal wards and neonatal units. The library has neonatal antibiotic dosing audits [2959][2960] but none measuring time from decision to first dose.

standard.source: NICE NG195 rec 1.15.2 (2021, updated 2026)
standard.wording: If a baby needs antibiotic treatment, give this as soon as possible and always within 1 hour of the decision to treat. [2021]

pass: Documented administration time of the first antibiotic dose is ≤60 minutes after the documented decision (or prescription) time.
population: Babies up to 28 days started on IV antibiotics for suspected early- or late-onset infection on the neonatal unit, transitional care or postnatal ward.
sample: 40 consecutive courses over the last 2 months.
data_source: Neonatal EPR (BadgerNet) or medical notes for decision time; EPMA/drug chart for prescription and administration times.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Use prescription time if decision time not written

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Introduce a neonatal 'sepsis grab bag' (cannula, culture bottle, pre-calculated benzylpenicillin and gentamicin dose card) and a 'decision time' field on the neonatal antibiotic prescription.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive courses, same template.
close_loop: Present at the perinatal governance meeting with midwifery. If it works, stock grab bags on every postnatal ward and add time-to-antibiotic to the unit dashboard.
evidence: [1583] open fractures: tracking and feedback of antibiotic timing improved order and administration within 1 hour
[2656] acute abdomen pathway: antibiotics within 1 hour 80% → 50% after pathway update alone (pathway without logistics fails)
[2960] neonatal gentamicin errors: 67% linked to calculation complexity; simplified dosing and monograph examples
pitfalls: Decision time not recorded → agree to use prescription time; note it underestimates delay.
Postnatal ward babies wait for a neonatal doctor to cannulate → capture cause of delay to target the right fix.
Babies on the NNU skew results → report postnatal ward and NNU separately.
Grab bags not restocked → assign a named band 5 nurse per shift.
pearls: Co-lead with a neonatal nurse or ANNP; they give most first doses.
Run a 'mock sepsis' drill on the postnatal ward in week 4.
Display monthly median time on the NNU safety board.
Agree grab-bag restocking with pharmacy before launch.
effort: ~20 min per 10 babies from neonatal EPR
pass_short: First antibiotic dose given within 60 minutes of decision to treat

question: What proportion of babies started on antibiotics for risk factors or possible early-onset infection have antibiotics stopped at 36 hours when the NICE stopping criteria are met?
why: Unneeded courses keep mothers and babies in hospital and drive resistance. Neonatal antibiotic audits in the library cover NEC regimens and drug levels [2981][2959]; none measure stopping at 36 hours.

standard.source: NICE NG195 rec 1.21.3 (2012, amended 2026)
standard.wording: For babies who are being treated with intravenous antibiotics because of risk factors for early-onset infection or clinical indicators of possible infection, stop antibiotics at 36 hours if: the blood culture is negative and the initial clinical suspicion of infection was not strong and the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no clinical indicators of possible infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset infection) and the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring. [2012, amended 2026]

pass: In babies meeting all four stopping criteria, the last antibiotic dose is given within 36 hours (allow up to 40 hours) of the first dose.
population: Babies started on IV antibiotics within 72 hours of birth for suspected early-onset infection. Exclude positive blood cultures, strong initial suspicion documented, and babies with ongoing clinical indicators at 36 hours.
sample: 50 consecutive courses over the last 3 months (expect 30–40 to meet stopping criteria).
data_source: EPMA for dose times; microbiology system for culture result time; neonatal EPR for clinical review and CRP.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 36-hour review prompt to the neonatal antibiotic prescription (EPMA stop date set at 36 hours for early-onset regimens, needing a documented reason to extend).
target: ≥90% stopped by 36 hours when criteria met
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 50 consecutive courses, same template.
close_loop: Present at the neonatal and antimicrobial stewardship meetings. If it works, keep the default stop date and report length of stay for these babies.

'Strong suspicion' is subjective → agree a local definition (for example red flag or two or more non-red-flag indicators) before cycle 1.
CRP repeat taken late → record CRP timing as a secondary item.
Seniors override the stop date → reasons are captured; review them at the stewardship meeting.
pearls: Recruit the neonatal pharmacist and a microbiologist.
Use the Kaiser or local EOS calculator result as a secondary descriptor, not a pass criterion.
Report bed-days saved; it wins management support.
Keep the stop-date default in the EPMA build, so it survives rotation.
effort: ~20 min per 10 courses from EPMA
pass_short: Antibiotics stopped within 36 hours of first dose when all four criteria met

question: What proportion of eligible babies born at 35 weeks or later on antibiotics beyond 36 hours are switched to oral amoxicillin when the 2026 NICE criteria are met?
why: NICE added an IV-to-oral switch for early-onset infection in 2026; units have not yet measured uptake. The paediatric IV-to-oral audit in the library [2999] covers older children, not neonates.

standard.wording: For babies born from 35+0 weeks' gestation with negative blood culture who need antibiotics for more than 36 hours because the initial clinical suspicion of infection was strong, consider switching treatment from intravenous to oral antibiotics at 36 hours or thereafter to complete the course (up to 7 days of antibiotics in total) if: the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no current clinical indicators of ongoing infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection) and the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring and the baby is tolerating oral feeds. [2026] ... Use amoxicillin as the oral antibiotic, unless local bacterial resistance data indicates the need for a different antibiotic. [2026]

pass: Eligible baby either switched to oral amoxicillin within 24 hours of meeting all criteria, or has a documented senior reason for staying on IV.
population: Babies ≥35+0 weeks, blood culture negative, continuing antibiotics beyond 36 hours for strong initial suspicion, clinically well, CRP reassuring and feeding orally. Exclude meningitis, positive cultures and babies under 35 weeks.
sample: 30 consecutive eligible babies over the last 6 months (screen all courses >36 hours).
data_source: EPMA (route and drug changes), neonatal EPR (senior review, feeding), microbiology and CRP results.

question: What proportion of babies having a lumbar puncture for suspected infection have a blood glucose measured immediately before the procedure?

standard.wording: Measure blood glucose in babies immediately before lumbar puncture, so that the cerebrospinal fluid to blood glucose ratio can be calculated. [2024]

pass: Blood glucose (point-of-care or lab) recorded within 30 minutes before the LP time.
population: Babies up to 28 days corrected age having an LP for suspected infection on the neonatal unit, postnatal ward, children's ward or ED.
sample: 40 consecutive LPs over the last 6 months (use CSF lab requests to find cases).
data_source: Lab system (CSF sample time, CSF glucose); blood gas/POCT glucose record; procedure note.

change: Add 'blood glucose immediately before LP: __ mmol/L at __:__' to the LP procedure sticker or EPR procedure note, and add a paired-glucose item to the LP trolley checklist.

question: What proportion of babies with jaundice noticed in the first 24 hours of life have a serum bilirubin measured within 2 hours?
why: Jaundice in the first day is pathological until proven otherwise. The library records a 6-hour bilirubin audit for older babies [145] and ED triage gaps [278]; no audit of the 2-hour standard for early jaundice has been published.

standard.source: NICE CG98 rec 1.2.10 and 1.2.12 (2010, updated 2023)
standard.wording: In all babies with suspected or obvious jaundice in the first 24 hours of life, measure and record the serum bilirubin level urgently (within 2 hours). [2010] ... Arrange a referral to ensure that an urgent medical review is conducted (as soon as possible and within 6 hours) for babies with suspected or obvious jaundice in the first 24 hours of life to exclude pathological causes of jaundice. [2010]

pass: Serum bilirubin sample time ≤2 hours after the first documented observation of jaundice.
population: Babies with jaundice first documented at under 24 hours of age on postnatal ward, transitional care or neonatal unit.
sample: 40 consecutive babies over the last 6 months (search bilirubin requests at age <24 hours plus midwifery notes).
data_source: Midwifery/postnatal notes (time jaundice first noted); pathology system (sample time); medical notes (review time).

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add an 'early jaundice (<24 h)' escalation box to the postnatal NEWTT chart that triggers a same-hour bilirubin request and neonatal review call, with the time recorded.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 babies (extend window if needed), same template.

question: What proportion of babies seen for prolonged jaundice have the full NICE screen, including a conjugated bilirubin?
why: Prolonged jaundice clinics exist to catch biliary atresia early, and missing a conjugated bilirubin defeats that purpose. No audit of prolonged jaundice screening has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG98 rec 1.7.1 (2010, amended 2023)
standard.wording: In babies with a gestational age of 37 weeks or more with jaundice lasting more than 14 days, and in babies with a gestational age of less than 37 weeks and jaundice lasting more than 21 days: look for pale chalky stools and/or dark urine that stains the nappy measure the conjugated bilirubin carry out a full blood count carry out a blood group determination (mother and baby) and DAT (Coombs' test). Interpret the result taking account of the strength of reaction, and whether mother received prophylactic anti‑D immunoglobulin during pregnancy consider a urine culture if there is clinical suspicion of a urinary tract infection ensure that routine metabolic screening (including screening for congenital hypothyroidism) has been performed. [2010, amended 2023]

pass: Stool and urine colour documented, conjugated bilirubin, FBC, blood group and DAT done, and newborn blood spot result confirmed, at the first prolonged jaundice visit.
population: Babies referred to the prolonged jaundice clinic or ward attender service (term >14 days, preterm >21 days).
sample: 40 consecutive babies over the last 3 months.
data_source: Prolonged jaundice clinic proforma or letter; pathology system; child health record for blood spot result.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 babies, same template.
close_loop: Present at the neonatal/paediatric audit meeting. If it works, adopt the proforma for midwife- and GP-referred babies too.

Blood spot result not visible to hospital staff → agree access to the child health record before cycle 1.
Babies seen by midwives in the community → include only hospital clinic attendances in both cycles.
DAT not needed in some units' local policy → keep to NICE and note any agreed local variation.
pearls: Include a stool colour card; it doubles as parent education.
Recruit the clinic nurse or phlebotomist who runs the session.
Track time to specialist referral for any conjugated bilirubin >25 µmol/L.
Keep the proforma in the clinic template library, not a personal folder.
effort: ~15 min per 10 babies
pass_short: Full NICE prolonged jaundice screen done at first visit, including conjugated bilirubin

question: What proportion of babies born at or before 30 weeks' gestation start caffeine citrate before 3 days of age?

standard.wording: Use caffeine citrate routinely in preterm babies born at or before 30 weeks, starting it as early as possible and ideally before 3 days of age.

pass: First caffeine citrate dose given before 72 hours of age.
population: Babies born at ≤30+6 weeks admitted to the unit within 24 hours of birth. Exclude babies who died or were transferred out before 72 hours.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible babies over the last 12 months (use BadgerNet gestation filter).
data_source: BadgerNet/neonatal EPR for gestation and birth time; EPMA for first caffeine dose time.

pass_short: First caffeine citrate dose before 72 hours of age

question: What proportion of preterm babies on supplemental oxygen have a documented target saturation range of 91–95%?
why: Both high and low saturations harm preterm babies; NICE sets 91–95%. Oxygen prescribing is poor across children's wards [2952], and no neonatal target-range audit has been published in the library.

standard.wording: After initial stabilisation, aim for an oxygen saturation of 91% to 95% in preterm babies.

population: Preterm babies (<37 weeks at birth, <44 weeks corrected) receiving supplemental oxygen or respiratory support on the audit day.
sample: Point-prevalence on 10 separate days over 2 weeks (aim for 40 baby-days).
data_source: Bedside observation chart, oxygen prescription in EPMA, monitor alarm limit check at the cot side (recorded by the auditor).

question: What proportion of babies under 6 months with a first urinary tract infection that responds to treatment have a urinary tract ultrasound within 6 weeks?
why: Ultrasound finds obstruction and reflux-related scarring in young infants; follow-up imaging is easily lost after discharge. The library lists one registry entry on UTI in under 16s [453] and no published closed-loop audit of imaging.

standard.wording: Send babies younger than 6 months with first-time UTI that responds to treatment for ultrasound within 6 weeks of the UTI, as outlined in table 4. [2007]

pass: Renal tract ultrasound performed (not just requested) within 42 days of the positive urine sample; for atypical UTI, ultrasound during the acute illness.
population: Babies aged under 6 months with a culture-confirmed first UTI managed by paediatrics. Exclude known renal anomalies already under follow-up.
sample: 40 consecutive babies over the last 12 months (microbiology positive urine cultures filtered by age).
data_source: Microbiology system (culture date, organism); PACS/RIS (ultrasound request and scan dates); discharge letter.

standard.wording: Evaluate people after a first suspected seizure with a 12-lead ECG to help identify cardiac-related conditions that could mimic an epileptic seizure. [2022]

population: Girls under 18 prescribed valproate for any indication by the paediatric service (including those not yet menstruating, per MHRA).
sample: All eligible girls on the paediatric caseload (typically 10–30); census on one date.
data_source: Pharmacy/EPMA and clinic prescribing lists; scanned ARAF in the EPR; clinic letters.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
If started or first review after Jan 2024

timeline: Wk 1–2 census; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 set up register; Wk 5–12 review all overdue patients; Wk 13–14 repeat census
change: Set up a paediatric valproate register held by the epilepsy nurse with ARAF due dates and an automatic clinic booking 1 month before expiry.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: repeat census of all girls on valproate, same template.
