question: What proportion of women had a documented venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk assessment at their antenatal booking appointment?
why: VTE remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in the UK, and a documented early risk assessment is the foundation of thromboprophylaxis decisions; no closed-loop audit of booking VTE risk assessment completion is in the library.

standard.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37a, Reducing the Risk of Venous Thromboembolism during Pregnancy and the Puerperium (April 2015, amended 2023), Executive summary of recommendations
standard.wording: All women should undergo a documented assessment of risk factors for VTE in early pregnancy or prepregnancy.

pass: A structured VTE risk assessment (using the local or national scoring tool) is completed and documented in the notes at the booking appointment
population: Inclusion: all women booking for antenatal care. Exclusion: women booking after 20 weeks whose first contact was an emergency admission.
sample: 40 consecutive women at their booking appointment over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Antenatal booking proforma/electronic maternity record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make the structured VTE risk assessment tool a mandatory, non-skippable section of the electronic booking proforma.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity governance and thrombosis committee meeting; if compliant, extend mandatory reassessment fields to hospital admission during pregnancy
pitfalls: Booking appointments are sometimes done by different staff groups (GP, community midwife) with different systems → confirm which system captures the assessment before cycle 1
Risk assessment done verbally but not documented → count only documented assessments as compliant
Missing risk factors (e.g. undocumented BMI or family history) can make the assessment incomplete even if a form was started → check completeness, not just presence of a form
Women booking late or via unbooked emergency attendance are hard to capture → report this group separately
Improvement fading if the mandatory field can be bypassed → confirm the EPR build genuinely blocks completion of booking without it
pearls: Involve the maternity thrombosis lead midwife/obstetrician as co-investigator
Use the RCOG/local VTE risk assessment tool your unit has already adopted, for consistency
Cross-check a sample of high-risk women to confirm the resulting thromboprophylaxis plan was actually carried out
Present findings alongside MBRRACE-UK data on VTE as a leading cause of direct maternal death, to support engagement
Keep the same risk assessment tool and definition of 'booking' at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the booking record
pass_short: Structured VTE risk assessment documented at the booking appointment

question: What proportion of women having a vaginal birth had a systematic perineal examination, including a digital rectal examination, documented before perineal suturing?
why: Undiagnosed obstetric anal sphincter injury causes long-term incontinence; systematic examination including a rectal examination is a core element of the national OASI care bundle, but is not consistently documented; no closed-loop audit of this specific step is in the library (perineal repair pain relief is separately audited [NNA-205, NNA-206]).

standard.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 29, The Management of Third- and Fourth-Degree Perineal Tears (2015)
standard.wording: All women having a vaginal delivery are at risk of sustaining OASIS or isolated rectal buttonhole tears. They should therefore be examined systematically, including a digital rectal examination, to assess the severity of damage, particularly prior to suturing.

pass: The perineal examination record documents a systematic assessment including a digital rectal examination, completed before suturing began
population: Inclusion: all women having a vaginal birth with any degree of perineal trauma. Exclusion: women with an intact perineum and no trauma.
sample: 40 consecutive vaginal births with perineal trauma over the last 4-6 weeks
data_source: Perineal repair record/electronic birth record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Redesign the perineal repair record as a structured proforma with a mandatory digital rectal examination tick box that must be completed before the suturing section can be signed.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the OASI care bundle/maternity governance meeting; if compliant, roll the proforma out to the midwifery-led unit
pitfalls: Rectal examination may be performed but not documented → accept only documented examination as compliant; consider a spot-check with the woman's consent if under-recording is suspected
Junior staff may be uncomfortable performing or documenting a rectal examination → provide OASI care bundle training and supervision
Free-text notes may describe the tear without confirming a rectal examination was done → use a structured tick-box proforma rather than free text
Under-recognition of OASI, not just under-documentation, is the real risk → track third/fourth-degree tear detection rates alongside documentation compliance
Improvement fading without embedding in training → include the proforma in annual perineal repair skills updates
pearls: Base the audit on the national OASI care bundle project methodology so results are comparable with other units
Involve the OASI care bundle champion or perineal trauma lead as co-investigator
Use simulation training (perineal repair mannequins) to reinforce the systematic examination technique
Track OASI detection rate as a linked outcome measure alongside documentation compliance
Keep the same tear degree categories and examiner grade field at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 births from the perineal repair record
pass_short: Systematic perineal examination including digital rectal examination documented before suturing

question: Of instrumental vaginal births with a mediolateral episiotomy, what proportion had the episiotomy angle documented as approximately 60 degrees from the midline at the time of distension?
why: An episiotomy cut too close to the midline increases the risk of extension into the anal sphincter; angle documentation is a core OASI care bundle element but is inconsistently recorded; no closed-loop audit of episiotomy angle documentation is in the library.

standard.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 29, The Management of Third- and Fourth-Degree Perineal Tears (2015)
standard.wording: Where episiotomy is indicated, the mediolateral technique is recommended, with careful attention to ensure that the angle is 60 degrees away from the midline when the perineum is distended.

pass: The birth record documents that a mediolateral episiotomy was performed and states the angle achieved (or confirms the 60-degree technique was used) at the time of distension
population: Inclusion: all instrumental vaginal births (forceps or ventouse) with an episiotomy. Exclusion: spontaneous vaginal births without instrumental delivery.
sample: 40 consecutive instrumental births with episiotomy over the last 6-8 weeks
data_source: Birth record/instrumental delivery proforma
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce an episiotomy angle guide (a single-use disposable protractor/angle indicator) at every instrumental birth, with a mandatory 'angle achieved' field on the instrumental birth proforma.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the OASI care bundle meeting; if compliant, extend the angle guide to spontaneous births requiring episiotomy
pitfalls: Angle is difficult to measure precisely in a fast-moving birth → accept a disposable angle-guide indicator mark as a reasonable proxy for documentation
Only the mediolateral technique should be counted; midline episiotomy carries a higher OASI risk and should be flagged separately → record technique type explicitly
Junior obstetric and midwifery staff performing episiotomies may lack confidence with angle guides → provide simulation training before roll-out
Retrospective note review may only capture 'episiotomy performed' without angle detail → introduce the field prospectively for cycle 2
Improvement fading if angle guides run out of stock → confirm reliable procurement before wider roll-out
pearls: Use the same OASI care bundle framework and champion as the rectal-examination audit above, since they share a data collection visit
Pilot the angle guide with a small group of obstetricians and senior midwives first
Track OASI rate alongside angle-guide use as the outcome measure
Share results with the local perineal trauma multidisciplinary meeting
Keep the same technique and angle definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 births from the instrumental delivery proforma
pass_short: Episiotomy angle of approximately 60 degrees documented at distension

question: What proportion of women presenting with reduced fetal movements after 26 weeks had fetal heart rate auscultation, symphysis-fundal height/growth review and a fetal heart rate assessment (CTG) all completed and documented at that presentation, in line with the national RFM checklist?
why: Unrecognised or poorly managed reduced fetal movements (RFM) is a recurring contributory factor in avoidable stillbirth identified by MBRRACE-UK; no closed-loop audit of full RFM checklist completion is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 3, 'Suggested checklist for the management of reduced fetal movements (RFM)' (2023)
standard.wording: 2. Act: Auscultate fetal heart (hand-held Doppler/Pinnard) to confirm fetal viability. Assess fetal growth by reviewing growth chart, perform SFH if not performed within last 2 weeks (if not on an ultrasound surveillance pathway already). Perform CTG to assess fetal heart rate in accordance with national guidelines (ideally computerised CTG should be used).

pass: At the RFM presentation, fetal heart rate auscultation, a fundal height/growth review (or confirmation of an existing surveillance scan within 2 weeks) and a CTG are all documented as completed
population: Inclusion: all women presenting to triage or the day assessment unit with reduced fetal movements after 26 weeks. Exclusion: women presenting in established labour.
sample: 40 consecutive women presenting with reduced fetal movements over the last 4-6 weeks
data_source: Triage/day assessment unit RFM record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a structured RFM triage proforma based on the national Ask-Act-Advise checklist, with all three Act steps as mandatory fields before the assessment can be closed.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity safety champions meeting; if compliant, embed the proforma as the standard triage RFM pathway
pitfalls: RFM presentations are often managed hastily on a busy triage shift → make the proforma the fastest route, not an extra step, by pre-populating fields from the booking record
Recurrent RFM (which carries higher risk) may not be flagged if previous episodes are not cross-referenced → build a search of previous RFM presentations into the proforma
Growth chart review is sometimes skipped if a scan was 'recent' without checking the exact date → require the date of the last scan to be entered
Staff unfamiliar with the national checklist → provide short RFM update training before cycle 1
Improvement fading without an EPR-embedded proforma → build the checklist into the triage EPR template, not a paper insert
pearls: Base the audit directly on the NHS England SBLCB v3 checklist so it aligns with national reporting
Involve the maternity safety champion and RFM/stillbirth prevention lead as co-investigators
Track induction of labour and caesarean birth rates alongside compliance to watch for unintended over-intervention
Use anonymised MBRRACE-UK case summaries in training to explain the rationale
Keep the same first/recurrent RFM definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 presentations from the triage record
pass_short: Heart rate auscultation, growth review and CTG all documented at the presentation

question: Of pregnant women identified as smokers and referred for tobacco dependence treatment, what proportion were contacted within 1 working day and seen face-to-face by a tobacco dependence adviser within 5 working days of referral?
why: Rapid opt-out referral to tobacco dependence treatment is central to reducing smoking in pregnancy, but referral-to-contact timeliness is not routinely tracked; no closed-loop audit of this specific timeliness standard is in the library (CO testing itself is already audited [NNA-195]).

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 1 implementation guidance, 'Opt-out referral pathways' (2023)
standard.wording: Immediate referral and consultation with the tobacco dependence adviser is the ideal, but as a minimum the woman should be contacted within 1 working day and seen (ideally face-to-face) by a TDA within 5 working days.

pass: The woman is contacted by the tobacco dependence service within 1 working day of referral and seen face-to-face within 5 working days
population: Inclusion: all pregnant women with an opt-out referral to the in-house tobacco dependence treatment service. Exclusion: women who self-refer outside the opt-out pathway.
sample: 40 consecutive opt-out tobacco dependence referrals over the last 8-12 weeks
data_source: Tobacco dependence service referral and contact log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set up an automatic same-day electronic referral from the maternity CO-testing record straight into the tobacco dependence adviser's worklist, replacing any manual fax or paper referral step.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity smoking in pregnancy steering group; if compliant, use the electronic referral pathway as the trust standard
pitfalls: Referral date and contact date are sometimes recorded in different systems → agree a single source of truth (the tobacco dependence service log) before cycle 1
Working days versus calendar days can be miscounted around weekends and bank holidays → define clearly and apply consistently
Women who decline contact should not be miscounted as a service delay → record 'declined contact' as a distinct outcome
Small tobacco dependence adviser team capacity may be the real bottleneck → report capacity alongside timeliness data to inform service planning
Improvement fading if referrals revert to a manual process → confirm the electronic referral route is the permanent default
pearls: Involve the tobacco dependence adviser team directly, since they hold the contact log
Benchmark local performance against the Maternity Services Dashboard smoking metrics
Track quit-date setting and 4-week quit rates alongside timeliness as a linked outcome
Present results at the local Smoking in Pregnancy Challenge Group network meeting for benchmarking
Keep the same working-day definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 referrals from the tobacco dependence service log
pass_short: Contacted within 1 working day and seen face to face within 5 working days

question: What proportion of women had a fetal growth restriction (FGR) risk assessment completed by 14 weeks' gestation, using a validated digital blood pressure monitor for the blood pressure component?
why: Early, structured FGR risk assessment determines the surveillance pathway a woman is offered; digital blood pressure measurement was newly mandated in the 2023 care bundle update, and no closed-loop audit of this combined standard is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 2, interventions 2.4 and 2.6 (2023)
standard.wording: 2.4 Perform a risk assessment for FGR by 14 weeks gestation using an agreed pathway (for example, Appendix D). ... 2.6 As part of the risk assessment for FGR, blood pressure should be recorded using a digital monitor that has been [validated for use in pregnancy].

pass: The FGR risk assessment is documented as completed by 14+0 weeks' gestation, and the blood pressure recorded as part of it was measured on a validated digital monitor
population: Inclusion: all women booked for antenatal care who reach 14 weeks under the unit's care. Exclusion: women booking after 14 weeks.
sample: 40 consecutive women who reached 14 weeks' gestation over the last 6-8 weeks
data_source: Antenatal booking and risk assessment record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make the FGR risk assessment pathway a mandatory field in the electronic booking record with a due-date prompt at 14 weeks, and replace remaining manual sphygmomanometers in booking clinics with validated digital monitors.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity safety champions meeting; if compliant, report ongoing compliance through the Maternity Services Dashboard
pitfalls: Booking sometimes happens after 14 weeks, making the deadline unachievable for some women → report late bookers separately, not as non-compliance
Non-validated manual sphygmomanometers may still be in use in some clinic rooms → audit equipment as well as documentation
Risk assessment pathway/tool varies locally → confirm which tool (for example, a locally agreed algorithm per Appendix D of the care bundle) is in use before cycle 1
Community midwives booking women may use a different system from the hospital → include both settings in the sample
Improvement fading if old equipment is not fully withdrawn → remove non-validated monitors from clinical areas, not just add new ones
pearls: Involve the fetal growth surveillance/screening lead midwife as co-investigator
Audit equipment (monitor validation status) at the same time as the notes review
Use the care bundle's own process indicators for benchmarking against national data
Link with community midwifery teams early since much of this assessment happens outside hospital
Keep the same risk assessment pathway and 14-week deadline definition at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the booking record
pass_short: FGR risk assessment completed by 14+0 weeks using a validated digital blood pressure monitor

question: What proportion of midwives and obstetricians providing intrapartum care had up-to-date annual training and competency assessment in intermittent auscultation and electronic fetal monitoring?
why: Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK repeatedly cite gaps in fetal monitoring training as a contributory factor in avoidable harm; no closed-loop audit of annual fetal monitoring training completion is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 4, intervention 4.1 (2023)
standard.wording: All staff who care for women in labour are required to undertake annual training and competency assessment on knowledge and skills required for effective fetal monitoring via Intermittent auscultation (IA) [Midwives] and electronic fetal monitoring [Midwives and Obstetricians].

pass: The staff member has a documented, in-date (within the last 12 months) fetal monitoring training and competency assessment record
population: Inclusion: all midwives and obstetricians who provide intrapartum care, including bank/agency and locum staff. Exclusion: staff on long-term leave for the full audit period.
sample: All midwives and obstetricians providing intrapartum care on the unit at the time of the audit (or 40 consecutive staff records if the unit is very large)
data_source: Trust training/learning management system records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set up an automatic training system alert to staff and their line manager 6 weeks before their fetal monitoring training expires, and block rostering onto the labour ward for staff more than 4 weeks overdue.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternity education and governance meeting; if compliant, use the alert system as the trust-wide model for other mandatory training
pitfalls: Bank, agency and locum staff are hardest to track and often missed by the trust's own training system → include a specific check for these staff groups at ward entry
Training completion recorded but competency assessment (a separate step) not done → audit both fields, not just attendance
Staff on leave (maternity, sickness) may appear overdue through no fault of their own → exclude or flag separately
Different training records systems for medical and midwifery staff can under- or double-count → reconcile both systems before reporting
Improvement fading without automatic alerts → confirm the alert system, not just a spreadsheet, is doing the tracking
pearls: Involve the practice development midwife/fetal monitoring lead and medical education lead as co-investigators
Use existing trust training system reports as the primary data source to avoid duplicate data entry
Report compliance by staff group so gaps (for example, obstetric trainees rotating in) are visible
Link training compliance data to the unit's Each Baby Counts and SBLCB v3 annual submission
Keep the same 12-month in-date definition at re-audit
effort: ~10 min per 10 staff records from the training system
pass_short: Documented fetal monitoring training and competency assessment within the last 12 months

question: What proportion of women with pre-existing diabetes had an HbA1c measured at the start of the third trimester, with a documented increased-surveillance plan if the result was above 48 mmol/mol?
why: Women with type 1 and type 2 diabetes continue to have persistently high perinatal mortality; third-trimester HbA1c monitoring with escalation is a new 2023 care bundle standard with no closed-loop audit yet in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 6, intervention 6.4 (2023)
standard.wording: Women with diabetes should have an HbA1c measured at the start of the third trimester and those with an HbA1c above 48mmol/mmol should be offered increased surveillance including additional diabetes nurse/dietetic support, more frequent face to face review and input from their named, specialist Consultant to plan ongoing care and timing of birth decisions.

pass: An HbA1c is recorded at 28+0 to 28+6 weeks (start of third trimester), and if above 48 mmol/mol, an increased-surveillance plan is documented
population: Inclusion: all women with pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes under joint diabetes-obstetric care. Exclusion: women diagnosed with gestational diabetes only.
sample: 30 consecutive women with pre-existing diabetes reaching the third trimester over the last 3-6 months
data_source: Joint diabetes antenatal clinic record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic HbA1c order and a due-date prompt at 28 weeks to the joint diabetes antenatal clinic pathway, with a mandatory 'surveillance plan' field triggered when the result exceeds 48 mmol/mol.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint diabetes-obstetric MDT and the National Pregnancy in Diabetes (NPID) audit review meeting; if compliant, submit the improved pathway as evidence to the NPID audit
pitfalls: Women with diabetes are a relatively small cohort per unit → extend the collection period to 3-6 months to reach an adequate sample
HbA1c may be requested but the result not reviewed or acted on → audit the surveillance plan, not just the blood test being done
Joint clinic records may be split between diabetes and obstetric systems → check both before concluding non-compliance
Definition of 'increased surveillance' varies between clinicians → agree a minimum data set (extra visit booked, dietitian/diabetes nurse referral, named consultant documented) before cycle 1
Improvement fading without an automatic order → build the 28-week HbA1c into the standard order set, not a manual reminder
pearls: Involve the joint diabetes antenatal clinic team (diabetes consultant, specialist nurse, dietitian) as co-investigators
Submit results to the National Pregnancy in Diabetes (NPID) audit for external benchmarking
Use the multidisciplinary joint clinic list as the sampling frame to minimise missed cases
Present findings against the unit's overall SBLCB v3 element 6 compliance
Keep the same 48 mmol/mol threshold and 28-week timing at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the joint diabetes clinic record
pass_short: HbA1c recorded at 28+0 to 28+6 weeks, with surveillance plan if above 48

question: What proportion of babies born before 34 weeks' gestation had their first temperature recorded between 36.5 and 37.5 degrees Celsius, measured within one hour of birth?
why: Neonatal hypothermia after preterm birth increases the risk of death and morbidity; normothermia is a scored element of the national perinatal optimisation pathway but is not yet separately audited in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 5, Normothermia (2023)
standard.wording: Babies born at less than 37 weeks gestational age should have a first temperature which is both between 36.5–37.5°C and measured within one hour of birth. Neonatal normothermia can have benefits for all babies.

pass: The baby's first recorded temperature is between 36.5 and 37.5 degrees Celsius and was measured within 1 hour of birth
population: Inclusion: all babies born before 34 weeks' gestation. Exclusion: stillbirths, babies who died before a temperature could be recorded.
sample: 30 consecutive babies born before 34 weeks over the last 6 months
data_source: Neonatal admission record/delivery room resuscitation record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a preterm delivery normothermia bundle (pre-warmed delivery room, polythene wrap/hat, transwarmer mattress) as a standard checklist item for every birth under 34 weeks, based on the BAPM normothermia toolkit.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the neonatal/perinatal optimisation pathway meeting; if compliant, report through the National Neonatal Audit Programme (NNAP) normothermia measure
pitfalls: Very preterm births are relatively infrequent → extend the collection period to 6 months and use network-level data if the unit's numbers are too small
Temperature taken later than 1 hour may be recorded without the delay being obvious → record both the time and the value
Emergency preterm births may not allow time for the full normothermia bundle to be prepared → record whether the birth was planned or emergency and compare
Different thermometers/sites (axillary vs other) can give inconsistent readings → standardise the measurement method across the unit
Improvement fading without embedding → make the normothermia bundle a standing item on the preterm birth checklist, not a one-off initiative
pearls: Base the change directly on the BAPM normothermia toolkit for a ready-made implementation package
Involve neonatal nursing staff and the labour ward as joint owners, since both are responsible for temperature control
Benchmark against National Neonatal Audit Programme (NNAP) data
Link this audit to the wider perinatal optimisation pathway compliance metric in the care bundle
Keep the same gestation cut-off and timing definition at re-audit
effort: ~10 min per 10 babies from the neonatal admission record
pass_short: First temperature between 36.5 and 37.5 degrees, measured within 1 hour of birth

question: What proportion of babies born before 34 weeks' gestation received their own mother's milk within 24 hours of birth?
why: Early maternal breast milk reduces necrotising enterocolitis and late-onset sepsis in preterm babies; this is a scored perinatal optimisation pathway element with no closed-loop audit yet in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 5, Early maternal breast milk (2023)
standard.wording: Babies born below 37 weeks gestational age should receive their own mother's milk, ideally within 6 hours, but aiming always within 24 hours of birth (except in rare situations where there are contraindications to MBM). Perinatal teams should work together to ensure consistent delivery of antenatal advice about MBM, with support (equipment, education, help) for mothers to express within two hours of birth.

pass: The baby receives their own mother's milk within 24 hours of birth, and the mother was supported to start expressing within 2 hours of birth, unless a documented contraindication exists
population: Inclusion: all babies born before 34 weeks' gestation. Exclusion: babies with a documented contraindication to maternal breast milk, stillbirths.
sample: 30 consecutive babies born before 34 weeks over the last 6 months
data_source: Neonatal unit feeding record/postnatal record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Ensure a breast pump, expressing consumables and written/verbal expressing support are available at the mother's bedside within 2 hours of a preterm birth, prompted by a checklist item on the neonatal admission pathway.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the neonatal/infant feeding governance meeting; if compliant, report through the perinatal optimisation pathway compliance metric
pitfalls: Mothers recovering from caesarean birth or illness may be physically unable to express within 2 hours → record and report this separately from equipment or support failures
Milk expressed but not given to the baby promptly (e.g. delayed transport to neonatal unit) → capture both expressing time and administration time
Equipment availability (pumps, kits) at night or on a busy unit can be a genuine bottleneck → audit equipment availability alongside documentation
Small numbers of very preterm births → extend the collection period to 6 months
Improvement fading without embedding → make expressing support a standing item on the preterm admission checklist
pearls: Involve the infant feeding lead and neonatal nursing team as co-investigators
Use the BAPM maternal breast milk toolkit for a ready-made implementation package
Track necrotising enterocolitis and late-onset sepsis rates as linked longer-term outcome measures
Ensure postnatal ward and neonatal unit protocols are aligned so support does not stop at transfer
Keep the same 24-hour and 2-hour definitions at re-audit
effort: ~10 min per 10 babies from the neonatal feeding record
pass_short: Baby received own mother's milk within 24 hours, and expressing started within 2 hours

question: What proportion of women presenting with suspected pre-eclampsia between 20 and 36+6 weeks had placental growth factor (PlGF)-based testing performed as part of their assessment?
why: PlGF-based testing helps rule out pre-eclampsia and speeds appropriate discharge or admission decisions; no closed-loop audit of PlGF testing uptake for suspected pre-eclampsia is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG133 Hypertension in pregnancy, rec 1.4.4 (2019)
standard.wording: Offer placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing to help rule out pre-eclampsia in women presenting with suspected pre-eclampsia (for example, with gestational hypertension) between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.

pass: PlGF-based testing is documented as performed (or a clear reason recorded for not performing it) at the assessment for suspected pre-eclampsia within the eligible gestation window
population: Inclusion: women assessed for suspected pre-eclampsia between 20+0 and 36+6 weeks. Exclusion: women with confirmed pre-eclampsia already on treatment, women outside the gestation window.
sample: 30 consecutive women assessed for suspected pre-eclampsia over the last 3 months
data_source: Maternal day assessment unit/triage record, laboratory results
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add PlGF-based testing as a default item on the suspected pre-eclampsia assessment order set in the maternal day assessment unit, alongside the standard bloods and urine protein tests.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternal medicine/obstetric governance meeting; if compliant, extend the order set to the antenatal day unit and triage
pitfalls: PlGF testing may not be available on-site out of hours → confirm laboratory turnaround and availability before setting the target
Clinicians unfamiliar with the test or its interpretation may default to not requesting it → provide a short interpretation guide alongside the order set
Cost or sample-handling requirements may cause under-use → involve the laboratory in planning capacity
Borderline gestations (just under 20 or over 36+6 weeks) can cause miscounting → apply the window strictly and record exact gestation
Improvement fading without an order-set default → embed the test as an automatic tick rather than a manual add-on
pearls: Involve the maternal medicine lead and laboratory point-of-care/biochemistry lead as co-investigators
Use the existing NICE diagnostics guidance on PlGF-based testing as supporting evidence for clinicians
Track time to discharge or admission decision as a linked outcome measure
Present early results to reassure staff about turnaround time before wider roll-out
Keep the same gestation window and definition of 'suspected pre-eclampsia' at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 assessments from the day unit record
pass_short: PlGF-based testing performed at assessment, or reason for not performing recorded

question: Of women with pre-eclampsia who had given birth and remained on antihypertensive treatment, what proportion had their blood pressure kept below 140/90 mmHg before discharge from postnatal care?
why: Uncontrolled postnatal hypertension after pre-eclampsia is a recognised cause of maternal harm, including postnatal eclampsia and stroke; no closed-loop audit of postnatal blood pressure control against the NICE target is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG133 Hypertension in pregnancy, postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment section, aim for women with pre-eclampsia after birth (2019)
standard.wording: aim to keep blood pressure lower than 140/90 mmHg

pass: The last blood pressure reading documented before discharge from postnatal inpatient care is below 140/90 mmHg, or, if not, a documented ongoing management plan is recorded
population: Inclusion: women with a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia in the current pregnancy who remain on antihypertensive treatment postnatally. Exclusion: women with chronic hypertension diagnosed before pregnancy managed under a separate pathway.
sample: 30 consecutive women with pre-eclampsia discharged from postnatal inpatient care over the last 3 months
data_source: Postnatal ward observation chart and discharge summary
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'discharge blood pressure below 140/90, or plan documented' field to the postnatal discharge checklist for women coded with pre-eclampsia.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the maternal medicine/obstetric governance meeting; if compliant, embed the field as a hard stop in the discharge workflow
pitfalls: Blood pressure can genuinely take days to settle after pre-eclampsia → discharge with a documented plan is an acceptable pass, not only an achieved target
Postnatal ward staff may not code pre-eclampsia consistently, making case-finding difficult → cross-check against the obstetric discharge summary and drug chart for antihypertensives
Early discharge (common practice) may mean the last reading in hospital is not representative → record whether community follow-up BP was also documented
Methyldopa should be changed to an alternative postnatally, which is a separate existing audit [NNA-194]; keep this audit focused on the BP target, not drug choice
Improvement fading without a mandatory field → build the check into the EPR discharge workflow
pearls: Involve the maternal medicine lead and postnatal ward matron as co-investigators
Cross-reference with the existing methyldopa-stopping audit [NNA-194] since both relate to postnatal hypertension management
Track readmission for hypertension/eclampsia as a linked outcome measure
Ensure community midwives and GPs receive a clear follow-up BP plan in the discharge letter
Keep the same 140/90 mmHg threshold at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the postnatal record
pass_short: Last blood pressure before discharge below 140/90 mmHg, or ongoing management plan documented

question: What proportion of women with a confirmed diagnosis of miscarriage were offered expectant management for 7 to 14 days as the first-line management strategy?
why: Expectant management avoids unnecessary medical or surgical intervention for miscarriage, but units often default to medical management; the library has audits on medical management drug regimens [NNA-209] but no audit of whether expectant management is offered first-line.

standard.source: NICE NG126 Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage, rec 1.10.1 (2019)
standard.wording: Use expectant management for 7 to 14 days as the first-line management strategy for women with a confirmed diagnosis of miscarriage.

pass: Expectant management for 7-14 days is documented as having been offered (and chosen, declined, or exceptions explained) before medical or surgical management is arranged
population: Inclusion: all women with a confirmed diagnosis of miscarriage seen in the early pregnancy assessment unit. Exclusion: women with the documented exceptions to expectant management listed in NG126 (for example, increased risk of haemorrhage or infection).
sample: 40 consecutive women with a confirmed miscarriage diagnosis over the last 6-8 weeks
data_source: Early pregnancy unit assessment record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Redesign the early pregnancy unit miscarriage counselling proforma so expectant management is listed and discussed first, with a mandatory field recording why it was not chosen if applicable.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the gynaecology/early pregnancy unit governance meeting; if compliant, review annually alongside miscarriage management outcome data
pitfalls: Women may express a preference for a quicker resolution, making 'not chosen' common even when correctly offered → audit whether it was offered, not just whether it was chosen
Documented exceptions (haemorrhage risk, infection risk) must be captured accurately, not assumed → require the specific exception to be named
Staff turnover and locum medical staff may be unfamiliar with the first-line recommendation → include in early pregnancy unit induction
Verbal counselling without documentation understates true practice → use a structured, tick-box proforma
Fading compliance without embedding → make the counselling proforma the standard document for every miscarriage consultation
pearls: Involve the early pregnancy unit lead nurse/sonographer as co-investigator
Provide women with a written information leaflet alongside verbal counselling to support informed choice
Track re-attendance and unplanned admission rates for each management option as a linked outcome
Share results with GPs who often see women in the days after miscarriage diagnosis
Keep the same definition of 'confirmed miscarriage' and exceptions list at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the early pregnancy unit record
pass_short: Expectant management for 7-14 days offered before medical or surgical management

question: Of women with an ectopic pregnancy treated with systemic methotrexate, what proportion had serum hCG measured on days 4 and 7 after treatment, with weekly measurement continued until a negative result?
why: Missed or delayed hCG follow-up after methotrexate treatment for ectopic pregnancy risks failing to detect treatment failure or rupture; no closed-loop audit of this specific follow-up schedule is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG126 Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage, rec 1.15.4 (2019)
standard.wording: For women with ectopic pregnancy who have had methotrexate, take 2 serum hCG measurements in the first week (days 4 and 7) after treatment and then 1 serum hCG measurement per week until a negative result is obtained. If hCG levels plateau or rise, reassess the woman's condition for further treatment.

pass: hCG is measured on both day 4 and day 7 after methotrexate, and weekly thereafter until a negative result, with a documented reassessment if levels plateau or rise
population: Inclusion: all women treated with systemic methotrexate for a tubal ectopic pregnancy. Exclusion: women converted to surgical management before the day 4 hCG.
sample: 20-30 consecutive women treated with methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy over the last 12 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Early pregnancy unit follow-up record and laboratory results
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Give every woman starting methotrexate a pre-printed follow-up appointment card with day 4, day 7 and subsequent weekly hCG dates filled in at the time of treatment, and add the same schedule as a recall task in the early pregnancy unit tracking system.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the early pregnancy unit governance meeting; if compliant, make the pre-printed follow-up schedule standard practice for every methotrexate treatment
pitfalls: Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy is relatively uncommon per unit → extend the collection period to 12 months
Women may have blood tests done at their GP practice, with results not always returned promptly to the early pregnancy unit → include a system to actively chase GP-taken bloods
Non-attendance for follow-up bloods is a genuine risk in this population → record non-attendance separately and have an escalation plan for women who do not attend
hCG plateau/rise noted but reassessment not documented → audit the action taken, not just the blood test being done
Fading compliance without a recall system → use an active tracking list, not reliance on the woman remembering appointments
pearls: Involve the early pregnancy unit nurse/coordinator who typically manages this follow-up
Use a dedicated methotrexate follow-up tracker (spreadsheet or EPR task list) to actively chase results
Give women a clear written safety-netting leaflet on symptoms of rupture to watch for between visits
Review any case of treatment failure or rupture at the departmental morbidity meeting to close the loop
Keep the same follow-up schedule definition at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per case from the early pregnancy unit record
pass_short: hCG measured on days 4 and 7 after methotrexate, then weekly until negative

question: Of women with heavy menstrual bleeding and no identified pathology, fibroids under 3cm, or suspected/diagnosed adenomyosis, what proportion were offered an LNG-IUS as the first treatment?
why: The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system is the recommended first-line treatment for most women with heavy menstrual bleeding, but non-hormonal or surgical options are often tried first; the library has an audit of FBC testing for HMB [NNA-212] but no audit of first-line treatment choice.

standard.source: NICE NG88 Heavy menstrual bleeding: assessment and management, rec 1.5.2 (2018)
standard.wording: Consider an LNG-IUS as the first treatment for HMB in women with: no identified pathology or fibroids less than 3 cm in diameter, which are not causing distortion of the uterine cavity or suspected or diagnosed adenomyosis.

pass: An LNG-IUS is documented as having been offered as the first treatment option, before any other pharmacological or surgical treatment was started, unless a reason for not offering it is recorded
population: Inclusion: women newly referred to gynaecology with heavy menstrual bleeding and no cavity-distorting pathology. Exclusion: women with fibroids of 3cm or more causing cavity distortion, endometrial pathology, or a contraindication to LNG-IUS documented at referral.
sample: 40 consecutive new HMB referrals meeting the eligibility criteria over the last 8-12 weeks
data_source: Gynaecology clinic letter/electronic outpatient record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an LNG-IUS 'offered/accepted/declined/not suitable (reason)' field as the first treatment option on the gynaecology HMB clinic letter template, positioned before other treatment options.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the gynaecology governance meeting; if compliant, extend the template to community gynaecology and GP referral pathways
pitfalls: Some women decline an LNG-IUS due to a previous poor experience or personal preference → count 'offered but declined' as compliant, distinct from 'not offered'
Clinic letters may describe a treatment plan without stating what was discussed first → use a structured template rather than free text
Insertion capacity/waiting times for LNG-IUS fitting may discourage clinicians from offering it → review fitting clinic capacity alongside the audit
GP referral letters may already state a treatment preference that anchors the gynaecology consultation → record whether the referral influenced the discussion
Fading compliance without a template change → build the field into the standard clinic letter, not a separate audit form
pearls: Involve a gynaecology consultant with a special interest in HMB as co-investigator
Provide a patient decision aid on HMB treatment options to support shared decision-making
Track LNG-IUS fitting waiting times as a linked service measure
Share results with GPs to support earlier community offering of LNG-IUS where appropriate
Keep the same eligibility criteria at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 referrals from the clinic letter
pass_short: LNG-IUS offered as first treatment, before other drug or surgical options

question: What proportion of people newly started on hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for menopause symptoms had a documented review at 3 months, with a further review at 12 months?
why: Structured review supports safe, effective long-term HRT use and catches ineffective treatment or side effects early; no closed-loop audit of the NICE-recommended HRT review schedule is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG23 Menopause: identification and management, rec 1.9.2 (2015)
standard.wording: Review each treatment for symptoms associated with menopause: at 3 months to assess efficacy and tolerability, annually thereafter, unless there are clinical indications for an earlier review (such as treatment ineffectiveness, side effects or adverse events).

pass: A documented review of efficacy and tolerability occurs at approximately 3 months after starting HRT, and again at approximately 12 months (or earlier if clinically indicated)
population: Inclusion: all patients newly started on HRT for menopause symptoms in general practice or the menopause clinic. Exclusion: patients who stopped HRT themselves before the 3-month review was due.
sample: 40 consecutive patients started on HRT over the last 12-15 months (allowing time for both reviews to fall due)
data_source: GP or menopause clinic electronic record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic recall task to the practice/clinic electronic record at 3 months and 12 months from the first HRT prescription, visible on the clinician's task list.
reaudit: At 15 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the practice/menopause clinic clinical governance meeting; if compliant, extend the recall system to all hormonal contraception and HRT prescribing
pitfalls: Patients started on HRT by different prescribers (GP, menopause clinic, private) may fall outside a single system's recall → clarify which service owns follow-up before cycle 1
Reviews done opportunistically (e.g. at an unrelated appointment) may not be labelled as an 'HRT review' → search consultation content, not just appointment type
Patients who stop HRT themselves and do not attend should not be counted as a missed review by the service → record and exclude these appropriately
The audit needs a run-in period of over a year to capture both reviews, delaying results → consider an interim analysis of 3-month reviews only while waiting for 12-month data
Fading compliance without an automatic recall → build the recall into the electronic record's task system, not a manual diary
pearls: Involve the practice's menopause lead GP or specialist nurse as co-investigator
Use a search of the electronic prescribing record to build an accurate cohort of new HRT starts
Record side effects and reasons for stopping at review to feed into future prescribing discussions
Consider running this alongside a wider menopause care quality improvement project
Keep the same 3-month and 12-month definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the GP/clinic record
pass_short: HRT reviewed at about 3 months and again at about 12 months

question: What proportion of women had a warm wet compress applied to the perineum from crowning until birth in the second stage of labour, where the birth was not in water?
why: A warm compress reduces the risk of obstetric anal sphincter injury, but its use is not routinely checked; the library audits perineal repair analgesia [NNA-205, NNA-206] but not this preventive intervention.

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, rec 1.9.13 (2023, amended 2025)
standard.wording: Once the presenting part distends the perineum in the second stage of labour, offer to apply a warm wet compress to the perineum and continue this until birth. Check the temperature of the compress is comfortable for the woman or pregnant person. Note, this recommendation does not apply to births in water.

pass: A warm wet compress is documented as offered and applied to the perineum from crowning until birth, for births not in water
population: Inclusion: all vaginal births not in water. Exclusion: waterbirths, births too precipitate for any intervention (documented).
sample: 40 consecutive vaginal births not in water over the last 4-6 weeks
data_source: Birth record/second stage record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Stock a warm compress kit (warming device, single-use pads) in every birth room and add a 'warm compress offered/applied' tick box to the second-stage section of the birth record.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the OASI care bundle/labour ward audit meeting; if compliant, review OASI rate as a linked outcome at 6 months
pitfalls: Compresses may be applied but not documented → add a simple tick box rather than relying on narrative notes
Equipment (compress warmers, single-use pads) may not be available in every room → audit equipment stocking alongside documentation
Precipitate births leave no time for a compress → record this as a distinct, acceptable exception
Staff unfamiliar with the 2023 update may not know this is now recommended → include in perineal care refresher training
Fading compliance if equipment runs out → add compress kits to the standard birth room stock list with a restocking check
pearls: Link this audit to the OASI care bundle programme and its existing champions
Trial the compress kit in one birth room before wider roll-out to solve practical issues
Track OASI rate over time alongside compress use as the outcome measure
Include the temperature-check step in training to ensure comfort and safety
Keep the same water-birth exclusion at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 births from the birth record
pass_short: Warm wet perineal compress applied from crowning until birth, except water births

question: When uterine hyperstimulation occurred during induction of labour, what proportion had a fetal assessment performed and any further induction medicines withheld, with vaginal pessaries or delivery systems removed where possible?
why: Uterine hyperstimulation during induction can cause fetal compromise if not promptly managed; no closed-loop audit of the NICE hyperstimulation management steps is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG207 Inducing labour, rec 1.7.1 (2008, amended 2021)
standard.wording: If uterine hyperstimulation occurs during induction of labour: carry out a fetal assessment, do not administer any more doses of medicines to induce labour and remove any vaginal pessaries or delivery systems if possible, consider tocolysis.

pass: All three steps (fetal assessment, no further induction doses given, pessary/delivery system removed where possible) are documented for every episode of hyperstimulation during induction
population: Inclusion: all women who had a documented episode of uterine hyperstimulation during induction of labour. Exclusion: hyperstimulation occurring during augmented (not induced) labour.
sample: All documented hyperstimulation episodes during induction over the last 6-12 months (or 20-30 consecutive episodes if the unit has a higher volume)
data_source: CTG trace annotations, drug chart, incident report
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'hyperstimulation response' sticker/proforma to the induction pathway documenting each of the three required steps, to be completed at the time of the event.
reaudit: At 6-12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward risk management meeting; if compliant, include the proforma in induction of labour training
pitfalls: Hyperstimulation is relatively infrequent, making case-finding important → use an incident/CTG database search rather than relying on staff recall
Emergency documentation under pressure may be incomplete → use a dedicated proforma rather than free text
Ambiguity about what counts as 'removing where possible' for a slow-release pessary already largely absorbed → record what was physically done and any limiting factors
Tocolysis use is a 'consider' recommendation, not mandatory, so should not be scored as a hard fail → record as a separate, non-mandatory field
Fading compliance without a structured proforma → embed the proforma in the induction pathway documentation set
pearls: Cross-reference incident reports and CTG categorisation logs to find all episodes
Involve the labour ward risk midwife/obstetrician as co-investigator
Use simulation training to rehearse the hyperstimulation response as a team
Present findings alongside outcome (mode of birth, neonatal outcome) for context
Keep the same three-step definition at re-audit
effort: ~20 min per episode from CTG and drug records
pass_short: Hyperstimulation: fetal assessment, no further induction doses, pessary or delivery system removed where possible

question: In babies with an acute fetal bradycardia (or a single prolonged deceleration of 3 minutes or more) that did not recover, what proportion were born within 9 minutes of the bradycardia being recognised, or had a documented reason for a longer interval?
why: An unresolved acute bradycardia is a time-critical fetal emergency; delayed recognition-to-birth intervals are a recurring theme in Each Baby Counts reports, but no closed-loop audit of this specific interval is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.5.9 (2017, amended 2022)
standard.wording: If there is an acute bradycardia, or a single prolonged deceleration for 3 minutes or more: ... expedite the birth if the acute bradycardia persists for 9 minutes, or less if there are significant antenatal or intrapartum risk factors for fetal compromise.

pass: The baby is born within 9 minutes of the acute bradycardia/prolonged deceleration being recognised, or a documented clinical reason for a longer interval is recorded
population: Inclusion: all babies with a documented acute bradycardia or single prolonged deceleration of 3 minutes or more that did not recover and led to expedited birth. Exclusion: bradycardia that resolved spontaneously without expedited birth.
sample: All such episodes over the last 12 months (or 20-30 consecutive episodes if the unit has a higher volume)
data_source: CTG trace, birth record, incident report/perinatal morbidity review
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a 'crash caesarean/instrumental birth' timer sheet, started automatically when an acute bradycardia is called, that is displayed in theatre/the birth room and reviewed at every case in the perinatal morbidity meeting.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present every case at the perinatal morbidity and mortality review meeting; if compliant, use the timer sheet as standard practice for all category 1 births
pitfalls: Recognition time is often reconstructed retrospectively and may be imprecise → use the CTG trace timestamp as the primary source where available
This is a rare, high-stakes event, so numbers will be small → review every case rather than a sample, and extend the collection period as needed
Blame-focused review can suppress honest reporting → use a just-culture, learning-focused review process
Genuine clinical reasons for delay (for example, maternal resuscitation first) must be captured accurately → require a documented reason field, not just a pass/fail
Fading attention after an initial cluster of cases → keep this as a standing perinatal morbidity meeting agenda item
pearls: Review every case at the perinatal morbidity meeting rather than sampling, given the rarity and severity
Use simulation and "obstetric emergency" drills (crash caesarean, category 1) to rehearse the target interval
Link outcome data (cord gases, Apgar, NNU admission) to each case for full context
Feed learning into the unit's Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK action plans
Keep the same definition of 'recognition time' and the 9-minute target at re-audit
effort: ~30 min per case from CTG trace and birth record
pass_short: Baby born within 9 minutes of recognised bradycardia, or reason for delay documented

question: Of women identified as high risk of preterm birth at booking, what proportion were referred to a preterm birth prevention pathway by 12 weeks and offered transvaginal cervical length scanning every 2-4 weeks between 16 and 24 weeks?
why: Timely referral and surveillance can allow preventive interventions such as cerclage or progesterone; no closed-loop audit of preterm birth prevention pathway referral and cervical scanning frequency is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 5, Appendix F risk assessment and management algorithm (2023)
standard.wording: 1. Referral to local or tertiary Preterm Prevention (PP) clinic by 12 weeks. ... 3. All pregnant women to be offered transvaginal cervix scanning every 2-4 weeks between 16 and 24 weeks as a secondary test to more accurately quantify the risk of preterm birth.

pass: A woman identified as high risk for preterm birth is referred to the preterm prevention pathway by 12 weeks, and transvaginal cervical scanning is offered at intervals of no more than 4 weeks between 16 and 24 weeks
population: Inclusion: women identified with a high-risk factor for preterm birth (for example, previous preterm birth, previous cervical cerclage) at booking. Exclusion: women who decline referral or scanning.
sample: 30 consecutive women identified as high risk for preterm birth over the last 6 months
data_source: Preterm birth prevention clinic record

template.note: e.g. cerclage, pessary, progesterone, none indicated

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic referral trigger to the preterm birth prevention clinic when a high-risk factor is coded at booking, with the clinic's own scheduling system generating each cervical scan appointment automatically.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the preterm birth prevention team/maternity governance meeting; if compliant, report through the SBLCB v3 element 5 process indicators
pitfalls: High-risk factors may not be consistently identified or coded at booking → audit booking risk-factor recognition as well as the downstream pathway
Clinic capacity constraints may limit scan frequency regardless of intent → report capacity alongside compliance
Women who move between services (community/tertiary) may have incomplete records in one place → check both if the woman was referred onward
Missed scans due to non-attendance should be recorded separately from scans not offered → capture both
Improvement fading without automation → use an automatic referral trigger rather than relying on staff to remember
pearls: Involve the preterm birth prevention clinic lead as co-investigator
Use the SBLCB v3 Appendix F risk assessment and management algorithm as the reference standard
Track preterm birth rate in this cohort over time as a linked outcome measure
Coordinate with community midwives who identify risk factors at booking
Keep the same risk factor list and scanning interval definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the preterm prevention clinic record
pass_short: High-risk women referred by 12 weeks, cervical scans at most 4-weekly from 16-24 weeks

question: What proportion of pregnant women with type 1 diabetes were offered real-time continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with appropriate education and support to use it?
why: Continuous glucose monitoring improves glycaemic control and neonatal outcomes in type 1 diabetes in pregnancy and is a new 2023 care bundle standard; no closed-loop audit of CGM offer completion is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 6, intervention 6.2 (2023)
standard.wording: Women with type 1 diabetes should be offered real time continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and be provided with appropriate education and support to use this.

pass: The woman with type 1 diabetes has a documented offer of real-time CGM, with education/support provided, recorded at or soon after the joint diabetes-antenatal booking
population: Inclusion: all pregnant women with type 1 diabetes under joint diabetes-antenatal care. Exclusion: women already established on CGM before pregnancy (record as already in place, not a new offer).
sample: 20-30 consecutive women with type 1 diabetes in pregnancy over the last 6-12 months
data_source: Joint diabetes antenatal clinic record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'CGM offered, education provided, outcome' field to the joint diabetes antenatal booking proforma for every woman with type 1 diabetes.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint diabetes-obstetric MDT; if compliant, submit as supporting evidence to the National Pregnancy in Diabetes (NPID) audit
pitfalls: CGM funding/access pathways vary and may cause delay unrelated to clinical practice → record whether the delay was clinical or logistic (funding, device supply)
Small numbers of type 1 diabetes pregnancies per unit → extend the audit period to 12 months
Education/support may be provided by diabetes specialist nurses outside the joint clinic record → check both diabetes and obstetric records
Some women decline CGM for personal reasons, which is appropriate and should not be scored as non-compliance → record 'offered and declined' as compliant with the offer
Fading compliance without a mandatory field → build the field into the joint clinic booking proforma
pearls: Involve the diabetes specialist nurse and joint antenatal diabetes clinic lead as co-investigators
Use the NPID audit's own data fields to align local and national reporting
Track glycaemic control (time in range) as a linked outcome measure where CGM is accepted
Ensure equitable access regardless of postcode or funding pathway complexity
Keep the same definitions of 'offered' and 'already in use' at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the joint diabetes clinic record
pass_short: Pregnant women with type 1 diabetes offered real-time CGM with education and support

question: Of women with a tubal ectopic pregnancy managed expectantly, what proportion met the NICE eligibility criteria (serum hCG of 1500 IU/L or less, size and symptoms criteria, and ability to return for follow-up) documented at the decision?
why: Expectant management outside the recommended hCG and clinical criteria risks a missed ruptured ectopic pregnancy; no closed-loop audit of expectant management eligibility documentation is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG126 Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage, rec 1.14.1 (2019)
standard.wording: have serum hCG levels of 1,000 IU/L or less ... are able to return for follow-up.

pass: The documented decision for expectant management records the serum hCG level and confirms it was 1,000 IU/L or less (or 1,000-1,500 IU/L under the extended criteria in rec 1.14.2), with confirmation the woman was able to return for follow-up
population: Inclusion: all women with a tubal ectopic pregnancy managed expectantly. Exclusion: women managed medically or surgically from the outset.
sample: 20-30 consecutive women managed expectantly for ectopic pregnancy over the last 12 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Early pregnancy unit assessment and decision record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a structured ectopic pregnancy management decision proforma into the early pregnancy unit record with the hCG threshold and follow-up criteria as mandatory fields before expectant management can be selected.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the early pregnancy unit/gynaecology governance meeting; if compliant, review any rupture or emergency admission cases at the departmental morbidity meeting
pitfalls: Ectopic pregnancy volumes are relatively low per unit → extend the collection period to 12 months
hCG result timing relative to the decision may be unclear in retrospective notes → record the hCG date and value explicitly
Women may be judged clinically stable without this being explicitly documented → require an explicit statement, not an assumption
Follow-up non-attendance is itself a safety risk requiring an escalation plan → record any non-attendance and the service's response
Fading compliance without a structured proforma → embed the eligibility fields into the decision record, not a separate audit form
pearls: Involve the early pregnancy unit lead as co-investigator
Use a dedicated ectopic pregnancy tracking log to actively follow up all expectantly managed women
Review any case of rupture or emergency surgery after expectant management at the morbidity meeting to close the loop
Give women a clear written safety-netting leaflet on symptoms of rupture
Keep the same hCG thresholds at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per case from the early pregnancy unit record
pass_short: Expectant management decision records hCG of 1,000 IU/L or less and ability to return

question: In women with a retained placenta, what proportion had intravenous access secured, with the reason explained to the woman, documented at the time retention was diagnosed?
why: Retained placenta carries a risk of sudden major haemorrhage; securing IV access early is a basic safety step that is not routinely checked; no closed-loop audit of this step is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG235 Intrapartum care, rec 1.10.21 (2014)
standard.wording: Secure intravenous access if the placenta is retained, and explain to the woman why this is needed.

pass: IV access is documented as secured at the time retained placenta is diagnosed, with a note that the reason was explained to the woman
population: Inclusion: all women with a placenta not delivered within 30 minutes (active management) or 60 minutes (physiological management) of birth. Exclusion: women who already had IV access in place for another reason before diagnosis (record as already in place).
sample: 20-30 consecutive women with a retained placenta over the last 6-12 months
data_source: Birth record/third stage record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'retained placenta' sticker/proforma triggered at 30 or 60 minutes (as applicable) on the third-stage record, with a mandatory IV access field.
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the labour ward audit meeting; if compliant, embed the proforma in standard third-stage documentation
pitfalls: Retained placenta is relatively infrequent → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
IV access may be secured but not documented as related to the retained placenta specifically → check the timing against the diagnosis time
Community/home births have different equipment and transfer implications → consider auditing hospital and home births separately
Explanation to the woman is often given verbally without being noted → add a simple documentation prompt
Fading compliance without an automatic prompt → build the 30/60-minute retained placenta alert into the electronic partogram
pearls: Involve the labour ward coordinator in designing the retained placenta proforma
Use simulation training on postpartum haemorrhage and retained placenta to reinforce the IV access step
Track subsequent haemorrhage rate as a linked outcome measure
Coordinate with the community/home birth team on transfer protocols for this scenario
Keep the same 30/60-minute definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per case from the birth record
pass_short: IV access secured when retained placenta diagnosed, with reason explained to the woman

question: Of women having outpatient induction of labour, what proportion had a full clinical assessment of the woman and baby, and an agreed review plan, documented before they were discharged home?
why: Outpatient induction relies on safe assessment and a clear review plan before the woman leaves the unit; no closed-loop audit of pre-discharge assessment completeness for outpatient induction is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG207 Inducing labour, rec 1.6.2 and rec 1.6.3 (2008, amended 2021)
standard.wording: Carry out a full clinical assessment of the woman and baby (see recommendations 1.5.1 and 1.5.2) and ensure safety and support procedures are in place. ... For induction being undertaken on an outpatient basis, agree a review plan with the woman before she returns home.

pass: A full clinical assessment (Bishop score, CTG) and an agreed, documented review plan (including when to return, or when to contact the unit) are both recorded before the woman is discharged home
population: Inclusion: all women having outpatient induction of labour. Exclusion: women converted to inpatient induction before any planned discharge home.
sample: 30 consecutive outpatient inductions over the last 3-6 months
data_source: Induction of labour outpatient pathway record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a structured outpatient induction discharge checklist with mandatory assessment and review-plan fields that must be completed before the woman can be marked as discharged home.
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the induction of labour/maternity governance meeting; if compliant, make the checklist the standard outpatient induction discharge document
pitfalls: Outpatient induction volumes may be modest → extend the collection period to 3-6 months
Review plan sometimes given verbally without being written down → require a written plan given to the woman as well as documented in the notes
Safety-netting advice content varies between staff → use a standard script or leaflet for consistency
Unplanned reattendance before the planned review may indicate inadequate initial safety-netting → track and review these cases
Fading compliance without a mandatory checklist → build the checklist into the EPR discharge workflow
pearls: Involve the outpatient induction pathway lead midwife as co-investigator
Provide a standard written safety-netting leaflet for all outpatient induction patients
Track unplanned reattendance rate as a linked safety outcome measure
Share learning from any adverse outcome after outpatient induction at the governance meeting
Keep the same assessment and review-plan definitions at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per 10 women from the outpatient induction record
pass_short: Full clinical assessment and agreed review plan documented before outpatient induction discharge

question: Of women who gave birth following spontaneous preterm labour before 34 weeks' gestation, what proportion received intravenous intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis against early-onset group B streptococcal infection?
why: Preterm birth carries a substantially higher risk of early-onset GBS infection regardless of known maternal GBS status, and this preterm-specific antibiotic standard is distinct from the existing audit of antibiotics for women with a known GBS-positive result at term [NNA-200]; no audit of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for preterm labour under 34 weeks is in the library.

standard.source: NHS England Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle version 3, Element 5, process indicator 5d (2023)
standard.wording: Percentage of women who give birth following preterm labour below 34 weeks of gestation who receive IV intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent early onset neonatal Group B Streptococcal (GBS) infection.

pass: IV intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis against GBS is given during labour to a woman giving birth following spontaneous preterm labour before 34 weeks
population: Inclusion: women giving birth following spontaneous preterm labour before 34+0 weeks. Exclusion: elective preterm birth for a maternal or fetal indication with no labour, women with a documented penicillin/antibiotic contraindication managed with an alternative agent (record as compliant with an alternative).
sample: 20-30 consecutive preterm births below 34 weeks following spontaneous labour over the last 6-12 months
data_source: Labour ward drug chart and birth record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'preterm labour under 34 weeks' order set to e-prescribing that defaults to IV benzylpenicillin (or the locally agreed alternative) regardless of known GBS status, triggered when gestation under 34 weeks is entered.
reaudit: At 6-12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the preterm birth/perinatal optimisation pathway meeting; if compliant, report through the SBLCB v3 element 5 process indicators
pitfalls: Very preterm births are infrequent per unit → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
Staff may only think to give antibiotics if GBS status is known positive, missing the preterm-specific indication → make the order set trigger on gestation alone, not GBS status
Rapid/precipitate preterm births may not allow time for antibiotics before birth → record time from labour onset (or arrival) to first dose to distinguish this from omission
This is a distinct standard from the term GBS-positive antibiotic audit already in the library → keep the two audits and their process indicators clearly separate in reporting
Fading compliance without an order-set default → embed the trigger by gestation in the electronic prescribing system
pearls: Cross-reference with the existing term GBS antibiotic audit [NNA-200] but report separately to avoid confusion
Involve the preterm birth team and labour ward pharmacist in building the order set
Track early-onset neonatal GBS infection rates in preterm babies as a linked outcome measure
Report through the perinatal optimisation pathway compliance metric alongside the other SBLCB v3 element 5 measures
Keep the same 34-week gestation cut-off at re-audit
effort: ~15 min per case from the drug chart and birth record
pass_short: IV intrapartum antibiotics against GBS given in spontaneous preterm labour before 34 weeks

question: What proportion of parents were given information, before discharge, on the 'red flag' signs of serious illness in young babies that should prompt an urgent or emergency review?
why: Delayed recognition of serious neonatal illness after discharge is a recurring theme in serious incident reviews; no closed-loop audit of red-flag safety-netting information given at discharge is in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG194 Postnatal care, rec 1.4.9 and rec 1.4.10 (2021)
standard.wording: Recognise the following as 'red flags' for serious illness in young babies: appearing ill to a healthcare professional, appearing pale, ashen, mottled or blue (cyanosis), unresponsive or unrousable ... If a baby is thought to be seriously unwell based on a 'red flag' ... or on an overall assessment of their condition, arrange an immediate assessment with an appropriate emergency service.

pass: The discharge record documents that parents were given verbal and/or written information on newborn red-flag symptoms and when to seek urgent or emergency help
population: Inclusion: all babies discharged home from the birth setting or postnatal ward. Exclusion: babies transferred directly to another hospital or the neonatal unit.
sample: 40 consecutive babies discharged home over the last 4-6 weeks
data_source: Postnatal discharge checklist/newborn record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a standard newborn red-flag safety-netting leaflet to the discharge pack, with a mandatory 'red flag information given' tick box on the electronic discharge checklist.
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the postnatal ward/neonatal governance meeting; if compliant, extend the leaflet to home birth discharge packs
pitfalls: Verbal-only advice is easily forgotten by tired new parents → always pair verbal advice with a written leaflet
Documentation of 'advice given' is often generic and does not specify red flags → require the specific red-flag leaflet to be named in the record
Parents with limited English or literacy needs may need alternative formats → ensure translated or accessible versions are available and their use recorded
