question: What proportion of patients on maintenance lithium therapy have a lithium blood level checked at least once every 3 months?
why: Lithium monitoring for physical health parameters is not audited in the library, unlike related psychiatric monitoring topics; this is the single highest-harm, highest-volume medicines-safety gap named in the underlying national alert.

standard.source: NPSA Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2009/PSA005, Safer lithium therapy (1 December 2009)
standard.wording: one in 10 patients had no documented lithium blood level. (National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) standard: one blood level measurement every three months. Not met for 70 per cent of patients)

pass: At least one lithium level result is recorded in the preceding 3 months
population: Inclusion: adults on established (more than 6 months) maintenance lithium therapy under primary or secondary mental health care. Exclusion: patients newly starting lithium (still in initial titration monitoring).
sample: 40 consecutive patients on the lithium monitoring register over the last 3 months
data_source: Lithium monitoring register (practice or trust), laboratory results system

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 3-month lithium level recall to the lithium monitoring register, with a hard stop on repeat prescribing if the level is overdue, as recommended in the original NPSA alert.
reaudit: 6 months after the recall/hard stop is switched on, same register, same sample size
close_loop: Present at the medicines safety or mental health pharmacy governance meeting; keep the hard stop if the target is met.
pitfalls: Patients under shared care between GP and mental health services can fall between the two → agree who owns the recall before cycle 1
Patients who avoid blood tests are hardest to reach → offer a point-of-care or home phlebotomy option where available
A hard stop on prescribing needs pharmacy system changes → involve pharmacy IT from the outset
Register accuracy depends on all lithium patients being correctly coded → check the register against a full drug search before starting
pearls: Base the recall directly on the original NPSA alert's own 3-month standard so the audit maps onto a nationally recognised benchmark
Use the NPSA lithium record book (patient-held) as a low-cost extra safety net alongside the electronic recall
Recruit a mental health pharmacist to lead, since they typically run the lithium register already
Report separately for primary and secondary care patients, since the fix may differ by setting
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from lithium register
pass_short: Lithium level recorded within the preceding 3 months

question: What proportion of patients on maintenance lithium therapy have renal and thyroid function checked at least once every 6 months?
why: Renal and thyroid monitoring is a distinct national standard from the lithium level itself, and non-compliance with it was even more marked than lithium level monitoring in the original national audit that founded this alert.

standard.source: NPSA Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2009/PSA005, Safer lithium therapy (1 December 2009)
standard.wording: one in five patients had no renal function tests documented (NICE standard: assessment every six months. Not met for 46 per cent of patients); one in six patients had no thyroid function tests documented (NICE standard: assessment every six months. Not met for 51 per cent of patients)

pass: Both a renal function test (U&E/eGFR) and a thyroid function test are recorded within the preceding 6 months
population: Inclusion: adults on established maintenance lithium therapy over the last 6 months. Exclusion: patients newly starting lithium (still in initial titration monitoring).
sample: 40 consecutive patients on the lithium monitoring register over the last 6 months
data_source: Lithium monitoring register, laboratory results system

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add renal and thyroid function to the same automatic 6-month recall used for the lithium level check, as a single combined blood test request, rather than a separate process.
reaudit: 6 months after the combined recall is switched on, same register, same sample size
close_loop: Present at the medicines safety or mental health pharmacy governance meeting; keep the combined recall if the target is met.
pitfalls: Renal and thyroid tests are sometimes requested separately from the lithium level, causing extra venepuncture visits → combine them on one request form
Deteriorating renal function may not trigger a dose review → link abnormal results to a documented lithium dose review action
Test results filed but not reviewed by a prescriber → require a clinician sign-off field, not just a filed result
Register may not distinguish patients newly started from established patients → exclude the first 6 months, which has its own more frequent monitoring schedule

Recruit the same mental health pharmacist leading the lithium level audit
Track abnormal results and the action taken as a secondary measure of monitoring quality, not just test completion
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from lithium register
pass_short: Renal and thyroid function both recorded within the preceding 6 months

question: What proportion of patients starting lithium therapy are given a patient information booklet and a record book to track their lithium blood levels and relevant clinical tests?

standard.wording: at the start of lithium therapy and throughout their treatment patients receive appropriate ongoing verbal and written information and a record book to track lithium blood levels and relevant clinical tests

Present this audit alongside the monitoring-frequency audits for a complete picture of the lithium safety pathway

question: What proportion of adults with a single acute paracetamol overdose and a plasma-paracetamol concentration on or above the treatment line start acetylcysteine within 8 hours of ingestion?

standard.source: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Medicines Information Leaflet, Guideline for the Management of Paracetamol Overdose (March 2024), based on TOXBASE/National Poisons Information Service guidance
standard.wording: It is most effective if given within 8 hours of paracetamol ingestion, after which effectiveness declines... a plasma-paracetamol concentration on or above the treatment line should be regarded as carrying a serious risk of liver damage.

pass: Acetylcysteine is started within 8 hours of the recorded time of ingestion
population: Inclusion: adults presenting with a single acute paracetamol overdose and a plasma-paracetamol concentration on or above the treatment line over the last 6 months. Exclusion: staggered or uncertain-time overdoses.
sample: 30 consecutive eligible presentations over the last 6 months
data_source: ED notes, drug chart (acetylcysteine start time), laboratory paracetamol level and time

evidence: [92 nearest related entry: staggered/uncertain-time paracetamol overdose acetylcysteine timing within 1 hour of arrival]
pitfalls: Ingestion time is often uncertain even in 'single acute' presentations → verify with ambulance or collateral history where possible

Present findings alongside the NPIS/TOXBASE contact audit below, since both use the same case list

question: What proportion of children, young people and adults newly diagnosed with epilepsy have their MRI scan carried out within 6 weeks of the MRI referral?
why: Referral timing to a first-seizure clinic is already audited [see NNA-127], but the timeliness of the neuroimaging itself, once referred, is not measured anywhere in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 1.3.1 (2022)
standard.wording: Offer an MRI scan to children, young people and adults diagnosed with epilepsy, unless they have idiopathic generalised epilepsy or self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes. pass: The MRI scan is performed within 6 weeks of the date the MRI referral was made
population: Inclusion: children, young people and adults newly diagnosed with epilepsy and referred for MRI over the last 6 months, excluding idiopathic generalised epilepsy or self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes. Exclusion: patients for whom MRI is contraindicated.
sample: 30 consecutive epilepsy MRI referrals over the last 6 months
data_source: Radiology information system, epilepsy clinic letter

close_loop: Present at the neurology/radiology joint governance meeting; keep the ring-fenced slot if the target is met.
