effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass_short: Pregnancy risks of anti-seizure medication discussed within the last 12 months

question: What proportion of people of childbearing potential prescribed an enzyme-inducing anti-seizure medication (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or topiramate) have documented advice about reduced hormonal contraceptive effectiveness?
why: Interaction advice for enzyme-inducing anti-seizure medications and hormonal contraception is a distinct recommendation from the valproate-specific pregnancy prevention audits already in the library, and is not measured anywhere.

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 4.3.10 (2022)
standard.wording: Be aware that some antiseizure medications, for example, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and topiramate, can impair the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Refer to the summary of product characteristics (SPC) and BNF or BNF for children for individual drug advice on the interactions between antiseizure medications and contraception.

pass: Documented advice about reduced hormonal contraceptive effectiveness and the need for an alternative or additional method
population: Inclusion: people of childbearing potential prescribed carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or topiramate for epilepsy, under active follow-up. Exclusion: patients using a copper intrauterine device or another method unaffected by enzyme induction, if already documented.
sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients on the epilepsy clinic caseload
data_source: Epilepsy clinic letters, GP contraception review records

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a drug-interaction alert to the epilepsy prescribing system that fires when one of the four enzyme-inducing medications is prescribed to a person of childbearing potential, prompting a documented contraception discussion.
reaudit: 6 months after the alert is switched on, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at neurology and sexual health/contraception joint governance; keep the alert if the target is met.
evidence: [324 nearest related entry: topiramate Pregnancy Prevention Programme highly effective contraception recorded]
pitfalls: This standard covers four specific drugs, not all anti-seizure medications, so the alert must be drug-specific to avoid unnecessary prompts
Contraception method may be managed entirely in primary care and not visible to the neurology clinic → check both GP and specialist records
Non-hormonal or copper IUD users need this explicitly recorded as 'not applicable' rather than being marked as a fail
Topiramate's own separate Pregnancy Prevention Programme requirements (already audited) may overlap with this general interaction advice → keep the pass criteria distinct
pearls: Coordinate with the existing topiramate Pregnancy Prevention Programme audit to avoid double data collection on the same patients
Provide a simple interaction quick-reference card (drug name, effect on contraception, alternative advice) for clinicians
Recruit a contraception/sexual health lead as an occasional co-reviewer for complex cases
Report by individual drug, since carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine and topiramate caseloads may differ in size
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass_short: Advice on reduced hormonal contraceptive effectiveness documented, with alternative or additional method

question: What proportion of people with epilepsy who continue to have seizures despite treatment are offered an epilepsy specialist nurse session after each emergency department attendance for a seizure?
why: Epilepsy specialist nurse contact after an ED attendance is a specific, checkable recommendation not currently measured by any audit in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 11.1.3 (2022)
standard.wording: For people with epilepsy who continue to have seizures, offer epilepsy specialist nurse sessions: at least twice a year and after emergency department visits.

pass: An epilepsy specialist nurse contact (session, call or clinic appointment) is documented within 2 weeks of the ED attendance
population: Inclusion: people with known epilepsy and ongoing seizures who attend the ED with a seizure over the last 6 months. Exclusion: ED attendances for a reason unrelated to epilepsy in a person who happens to have the condition.
sample: 30 consecutive epilepsy-related ED attendances over the last 6 months
data_source: ED attendance record, epilepsy specialist nurse contact log

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic epilepsy specialist nurse referral to the ED discharge system, triggered whenever a seizure-related attendance is coded in a patient with known epilepsy.
reaudit: 6 months after the automatic referral is switched on, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint ED/neurology governance meeting; keep the automatic referral if the target is met.
pitfalls: ED coding may not clearly distinguish a seizure-related attendance from other reasons → cross-check with the triage complaint as well as the diagnosis code
Epilepsy specialist nurse capacity may not match ED attendance volume → agree a realistic response model (call-back, not always a face-to-face session) with the service before cycle 1
Attendances out of hours or at weekends may be harder to flag for follow-up → build the referral into the discharge process itself, not a manual daily list
Patients who decline contact should be recorded as offered but declined, not as non-compliance
pearls: Base the automatic referral trigger on the same seizure-related attendance coding used for existing seizure audits
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse team directly, since they are best placed to say what response is realistic
Track whether ED re-attendance rates change over time as a secondary outcome of better specialist nurse contact
Present this alongside the referral-to-first-seizure-clinic audit for a fuller picture of the epilepsy urgent care pathway
effort: ~15 min per 10 attendances from ED/specialist nurse records
pass_short: Epilepsy specialist nurse contact within 2 weeks of ED attendance

question: What proportion of adults have a corrected serum calcium checked within 12 hours of thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy?
why: Post-operative hypocalcaemia is a common, preventable cause of delayed discharge and re-admission after thyroid and parathyroid surgery, and no closed-loop audit of the timing of the first postoperative calcium check has been published in the library.

standard.source: BAETS Post-operative Hypocalcaemia Guidance
standard.wording: POST THYROIDECTOMY / PARATHYROIDECTOMY CORRECTED CALCIUM LEVELS: Check within 12h postoperatively

pass: Corrected serum calcium result is filed and actioned within 12 hours of the end of surgery
population: Inclusion: all adults undergoing total or completion thyroidectomy, or parathyroidectomy. Exclusion: hemithyroidectomy or thyroid lobectomy only
sample: 40 consecutive adult thyroid or parathyroid operations over the last 4 months
data_source: Theatre system for operation type and time, laboratory system for calcium sample time, EPR for the documented action
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a 'post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery' order set that auto-requests a corrected calcium for 12 hours post-op and displays the BAETS treatment algorithm next to the result
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size, on the next 40 consecutive operations
close_loop: Present at the endocrine surgery/ENT MDT and departmental audit meeting; embed the order set as the default post-op set if the target is met
pitfalls: Sample drawn but result not checked out of hours → build the check into the nursing handover, not just the request
Small numbers at units doing few parathyroidectomies → combine thyroid and parathyroid cases for the denominator
Definition of 'checked' drifts between cycles (requested vs resulted) → fix the definition as 'result available in EPR' before cycle 1
New starters unaware of the algorithm → laminate the algorithm in recovery and on the ward
pearls: Recruit the endocrine surgery clinical nurse specialist to check for missed 12-hour bloods each morning
Agree the exact cut-off time (12h from skin closure, not from admission) before cycle 1 starts
Link the order set to the procedure code so it fires automatically
Keep the same nurse-led calcium round after the surgical trainees rotate
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from theatre system and EPR
pass_short: Corrected calcium result filed and actioned within 12 hours of surgery ending

question: What proportion of adults undergoing thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy have a documented post-operative laryngoscopy to assess vocal cord movement?
why: Vocal cord palsy is a leading cause of litigation after thyroid and parathyroid surgery, yet the true incidence is only known where laryngoscopy is performed routinely; no audit of compliance with mandatory post-operative laryngoscopy has been published in the library.

standard.source: BAETS Consensus, Pre and Post Operative Laryngoscopy in Thyroid and Parathyroid Surgery (FF Palazzo for BAETS, June 2010)
standard.wording: Post-operative laryngoscopy is required as a key quality control measure and should become mandatory.

pass: A fibreoptic or transcutaneous laryngoscopy assessment of vocal cord movement is documented at any point after surgery, up to and including the first outpatient follow-up
population: Inclusion: all adults undergoing thyroid or parathyroid surgery. Exclusion: patients refusing the examination (documented separately)
sample: 40 consecutive adult thyroid/parathyroid operations over the last 4 months
data_source: Operation note, ENT/voice clinic letters, EPR results
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make a laryngoscopy booking (by the surgical team or ENT) a mandatory step on the electronic discharge checklist for every thyroid/parathyroid operation
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the endocrine surgery MDT and joint ENT/endocrine surgery governance meeting; embed the discharge checklist step if effective
pitfalls: No ENT or voice clinic slots available → negotiate a ring-fenced weekly slot before cycle 1
Refusals not distinguished from omissions → add a separate 'declined' field so the denominator is fair
Surgeons doing their own transcutaneous ultrasound assessment not counted → agree what counts as 'laryngoscopy' before starting
Result not filed back into the surgical record → ask ENT to copy the surgical team into every report
pearls: Agree with ENT a same-day or next-day slot before starting the first cycle
Use a transcutaneous laryngeal ultrasound pathway where trained staff exist, to reduce reliance on ENT capacity
Put the laryngoscopy step on the WHO-style discharge checklist so it cannot be missed
Feed back cord palsy rates to the department each year so the mandatory step is not seen as a paperwork exercise
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPR and clinic letters
pass_short: Post-operative laryngoscopy of vocal cord movement documented by first outpatient follow-up

question: What proportion of adults with a voice change or suspected/confirmed thyroid malignancy have a documented pre-operative laryngoscopy before thyroid or parathyroid surgery?
why: Pre-operative vocal cord assessment changes intraoperative and consent decisions when malignancy or voice change is present; no audit targeting this selective indication (rather than routine laryngoscopy in all patients) has been published in the library.

standard.source: BAETS Consensus, Pre and Post Operative Laryngoscopy in Thyroid and Parathyroid Surgery (FF Palazzo for BAETS, June 2010)
standard.wording: Pre-operative laryngoscopy in non-cancer patients with no history of voice change has a low rate of abnormal findings.

pass: A pre-operative laryngoscopy result is documented in the notes before surgery for any patient with a voice change or a cytological/clinical suspicion of malignancy
population: Inclusion: adults listed for thyroid or parathyroid surgery with documented voice change or suspected/confirmed malignancy. Exclusion: benign disease with a normal voice
sample: All patients with voice change or suspected malignancy listed for thyroid/parathyroid surgery over the last 6 months (expect 30-40)
data_source: Pre-assessment clinic letters, MDT proforma, ENT clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'voice change / suspected malignancy → pre-op laryngoscopy booked' field to the thyroid MDT outcome proforma
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the thyroid cancer MDT; embed the proforma field if it improves compliance
pitfalls: Voice change not systematically asked about at clinic → add a standard voice question to the pre-assessment template
Small numbers if malignancy is rare locally → run over 6 months rather than 3
Laryngoscopy done but not documented in the surgical notes → require the ENT report to be filed in the same record
MDT proforma completed retrospectively → complete it in real time at the MDT
pearls: Add the voice question to every thyroid nodule clinic template, not just cancer clinics
Use the MDT coordinator to check the field is complete before the case is listed
Share abnormal pre-op findings with the operating surgeon before consent
Keep a log of pre-op abnormal cords to compare with post-op findings
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from MDT proforma
pass_short: Pre-operative laryngoscopy documented for voice change or suspected thyroid malignancy

question: What proportion of adults with structural persistent thyroid cancer after total or completion thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine are discussed at the thyroid cancer multidisciplinary team meeting?
why: Persistent structural disease after primary treatment changes management (further surgery, radiotherapy or systemic treatment) and should not be managed outside the MDT; no audit of MDT discussion for this specific group has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.6.4 (2022)
standard.wording: Discuss at the multidisciplinary team meeting any person who has had a total or completion thyroidectomy and RAI and has evidence of structural persistent disease.

pass: Documented discussion and outcome at the thyroid cancer MDT within 4 weeks of imaging or biochemistry showing structural persistent disease
population: Inclusion: adults with thyroid cancer who have had total or completion thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine and subsequent evidence of structural persistent disease. Exclusion: biochemical-only persistence with no structural correlate
sample: All such patients identified over the last 12 months (expect 20-30 in a regional cancer centre)
data_source: MDT database, oncology and endocrine clinic letters, imaging reports
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'structural persistent disease' MDT-list trigger from the radiology reporting system when a report contains that phrase for a coded thyroid cancer patient
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the thyroid cancer MDT and cancer services governance meeting; embed the radiology trigger if effective
pitfalls: Structural persistence identified in a non-cancer clinic and not flagged → educate all clinicians reviewing thyroid cancer follow-up scans
MDT list overloaded, cases delayed → create a fast-track 'persistent disease' slot
Ambiguity over what counts as 'structural' vs biochemical → agree the definition with radiology and oncology before cycle 1
Retrospective identification bias if reliant on memory → use a coded database search
pearls: Ask radiology to use a standard phrase ('structural persistent disease') in reports to enable searching
Give the MDT coordinator a standing search of the radiology system each week
Keep a register of persistent disease cases for continuity when staff rotate
Feed outcomes back to the referring endocrinologist so follow-up plans are updated
effort: ~30 min per month from MDT database and radiology search
pass_short: Thyroid cancer MDT discussion within 4 weeks of structural persistent disease being shown

question: What proportion of fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) samples for a thyroid nodule are reported as Thy1 (non-diagnostic/inadequate)?
why: A high non-diagnostic rate delays diagnosis and increases repeat procedures; no audit of local Thy1 rates against the NICE quality trigger has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.2.10 (2022)
standard.wording: Consider rapid on-site evaluation of FNAC adequacy rates to improve the diagnostic yield of samples if the Thy1 (inadequate) rate for the centre or individual healthcare professionals is higher than 15% (when Thy1c is excluded).

pass: Thy1 (excluding Thy1c) rate for the service is 15% or lower over the audit period
population: Inclusion: all thyroid nodule FNAC samples taken over the audit period. Exclusion: repeat FNAC on the same nodule within 4 weeks
sample: All thyroid FNAC samples over the last 6 months (expect 40-60)
data_source: Cytology reporting system, radiology (ultrasound-guided FNAC) records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) of FNAC adequacy for ultrasound-guided thyroid biopsies
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint cytology/radiology/endocrine surgery governance meeting; embed ROSE if the target is met
pitfalls: ROSE requires a cytotechnologist or pathologist present at every list → negotiate cover before starting the change
Operator-level data seen as punitive → present anonymised operator codes first, agree feedback approach with the team
Thy1c cases wrongly counted as inadequate → use the coded cytology categories, not free text
Small numbers per individual operator → report at service level first, individual level only with consent
pearls: Agree with cytology in advance which category counts as 'inadequate' for the audit
Use a dedicated ultrasound-guided FNAC list run by trained operators to improve consistency
Share Thy1 rates quarterly at the endocrine surgery/radiology joint meeting
Track repeat-biopsy rate as a secondary outcome
effort: ~20 min per month from cytology reporting system
pass_short: Thy1 rate (excluding Thy1c) of 15% or lower

question: What proportion of patients with T1a/T1b or greater differentiated thyroid cancer who have had a hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without radioactive iodine receive the recommended surveillance ultrasound and annual clinical follow-up?
why: Under-surveillance risks missed recurrence in low-risk thyroid cancer managed without RAI; no audit of adherence to the NICE surveillance schedule has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.6.2 (2022)
standard.wording: Consider an ultrasound at 6 to 12 months initially then annual clinical follow-up for up to 5 years for people with T1a (m) or T1b stage or greater thyroid cancer, who have had a hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without RAI.

pass: An ultrasound is booked or performed 6-12 months after surgery and an annual clinical follow-up appointment is booked for each year up to 5 years
population: Inclusion: adults with T1a(m)/T1b or greater differentiated thyroid cancer treated by hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without RAI. Exclusion: patients who received RAI
sample: All such patients treated in the last 18 months (expect 20-30)
data_source: Cancer MDT database, radiology booking system, clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'low-risk thyroid cancer surveillance' pathway on the cancer follow-up system that books the 6-12 month ultrasound and annual reviews at the point of MDT outcome
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the thyroid cancer MDT; embed the automated pathway if effective
pitfalls: Patients lost to follow-up after discharge from surgical clinic → use a single named follow-up pathway owner
Ultrasound slots not protected for surveillance → agree a standing allocation with radiology
Definition of T1a(m) vs T1a ambiguous to non-specialists → confirm staging with the MDT coordinator for each case
Surveillance stopped early without documented reason → require a reason field if follow-up is curtailed before 5 years
pearls: Use the MDT outcome form to auto-generate the follow-up schedule
Give patients a printed follow-up plan at their post-op clinic visit
Audit alongside the cancer MDT's annual outcomes review
Nominate a CNS to track the pathway centrally
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from MDT database
pass_short: Ultrasound 6-12 months after surgery and annual clinical follow-up booked for 5 years

question: What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery who are not already taking a beta-blocker are offered pharmacological prophylaxis (amiodarone, a standard beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker) to reduce the risk of postoperative atrial fibrillation?
why: Postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery prolongs stay and increases stroke risk; while restarting a pre-existing beta-blocker is already tracked in the library [NNA-047], no audit has measured whether patients who are not already on a beta-blocker are offered any of the recommended prophylactic options.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.1 (2021)
standard.wording: In people having cardiothoracic surgery: reduce the risk of postoperative atrial fibrillation by offering 1 of the following: amiodarone a standard beta‑blocker (that is, a beta-blocker other than sotalol) a rate‑limiting calcium‑channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) do not offer digoxin.

pass: One of amiodarone, a standard beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker is prescribed for AF prophylaxis by the end of the first postoperative day, and digoxin is not used for this purpose
population: Inclusion: adults having elective cardiac surgery who were not on a beta-blocker before admission. Exclusion: patients on a pre-existing beta-blocker (covered by the restart pathway)
sample: 40 consecutive beta-blocker-naive adult cardiac surgery patients over the last 4 months
data_source: Anaesthetic chart, ICU drug chart, EPMA
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a default 'AF prophylaxis: amiodarone / beta-blocker / calcium-channel blocker (tick one) or contraindicated (reason)' line to the post-cardiac surgery ICU order set
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery/anaesthesia governance meeting; embed the order set default if effective
pitfalls: Digoxin still used from habit → remove it as an option from the order set
Bradycardia or hypotension used as a blanket reason to omit prophylaxis without considering alternatives → require the alternative agent to be considered first
AF occurring after ICU discharge missed by the audit → extend data collection to hospital discharge
Anaesthetists and surgeons prescribing inconsistently → agree a single default order set for both teams
pearls: Build the three options into a single tick-box so an active choice is required
Involve pharmacy in checking interactions before amiodarone loading
Review the order set uptake weekly during the first cycle
Keep the postoperative AF rate as a linked outcome measure
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from ICU drug chart
pass_short: Amiodarone, beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker prescribed by postoperative day 1, no digoxin

question: What proportion of patients started on a rhythm-control strategy for new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery have their need for continued antiarrhythmic treatment reassessed at around 6 weeks?
why: Postoperative AF often resolves once the precipitant settles, but antiarrhythmic drugs are frequently continued by default; no audit of the 6-week reassessment has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.6 (2021)
standard.wording: If a rhythm‑control strategy is chosen, reassess the need for antiarrhythmic drug treatment at a suitable time point (usually at around 6 weeks).

pass: A documented reassessment of the need for continued antiarrhythmic treatment occurs between 4 and 8 weeks after starting rhythm control
population: Inclusion: adults started on a rhythm-control strategy for new postoperative AF after cardiac surgery. Exclusion: rate-control strategy chosen
sample: All patients started on rhythm control for postoperative AF in the last 6 months (expect 20-30)
data_source: Discharge summary, cardiology/cardiac surgery follow-up clinic letters, GP correspondence
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 6-week antiarrhythmic review task to the discharge summary for any patient discharged on antiarrhythmic treatment for postoperative AF
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery follow-up governance meeting; embed the discharge task if effective
pitfalls: Patients discharged to GP follow-up only, with no cardiology review booked → give GPs a clear stop/review date on the discharge letter
Reassessment done but not documented in a retrievable place → use a coded discharge summary field
Loss to follow-up if patients move between services → name a single team responsible for the review
Antiarrhythmics continued indefinitely 'to be safe' → present the evidence for time-limited use at teaching sessions
pearls: Give a clear stop/review date on every antiarrhythmic prescription at discharge
Use the cardiac surgery nurse specialist to track outstanding reviews
Feed reassessment outcomes back to the prescribing team
Align the review with an existing 6-week post-cardiac-surgery follow-up appointment where possible
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from discharge summaries
pass_short: Antiarrhythmic need reassessed between 4 and 8 weeks after starting rhythm control

question: What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery who are already taking a statin have it continued after surgery?
why: Unintentional omission of a pre-existing statin at the time of surgery is a recognised, avoidable medicines-reconciliation failure; no audit of statin continuation after cardiac surgery has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.4 (2021)
standard.wording: In people having cardiothoracic surgery who are already on statins, continue this treatment.

pass: A pre-existing statin is represented on the post-operative drug chart by the end of the first postoperative day, or a documented reason for stopping it is recorded
population: Inclusion: adults on a statin before elective cardiac surgery. Exclusion: statin started for the first time postoperatively
sample: 40 consecutive adult cardiac surgery patients known to be on a statin pre-operatively, over the last 4 months
data_source: Medicines reconciliation record, ICU/ward drug chart

template.note: Initials of person collecting the data and date collected

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add pre-existing statins to the medicines reconciliation prompt that appears automatically when writing the post-cardiac-surgery drug chart
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery/pharmacy medicines safety meeting; embed the reconciliation prompt if effective
pitfalls: Statin omitted because the patient is nil by mouth and not represented once feeding resumes → add a re-check step once oral intake restarts
Reconciliation done by a junior doctor without pharmacy cross-check → involve pharmacy in every post-op reconciliation
Statin stopped for a genuine reason (e.g. rhabdomyolysis risk) but not documented → require a reason field
Discharge summary omits the statin even though it was continued in hospital → check the discharge letter as well as the inpatient chart
pearls: Use the electronic medicines reconciliation list as the single source of truth for pre-op medicines
Ask pharmacy to review post-cardiac-surgery drug charts within 24 hours
Flag any statin omission for consultant sign-off
Repeat the check at discharge as well as on the ward
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from drug charts
pass_short: Pre-existing statin continued by postoperative day 1, or reason for stopping documented

question: What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery receive mechanical VTE prophylaxis from admission and, where indicated, pharmacological prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days?
why: Cardiac surgery patients are at increased VTE risk from immobility and central access, but VTE prophylaxis is often deprioritised around anticoagulation for bypass; no audit of compliance with the NICE cardiac-surgery-specific VTE recommendations has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG89 Venous thromboembolism in over 16s, recs 1.15.1 and 1.15.2 (2018)
standard.wording: 1.15.1 Consider mechanical VTE prophylaxis on admission for people who are undergoing cardiac surgery who are at increased risk of VTE. 1.15.2 Consider adding pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days for people who are undergoing cardiac surgery and are not having other anticoagulation therapy: Use LMWH as first-line treatment.

pass: Mechanical VTE prophylaxis is documented from admission, and pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH is prescribed for at least 7 days in patients not otherwise anticoagulated
population: Inclusion: adults undergoing cardiac surgery at increased VTE risk. Exclusion: patients already anticoagulated for another indication
sample: 40 consecutive adult cardiac surgery patients over the last 4 months
data_source: VTE risk assessment form, drug chart, nursing records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a cardiac-surgery-specific VTE prophylaxis bundle (mechanical from admission plus a 7-day LMWH course) to the admission and post-op order sets
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery governance meeting; embed the bundle if effective
pitfalls: Mechanical prophylaxis omitted because of leg swelling or drains → give clear guidance on device choice around chest drains and vein harvest sites
LMWH delayed because of concern about bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass → agree a standard start day with the surgical team before cycle 1
7-day course not completed because of early discharge → include a discharge prescription for the remaining days
VTE risk assessment completed but not linked to a prescribing action → link the assessment directly to the order set
pearls: Build both mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis into a single order-set bundle
Agree the LMWH start time with cardiac surgery and anaesthesia in advance
Audit alongside existing VTE risk-assessment compliance data
Keep a discharge checklist item for completing the 7-day course
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from drug chart and VTE assessment
pass_short: Mechanical prophylaxis from admission and LMWH for at least 7 days if not anticoagulated

question: What proportion of adults with an undiagnosed or symptomatic pleural effusion who need a pleural procedure have it within 5 days of the decision being made?
why: Delays to pleural drainage prolong breathlessness and hospital stay; no audit of time from decision to pleural procedure against the national access standard has been published in the library.

standard.source: BTS Quality Standard for Pleural Disease, quality statement on access to pleural services
standard.wording: For symptomatic or undiagnosed pleural effusion, where a pleural procedure is clinically indicated, it should be offered within five days of the decision being made, unless the patient's symptoms or evidence of infection makes a more urgent procedure necessary.

pass: The pleural procedure is performed within 5 calendar days of the documented decision to proceed, or sooner if urgent
population: Inclusion: adults with a symptomatic or undiagnosed pleural effusion referred to the cardiothoracic/pleural service for a procedure. Exclusion: emergency drainage for tension physiology or empyema requiring immediate intervention
sample: 40 consecutive referrals for pleural procedures over the last 3 months
data_source: Referral log, procedure booking system, clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set up a weekly protected pleural procedure list with direct electronic referral from the point of decision
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the pleural service/cardiothoracic MDT; embed the protected list if effective
pitfalls: 'Decision made' not consistently documented, making the start point unclear → agree a single documentation point (referral form date) before cycle 1
Procedure delayed by lack of ultrasound-trained operators → identify capacity gaps early
Urgent cases wrongly counted against the 5-day target → add an explicit urgent-indication field
Referrals lost between teams → use a single electronic referral pathway
pearls: Use a single electronic referral form that timestamps the decision
Protect a weekly list specifically for non-urgent pleural procedures
Involve the pleural nurse specialist in tracking waiting referrals
Review the waiting list weekly at the pleural MDT
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from referral log
pass_short: Pleural procedure within 5 calendar days of the decision

question: What proportion of patients are given information and advice about how to recognise a surgical site infection and who to contact, documented before discharge after cardiac surgery?
why: Sternal wound infection after cardiac surgery is a high-harm complication, and early patient recognition and re-presentation depend on clear safety-netting advice; no audit of documented SSI safety-netting specifically after cardiac surgery has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG125 Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment, rec 1.1.3 (2019)
standard.wording: Offer patients and carers information and advice about how to recognise a surgical site infection and who to contact if they are concerned.

pass: The discharge summary or a discrete leaflet documents that wound infection safety-netting advice (signs to watch for and a contact number) was given
population: Inclusion: all adults discharged after cardiac surgery via median sternotomy. Exclusion: patients who die before discharge
sample: 40 consecutive cardiac surgery discharges over the last 3 months
data_source: Discharge summary, nursing discharge checklist

template.note: Initials of person collecting the data and date collected

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'sternal wound infection advice and contact number given' tick box to the cardiac surgery discharge summary template, linked to a standard leaflet
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the cardiothoracic surgery governance and infection prevention meeting; embed the discharge tick box if effective
pitfalls: Advice given verbally but not documented → make documentation itself, not just the conversation, the pass criterion
Leaflet given but generic (not sternal-wound specific) → develop a cardiac-surgery-specific leaflet
Patients discharged out of hours without the usual checklist → audit weekend/evening discharges separately
Field ticked as a default without the conversation happening → spot-check with post-discharge phone calls
pearls: Make the leaflet part of the standard cardiac surgery discharge pack
Give the same information to family/carers where the patient has reduced capacity
Include the sternal wound infection bundle as an agenda item at governance meetings
Track re-presentation rates for wound infection as a linked outcome
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from discharge summaries
pass_short: Wound infection advice, including signs and contact number, documented before discharge

question: What proportion of children undergoing scrotal exploration for suspected testicular torsion reach theatre within 3 hours of the decision to operate?
why: Testicular salvage falls sharply with delay to surgery; no closed-loop audit of time from decision to operate to incision for suspected torsion has been published in the library.

standard.source: NHS England (Midlands) Commissioning Guide for the Management of Paediatric Testicular Torsion
standard.wording: Timely intervention: Percentage of explorations within 3 hours of decision to operate (NCEPOD 2) (excluding those with co-morbidities) 100%

pass: Time from documented decision to operate to skin incision is 3 hours or less
population: Inclusion: all children undergoing scrotal exploration for suspected testicular torsion. Exclusion: children with significant co-morbidities delaying anaesthesia
sample: All scrotal explorations for suspected torsion over the last 12 months (expect 20-40)
data_source: Theatre system, emergency department and surgical clerking notes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a 'suspected testicular torsion' theatre booking category that bypasses the routine emergency list queue and alerts theatre coordination directly
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the paediatric surgery/emergency theatre governance meeting; embed the booking category if effective
pitfalls: Decision-to-operate time not documented consistently → agree a single trigger point (consultant/registrar decision documented in notes) before cycle 1
Theatre unavailable out of hours → confirm the emergency theatre escalation pathway covers torsion explicitly
Low case numbers per quarter → collect over 12 months to get a meaningful sample
Fasting status used to justify delay despite clinical urgency → reiterate that assessment should not be delayed by fasting status
pearls: Agree the torsion pathway with emergency medicine, theatres and anaesthesia before starting
Use a single-page torsion pathway sheet that timestamps each step
Review every case with a time over 3 hours at the morbidity and mortality meeting
Track testicular salvage rate as the outcome that matters to families
effort: ~15 min per case from theatre and ED records
pass_short: Decision to skin incision within 3 hours

question: What proportion of children presenting to a secondary care hospital with suspected testicular torsion are explored locally rather than transferred to a tertiary paediatric surgery centre?
why: Transfer delays testicular salvage and should be exceptional; no audit of unnecessary inter-hospital transfer for suspected torsion has been published in the library.

standard.source: NHS England (Midlands) Commissioning Guide for the Management of Paediatric Testicular Torsion
standard.wording: Transfer of a boy with a suspicion of torsion from a Secondary Care Institution to a Tertiary Care Centre should therefore be an exceptional occurrence (e.g. medical comorbidities).

pass: The child is explored at the presenting secondary care hospital unless a documented medical co-morbidity or other exceptional reason requires transfer
population: Inclusion: children presenting to a secondary care hospital with suspected testicular torsion. Exclusion: children presenting directly to a tertiary centre
sample: All secondary care presentations with suspected torsion over the last 12 months (expect 15-30)
data_source: Emergency department notes, transfer records, theatre system
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Agree and circulate a local on-call rota and skills sign-off so that a competent surgeon and anaesthetist are always available locally for suspected torsion, with transfer requiring consultant-to-consultant agreement
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the paediatric surgery network governance meeting; embed the local competency rota if effective
pitfalls: Transfer driven by lack of confidence rather than genuine need → provide simulation training for on-call teams
Reasons for transfer not documented → make a reason field mandatory in the transfer request
Network guidance not known to on-call staff → include the pathway in induction
Transfer perceived as 'safer' despite adding delay → present time-to-theatre and salvage outcome data alongside transfer rates
pearls: Use network-level data sharing so all sites can benchmark
Keep an up-to-date on-call competency list for out-of-hours cover
Debrief every transferred case at the regional network meeting
Track testicular salvage rate for transferred versus locally-managed cases
effort: ~15 min per case from ED and transfer records
pass_short: Explored at presenting hospital unless documented comorbidity or exceptional reason needs transfer

question: What proportion of boys referred with physiological phimosis are managed with reassurance, education and (where appropriate) a trial of topical steroid rather than referral for circumcision?
why: Referrals for physiological phimosis account for avoidable surgical workload and expose children to the small but real risks of circumcision; no audit of adherence to the non-operative-first pathway has been published in the library.

standard.source: RCS/BAPU/BAPS Commissioning guide: Foreskin conditions (2016)
standard.wording: When physiological phimosis is diagnosed in a primary care assessment of foreskin condition, consultation should focus on reassurance and education of parents and child.

pass: Boys with physiological (non-scarred) phimosis and no pathological features have a documented plan of reassurance/education, with or without a topical steroid trial, before any referral for circumcision
population: Inclusion: boys under 18 referred to paediatric surgery/urology for a foreskin problem. Exclusion: pathological phimosis with scarring, recurrent balanitis or paraphimosis
sample: 40 consecutive new foreskin condition referrals over the last 6 months
data_source: Outpatient clinic letters, GP referral letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Send GPs a standard foreskin-conditions leaflet and referral proforma that documents whether physiological phimosis has already had reassurance/education and a steroid trial before referral is accepted
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the paediatric surgery outpatient governance meeting; embed the referral proforma if effective
pitfalls: Parental expectation of surgery at first visit → provide written information explaining the conservative-first approach
GP referrals arriving without a trial of conservative management → use the proforma to triage these back with advice
Diagnosis of 'physiological' vs 'pathological' inconsistent between clinicians → agree diagnostic criteria before cycle 1
Steroid trial started but not followed up to assess response → build in a documented review
pearls: Give GPs a simple traffic-light referral form so conservative options are tried first
Use a patient information leaflet to manage parental expectations before the clinic visit
Audit alongside circumcision rates for physiological phimosis as an outcome measure
Keep the pathway visible in the electronic referral system
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass_short: Reassurance, education or topical steroid plan documented before any circumcision referral

question: What proportion of boys with pathological phimosis have a documented trial of a topical steroid before being listed for circumcision?
why: A trial of topical steroid is a safe, less invasive alternative to surgery, but is inconsistently offered before listing for circumcision; no audit of this step has been published in the library.

standard.source: RCS/BAPU/BAPS Commissioning guide: Foreskin conditions (2016)
standard.wording: Topical steroids may be considered and appear to be a safe, less invasive treatment option and a prescription of this would not normally exceed three months... A topical steroid such as Betamethasone (0.05%) is commonly prescribed for approximately 4 weeks.

pass: A topical steroid trial of up to 4-12 weeks is documented and completed (or a documented contraindication is recorded) before circumcision is listed
population: Inclusion: boys diagnosed with pathological phimosis listed for circumcision. Exclusion: emergency circumcision for paraphimosis or acute infection
sample: All boys listed for circumcision for pathological phimosis over the last 6 months (expect 25-40)
data_source: Outpatient clinic letters, theatre listing forms
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'topical steroid trial: dates and response, or contraindication' field to the outpatient clinic template before circumcision can be listed electronically
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the paediatric surgery outpatient governance meeting; embed the mandatory field if effective
pitfalls: Steroid prescribed by GP but response not fed back to secondary care → ask GPs to document response on the referral back to clinic
Trial too short to assess benefit → specify the recommended 4-week minimum course in the template
Steroid cream not available or not prescribed correctly (wrong strength) → provide a standard prescription card
Circumcision listed 'just in case' before the steroid trial completes → make the field a hard stop on the listing form
pearls: Give parents written instructions on how to apply the steroid and for how long
Ask the GP to review response after 4 weeks rather than waiting for the next hospital appointment
Track circumcision avoidance rate as a secondary outcome
Review any listing without a documented trial at the departmental meeting
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass_short: Topical steroid trial of 4-12 weeks completed before circumcision listing, unless contraindicated

question: What proportion of children having elective day-case surgery are permitted clear fluids up to 1 hour before anaesthesia, rather than being fasted for longer?
why: Unnecessarily long clear-fluid fasting causes distress, dehydration and cancelled theatre slots in children; no audit of compliance with the reduced 1-hour clear-fluid fasting standard has been published in the library.

standard.source: APAGBI/ESPA/ADARPEF Consensus statement on clear fluids fasting for elective paediatric general anaesthesia (Thomas et al., Pediatric Anesthesia 2018)
standard.wording: based on the current evidence base, unless there is a clear contraindication, it is safe and recommended for all children able to take clear fluids, to be allowed and encouraged to have them up to 1 hour before elective general anesthesia.

pass: The documented last clear fluid intake is within 1-2 hours of anaesthetic induction, with no unexplained longer fast
population: Inclusion: children undergoing elective day-case surgery under general anaesthesia. Exclusion: emergency surgery, documented contraindication to reduced fasting
sample: 40 consecutive elective paediatric day cases over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Pre-operative fasting instructions, anaesthetic chart, ward nursing record of last oral intake
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Reissue pre-admission fasting instructions and ward whiteboards to state '1 hour for clear fluids' explicitly, with clear fluids actively offered on the morning of surgery
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the paediatric anaesthesia/day surgery governance meeting; embed the updated instructions if effective
pitfalls: List order changes on the day, leaving children over-fasted despite correct initial instructions → actively offer fluids to children further down the list
Ward staff defaulting to traditional 'nil by mouth from midnight' habits → retrain ward and pre-admission staff
Parents fasting children for longer than instructed out of caution → explain the rationale clearly in pre-admission information
Fluid type not actually 'clear' (e.g. milk given) → define clear fluids explicitly in patient information
pearls: Actively offer clear fluids on the ward rather than relying on parents to remember
Update pre-admission letters and phone calls to state the 1-hour rule clearly
Reorder theatre lists to minimise fasting time for younger children
Audit fasting times alongside cancellation rates for over-fasted children
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from ward and anaesthetic records
pass_short: Last clear fluid intake within 1-2 hours of induction, with no unexplained longer fast

question: What proportion of children having elective day-case surgery are fasted from solid food and formula milk for no more than 6 hours, and from breast milk for no more than 4 hours?
why: Excessive fasting from solids and milk feeds, not just clear fluids, remains common in children's day surgery and is distressing and clinically unnecessary; no audit of adherence to the recommended maximum solid/milk fasting times has been published in the library.

standard.source: APAGBI/ESPA/ADARPEF Consensus statement on clear fluids fasting for elective paediatric general anaesthesia (Thomas et al., Pediatric Anesthesia 2018), Table 1
standard.wording: Preoperative fasting for elective procedures in children, Age (y) 0-16: Solid food, Formula milk 6h; Breast milk 4h; Clear fluids 1h.

pass: Documented fasting time for solids/formula is no more than 6 hours and for breast milk no more than 4 hours before induction, without unexplained excess
population: Inclusion: children aged 0-16 having elective day-case surgery under general anaesthesia. Exclusion: emergency surgery or documented contraindication
sample: 40 consecutive elective paediatric day cases over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Pre-operative fasting instructions, ward nursing record of last feed, anaesthetic chart
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add feed-type-specific maximum fasting times (6h solids/formula, 4h breast milk, 1h clear fluids) to the pre-admission fasting letter and the ward fasting whiteboard
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the paediatric anaesthesia/day surgery governance meeting; embed the updated fasting letter if effective
pitfalls: Breastfeeding mothers given the same 6-hour instruction as formula feeders → make the distinction explicit in written information
List order changes causing unplanned prolonged fasting → build a fallback offer of a snack/feed if delay is expected
Fasting times recorded inconsistently (last 'meal' vs last 'snack') → define clearly what counts as a solid feed
Ward staff unaware of the different breast milk time → include in induction training
pearls: Print the age-specific fasting table on ward information boards
Give parents a written personalised fasting time on the day-before phone call
Prioritise younger children and breastfed infants earlier on the list
Review any case with fasting over 8 hours as an outlier
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from ward records
pass_short: Fasting no more than 6 hours for solids and formula, 4 for breast milk

question: What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients have a clinic blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg (or 130/80 mmHg if significant proteinuria) recorded at their most recent follow-up visit?
why: Blood pressure control after kidney transplantation reduces graft loss and cardiovascular events, but is not universally achieved; no audit of blood pressure target attainment in transplant follow-up has been published in the library.

standard.source: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017)
standard.wording: Clinic blood pressure should be <140/90 mmHg in clinic (130/80 mmHg if PCR >50 or ACR >35) (2C)

pass: The most recent recorded clinic blood pressure meets the applicable target (<140/90, or <130/80 with significant proteinuria)
population: Inclusion: adult kidney transplant recipients attending routine transplant follow-up. Exclusion: patients within 6 weeks of transplantation
sample: 40 consecutive transplant follow-up clinic attendances over the last 2 months
data_source: Transplant clinic letters, EPR vital signs, urine protein:creatinine ratio results
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a blood pressure target flag to the transplant clinic template that highlights the applicable target based on the patient's most recent proteinuria result
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the transplant surgery/nephrology governance meeting; embed the target flag if effective
pitfalls: Home blood pressure readings not considered when clinic readings are borderline → offer home/ambulatory monitoring where available
Proteinuria result out of date, leading to the wrong target being applied → require an annual protein:creatinine ratio
Single reading used rather than an average → standardise to the documented clinic reading process
Target-focused prescribing without checking calcineurin inhibitor levels → review nephrotoxic drug levels alongside blood pressure
pearls: Display the applicable target automatically in the clinic template based on the latest proteinuria result
Offer home blood pressure monitoring kits to patients with white-coat effect
Review antihypertensive regimens at every visit, not only when out of target
Feed results back to referring GPs so shared care is aligned
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass_short: Latest clinic blood pressure below 140/90, or below 130/80 with proteinuria

question: What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients due an annual review are assessed in an annual review clinic within the expected time frame?
why: Late morbidity after kidney transplantation (skin, sexual, psychological and metabolic problems) is unlikely to be identified in routine outpatient follow-up alone; no audit of attendance at a structured annual review has been published in the library.

standard.source: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017)
standard.wording: Audit Measure: Percentage of total patients assessed in an annual review clinic

pass: The patient has a documented annual review clinic assessment within 13 months of their previous one
population: Inclusion: adult kidney transplant recipients more than 1 year post-transplant. Exclusion: recipients within their first post-transplant year
sample: 40 consecutive transplant recipients due an annual review over the last 3 months
data_source: Transplant follow-up database, clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create an automated recall list from the transplant database that flags patients due an annual review 6 weeks in advance
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the transplant follow-up governance meeting; embed the automated recall if effective
pitfalls: Patients lost to follow-up after moving GP or address → confirm contact details are updated at every clinic visit
Annual review conflated with a routine transplant clinic visit without the full review content → define what the annual review must include
DNA rates not tracked → record and follow up non-attenders
Recall list not maintained centrally → assign a named administrator
pearls: Use a single database to track annual review due dates across the service
Combine the annual review with existing blood test visits to reduce patient burden
Record DNA reasons to target support at high-risk patients
Feed annual review outcomes to GPs for shared-care patients
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from transplant database
pass_short: Annual review clinic assessment within 13 months of the previous one

question: What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients have a documented skin surveillance review at the recommended frequency (at least twice yearly up to 5 years post-transplant, then annually)?
why: Kidney transplant recipients have a markedly increased risk of skin cancer from long-term immunosuppression, but skin surveillance is easily overlooked amid other follow-up priorities; no audit of adherence to the recommended surveillance frequency has been published in the library.

standard.source: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017)
standard.wording: We suggest that self-examination should be encouraged with guidance provided. This should be supplemented by at least biannual review by a trained healthcare professional up to 5 years post-transplant and annual review from 5 years (2C)

pass: A documented skin review by a trained healthcare professional has occurred within the last 6 months (if ≤5 years post-transplant) or 12 months (if >5 years post-transplant)
population: Inclusion: adult kidney transplant recipients attending follow-up. Exclusion: recipients within the first 3 months post-transplant
sample: 40 consecutive transplant follow-up attendances over the last 3 months
data_source: Transplant clinic letters, dermatology referral records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a skin surveillance due-date field to the transplant follow-up database that flags overdue reviews and prompts referral to a dermatology or transplant skin clinic
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the transplant follow-up governance meeting; embed the due-date flag if effective
pitfalls: No dedicated skin surveillance clinic, relying on ad hoc opportunistic checks → set up a named transplant skin surveillance clinic or pathway
Self-examination advice given once at transplant and not reinforced → repeat advice at each annual review
Patients living far from the transplant centre missing reviews → arrange shared care with local dermatology where possible
Frequency requirement not distinguished by years post-transplant → build the changing frequency into the recall system
pearls: Combine skin checks with the annual review visit to improve attendance
Give patients a self-examination guide and photograph diary
Refer early for any suspicious lesion rather than waiting for the next scheduled review
Audit alongside skin cancer incidence in the transplant cohort
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass_short: Skin review within 6 months if up to 5 years post-transplant, otherwise 12 months

question: What proportion of kidney transplant recipients treated for a presumed acute rejection episode have a transplant biopsy carried out before treatment is started?
why: Treating rejection without histological confirmation risks over-treatment with immunosuppression and masks alternative diagnoses; no audit of biopsy-before-treatment compliance has been published in the library.

standard.source: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017)
standard.wording: We recommend that a transplant renal biopsy should be carried out before treating an acute rejection episode unless this will substantially delay treatment or pose a significant risk to the patient (1C)

pass: A transplant biopsy result is available before treatment for rejection is started, or a documented reason (delay risk/patient risk) is recorded when treatment precedes biopsy
population: Inclusion: adult kidney transplant recipients treated for presumed acute rejection. Exclusion: hyperacute rejection requiring immediate treatment
sample: All rejection episodes treated over the last 12 months (expect 15-30)
data_source: Transplant MDT records, histopathology reports, drug chart
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'biopsy result before treatment, or documented reason for treating first' field to the rejection treatment order in EPMA
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the transplant surgery/nephrology MDT; embed the EPMA field if effective
pitfalls: Biopsy delayed by radiology or histopathology capacity, forcing empirical treatment → agree a rapid-access biopsy slot for suspected rejection
Reason for treating before biopsy not documented → make the reason field mandatory
Coagulopathy or single-kidney risk used inconsistently to justify treating first → agree criteria in advance with the MDT
Biopsy performed but result not available before treatment starts → track turnaround time separately
pearls: Negotiate a same-day or next-day biopsy slot with interventional radiology for suspected rejection
Fast-track histopathology reporting for transplant biopsies
Review every case where treatment preceded biopsy at the transplant MDT
Track biopsy turnaround time as a linked process measure
effort: ~15 min per case from MDT records
pass_short: Transplant biopsy result available before rejection treatment, or reason documented

question: What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients receive an annual influenza vaccination unless contraindicated?
why: Kidney transplant recipients are at increased risk of severe infection, and influenza vaccination is a simple, high-value preventive measure that is easily missed in surgical follow-up; no audit of annual influenza vaccination uptake in this population has been published in the library.

standard.source: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017), Guideline 8.1.1
standard.wording: Should receive annual influenza vaccination unless contraindicated (1C)

pass: Documented receipt of influenza vaccination in the current influenza season, or a documented contraindication
population: Inclusion: adult kidney transplant recipients under active follow-up. Exclusion: recipients transplanted within the last 6 weeks
sample: 40 consecutive transplant follow-up attendances during influenza season
data_source: GP vaccination record, transplant clinic letters, national immunisation record where accessible

template.note: Initials of person collecting the data and date collected

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an influenza vaccination status field to the transplant clinic template, checked and acted on at every autumn clinic visit, with on-site vaccination offered if not yet done
reaudit: At the following influenza season, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the transplant follow-up governance meeting; embed the clinic template field and on-site vaccination offer if effective
pitfalls: Vaccination assumed to be the GP's responsibility and not checked in clinic → make status-checking part of every autumn transplant clinic visit
No record-sharing between GP and transplant centre → ask patients to bring or confirm vaccination status
Live vaccines incorrectly given to immunosuppressed patients → ensure only inactivated influenza vaccine is used
Vaccination status not re-checked each season → build an annual reminder into the recall system
pearls: Offer on-site vaccination during the autumn transplant clinic to remove the barrier of a separate GP visit
Give patients written confirmation of vaccination for their records
Coordinate with GP practices to avoid duplicate or missed vaccination
Audit alongside pneumococcal vaccination and booster status
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass_short: Influenza vaccination documented this season, or contraindication recorded

question: What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients have their hepatitis B surface antibody (HBsAb) level rechecked annually, with revaccination given if titres fall below 10 mIU/mL?
why: Waning hepatitis B immunity in immunosuppressed transplant recipients is a preventable infection risk that requires active annual surveillance; no audit of adherence to annual HBsAb rechecking has been published in the library.

standard.source: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017), Guideline 8.1.2
standard.wording: Should have hepatitis B surface antibody (HBsAb) levels rechecked annually and be revaccinated if antibody titres fall below 10 mIU/mL (2D)

pass: An HBsAb level is checked within the last 12 months, with revaccination given if the result is below 10 mIU/mL
population: Inclusion: adult kidney transplant recipients previously immunised against hepatitis B under annual follow-up. Exclusion: recipients within their first post-transplant year
sample: 40 consecutive transplant follow-up attendances over the last 3 months
data_source: Laboratory results, transplant clinic letters, immunisation record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an annual HBsAb check to the standard transplant follow-up blood test panel, with an automatic flag to prompt revaccination when the result is below 10 mIU/mL
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the transplant follow-up governance meeting; embed the automated blood panel and flag if effective
pitfalls: HBsAb not included in the routine annual blood panel → add it as a standing annual test
Low result identified but revaccination not actioned → build an automatic alert into the results system
Patients revaccinated elsewhere (e.g. by GP) without the result being shared → ask patients to confirm at each visit
Turnaround time for the result delays action → track result-to-action time
pearls: Bundle the HBsAb check with the existing annual review blood tests
Use an automated laboratory flag for results below 10 mIU/mL
Keep a vaccination record accessible to both transplant and primary care teams
Review results alongside other post-transplant infection surveillance data
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from laboratory results
pass_short: HBsAb checked within 12 months, with revaccination if below 10 mIU/mL

question: What proportion of patients with a new, surgically significant abnormality on head injury imaging have their care discussed with a neurosurgeon?
why: Timely neurosurgical input changes management of significant traumatic brain injury findings; no audit of documented neurosurgical discussion for new significant imaging abnormalities has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.4.15 (2023)
standard.wording: Discuss with a neurosurgeon the care of anyone with new and surgically significant abnormalities on imaging.

pass: A documented discussion with a neurosurgeon occurs within 1 hour of the imaging report identifying a new, surgically significant abnormality
population: Inclusion: adults and children with a head injury and a new surgically significant abnormality on CT/MRI. Exclusion: known chronic stable abnormalities
sample: 40 consecutive head injury CT scans reported as showing a new significant abnormality over the last 4 months
data_source: Radiology reports, ED/ward notes, neurosurgical referral log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a direct electronic 'significant finding' alert from radiology to the referring team and neurosurgical registrar as soon as the report is authorised
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the trauma/neurosurgery network governance meeting; embed the electronic alert if effective
pitfalls: 'Surgically significant' not defined locally, causing inconsistent referral → agree a local definition with the neuroscience unit before cycle 1
Discussion happens but is not documented in a retrievable place → require a coded referral log entry
Out-of-hours reporting delays discussion → audit day and night separately
Referring team unaware imaging has been reported → use an automated alert rather than relying on staff checking results
pearls: Agree the local definition of 'surgically significant' with the neuroscience unit in advance
Use a single logged referral pathway (phone plus electronic record) for every discussion
Review any delay over 1 hour at the trauma governance meeting
Keep the audit simple by using the radiology report timestamp as the start point
effort: ~15 min per case from radiology and referral records
pass_short: Neurosurgeon discussion documented within 1 hour of imaging report showing surgical abnormality

question: What proportion of patients with a severe head injury (GCS 8 or less) requiring transfer to a neuroscience unit are transferred in line with local, agreed transfer guidelines?
why: Delayed or poorly organised transfer of severely head-injured patients worsens outcome; no audit of adherence to agreed local transfer guidelines has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.8.1 (2023)
standard.wording: Ensure local guidelines on the transfer of people with a severe traumatic brain injury are drawn up between the referring hospital trusts, the neuroscience unit and the local ambulance service, and recognise that: transfer would benefit anyone with serious head injuries (a GCS score of 8 or less), irrespective of the need for neurosurgery.

pass: Transfer of a patient with GCS 8 or less follows the documented local transfer guideline (designated referring/receiving consultants, escort standards and communication during transfer)
population: Inclusion: adults with GCS 8 or less transferred to a neuroscience unit for a head injury. Exclusion: patients managed entirely within the neuroscience unit's own catchment without transfer
sample: All such transfers over the last 12 months (expect 15-30)
data_source: Transfer documentation, ambulance records, receiving unit notes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Refresh and redistribute the network head injury transfer guideline, with a transfer checklist built into the ambulance handover documentation
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the trauma network governance meeting; embed the transfer checklist if effective
pitfalls: Local guideline out of date or not known to junior staff → include the transfer pathway in trauma induction
Escort training not verified before transfer → use a standard escort competency checklist
Unstable patients transferred without adequate resuscitation → reinforce the requirement to stabilise before transfer
Transfer delayed by bed availability, not process → record reasons for any delay separately
pearls: Review the transfer guideline jointly with the ambulance service and neuroscience unit annually
Use a standard transfer checklist that mirrors the NICE recommendations
Debrief any transfer that deviates from the guideline
Track transfer times alongside guideline adherence
effort: ~15 min per case from transfer records
pass_short: Transfer follows the documented local guideline for patients with GCS 8 or less

question: What proportion of adults undergoing cranial surgery receive mechanical VTE prophylaxis from the time of admission?
why: Cranial surgery patients are at high VTE risk but pharmacological prophylaxis is often delayed because of bleeding concerns, making early mechanical prophylaxis important; no audit of mechanical VTE prophylaxis timing for cranial surgery has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG89 Venous thromboembolism in over 16s, rec 1.12.5 (2018)
standard.wording: Consider mechanical VTE prophylaxis for people undergoing cranial surgery, start it on admission. Choose either: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression.

pass: Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression are documented as started on the day of admission
population: Inclusion: adults admitted for elective or emergency cranial surgery. Exclusion: patients with a documented contraindication to mechanical prophylaxis
sample: 40 consecutive cranial surgery admissions over the last 3 months
data_source: VTE risk assessment form, nursing admission record, drug/device chart

template.note: Initials of person collecting the data and date collected

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add mechanical VTE prophylaxis as a default nursing admission task for every cranial surgery admission, triggered by the admission diagnosis code
reaudit: At 12 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the neurosurgery governance meeting; embed the default admission task if effective
pitfalls: Emergency admissions bypassing the standard admission checklist → build the prompt into the emergency neurosurgical admission proforma as well
Correct stocking size not available → stock a full range of sizes on the ward
Device removed for imaging/theatre and not restarted → include a restart check in the post-procedure checklist
Documentation of 'prophylaxis given' without specifying which device or when → require the specific device and start time
pearls: Make mechanical prophylaxis a same-day nursing task linked to the admission diagnosis
Audit alongside VTE risk assessment completion rates
Keep spare stockings and compression sleeves readily available on the ward
Review any gaps at the weekly ward safety huddle
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from admission records
pass_short: Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent compression started on day of admission

question: What proportion of adults undergoing cranial surgery whose VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk are started on pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH 24 to 48 hours after surgery?
why: Delaying pharmacological VTE prophylaxis too long, or omitting it altogether, exposes high-risk neurosurgical patients to avoidable VTE; no audit of adherence to the recommended 24-48 hour start window has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG89 Venous thromboembolism in over 16s, rec 1.12.8 (2018)
standard.wording: Consider adding pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH, starting 24 to 48 hours after surgery for people undergoing cranial surgery whose risk of VTE outweighs their risk of bleeding.

pass: LMWH is started between 24 and 48 hours postoperatively in patients assessed as having VTE risk outweighing bleeding risk, or a documented reason is given for a different timing
population: Inclusion: adults having cranial surgery assessed as VTE risk outweighing bleeding risk. Exclusion: patients where bleeding risk is assessed as outweighing VTE risk throughout admission
sample: 40 consecutive cranial surgery patients meeting this risk profile over the last 4 months
data_source: VTE/bleeding risk assessment, drug chart, post-operative ward round notes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 48-hour post-cranial-surgery VTE prophylaxis decision to the ward round checklist, with a prompt to start LMWH if not already documented
reaudit: At 14 weeks, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the neurosurgery governance meeting; embed the ward round checklist prompt if effective
pitfalls: Decision deferred repeatedly without documentation → require an explicit decision at each ward round after 24 hours
Post-operative CT not repeated to confirm no bleeding before starting LMWH → agree a standard imaging check where required locally
Different consultants applying different thresholds → agree a single departmental risk-assessment tool
LMWH started but not documented as being for VTE prophylaxis specifically → use a coded prescription indication
pearls: Build the 24-48 hour decision point into the standard post-operative ward round proforma
Agree a single risk-assessment tool across the department before cycle 1
Review any prolonged delay at the morbidity and mortality meeting
Track post-operative VTE and bleeding events as balancing measures

pass_short: LMWH started 24-48 hours after surgery when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk

question: What proportion of adults on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy who present with a chronic subdural haematoma have a documented multidisciplinary decision on when to stop and, if appropriate, restart the drug?

standard.source: Protocol for the development of a multidisciplinary clinical practice guideline for the care of patients with chronic subdural haematoma (British Journal of Neurosurgery guideline programme)
standard.wording: Perioperative care pathway • Management of anticoagulation/antiplatelet agents • Optimal anaesthetic technique • Location and timing of optimization • Acute post-operative medical management

pass: A documented decision on stopping and restarting anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy, made with input from neurosurgery and the prescribing specialty (e.g. cardiology, stroke, haematology), is present in the notes
population: Inclusion: adults on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy diagnosed with chronic subdural haematoma. Exclusion: patients not on any anticoagulant/antiplatelet drug
sample: All such patients presenting over the last 6 months (expect 20-30)
data_source: Neurosurgical admission and discharge notes, MDT/ward round records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'anticoagulation/antiplatelet plan' field to the chronic subdural haematoma admission and discharge proforma, requiring a documented joint decision
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the neurosurgery governance meeting; embed the proforma field if effective
