pitfalls: Decompensated liver disease may not be clearly coded, especially if the presentation is dominated by withdrawal symptoms: cross-check liver function tests and clinical notes, not just the coding system
Advice may be given informally by phone without a written record: require the advice or plan to be documented in the notes regardless of how it was obtained
Choice of sedative may need adjustment in liver failure (e.g. shorter-acting benzodiazepines): record whether the medication choice reflects this, as a secondary marker of specialist input
Numbers will be small: consider a 12-month or longer collection window and report raw numbers alongside any percentage
Weekend and out-of-hours presentations may have delayed access to liver specialist advice: record and report time-of-week separately
pearls: Recruit a hepatology or gastroenterology liaison consultant as a joint audit lead with addiction liaison psychiatry
Use liver function tests and coding together to build a more complete case-finding search than either alone
Present the audit as protecting a small, very high-risk group, to secure engagement despite the modest case numbers
Build the electronic referral trigger to also suggest a liver-safe benzodiazepine choice, closing two safety gaps at once
Keep this as an ongoing, rolling audit given the low case volume, rather than a single fixed 3-month cycle
effort: ~20 min per identified case from the medical and hepatology record
pass: Advice from, or a joint plan with, a healthcare professional experienced in liver disease (hepatology, gastroenterology or a liver-specialist nurse) is documented within 24 hours of decompensated liver disease being identified during alcohol withdrawal treatment
pass_short: Liver specialist advice or joint plan documented within 24 hours of decompensation being identified

question: What proportion of patients discharged from inpatient drug treatment services (including specialist community and inpatient detoxification services) after treatment for opioid use are supplied with take-home naloxone, or have a documented reason why not?
why: No audit in the library measures naloxone supply on discharge from inpatient drug treatment settings, despite national guidance permitting a wide range of drug treatment services, including inpatient services, to supply naloxone without a prescription to reduce overdose deaths.

standard.source: GOV.UK Supplying take home naloxone without a prescription (Human Medicines Regulations 2012, regulation 238; guidance updated 12 September 2025)
standard.wording: The types of drug treatment services that can supply naloxone include, but may not be limited to: drug services provided by primary care services; drug services provided by secondary care services (including a range of specialised community and inpatient drug services)...

population: Inclusion: adults discharged from an inpatient drug/alcohol treatment unit or psychiatric ward following treatment where opioid use was part of the presentation. Exclusion: patients with no history of opioid use in the current or past 12 months.
sample: 30 consecutive discharges with a history of opioid use from the inpatient drug treatment or dual diagnosis service over the last 6 months
data_source: Inpatient drug treatment service discharge record and pharmacy dispensing log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'naloxone supplied or reason not supplied' field to the inpatient drug treatment discharge checklist, which cannot be completed without an entry, and stock take-home naloxone kits on the ward
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the drug treatment service and pharmacy governance meeting; if effective, embed the mandatory field and ward stock as standard practice
evidence: [1341] Audit of safe opioid prescribing across surgical departments found naloxone co-prescribing improved from below 50% to over 70% in several departments after education and reminders, showing naloxone supply is a modifiable, auditable practice even though this specific audit is in a surgical rather than drug treatment context
pitfalls: Patients may already hold a naloxone kit from a community drug service: record this as a valid reason for non-supply rather than a fail
Ward staff may be unfamiliar with the legal basis for supplying naloxone without an individual prescription: provide brief training alongside the mandatory field
Family members or carers present at discharge may also need training in use, which is easy to miss if only the patient is addressed
Stock and expiry management of naloxone kits on the ward needs a named responsible person, or supply will lapse
A patient who leaves against medical advice before formal discharge may miss the opportunity for supply: consider a rapid-access naloxone offer earlier in the admission for high-risk patients
pearls: Partner with the local community drug and alcohol service, which will already have a naloxone supply protocol that can be adapted for inpatient use
Use the gov.uk guidance's explicit inclusion of inpatient drug services to reassure ward staff of the legal basis for supply without an individual prescription
Build training on naloxone use into existing discharge planning conversations rather than as a separate appointment
Track whether kits supplied are ever used (via ambulance service or community data, where locally available) as a longer-term outcome measure
Keep a standing stock of naloxone kits on the ward with a named pharmacy lead responsible for restocking and expiry checks
effort: ~10 min per 10 discharges from the discharge checklist and pharmacy log
pass: A take-home naloxone kit is documented as supplied at discharge, or a specific reason for not supplying it (e.g. already holds a kit, clinically inappropriate, declined) is recorded
pass_short: Take-home naloxone supplied at discharge, or specific reason for not supplying recorded

question: When a multidisciplinary, medical or independent review determines that seclusion is no longer warranted, does the patient leave seclusion without unnecessary delay?
why: No audit in the library measures the time between a review decision to end seclusion and the patient actually being allowed free and unrestricted access to the ward, despite this being a specific Mental Health Act Code of Practice requirement distinct from the well-audited review-timing measures already in the library.

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraphs 26.144-26.145
standard.wording: Seclusion should immediately end when a MDT review, a medical review or the independent MDT review determines it is no longer warranted... Seclusion ends when a patient is allowed free and unrestricted access to the normal ward environment or transfers or returns to conditions of long-term segregation.

population: Inclusion: all seclusion episodes ended by a documented review decision in the audit period. Exclusion: episodes ended by the patient absconding or being transferred for an unrelated reason.
sample: All seclusion episodes ended in the last 3 months (typically 20-40 episodes across a secure or acute inpatient service)
data_source: Seclusion record, showing the time of the review decision and the time seclusion actually ended
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'time of review decision' and 'time seclusion ended' pair of fields to the seclusion record, both time-stamped by the system rather than handwritten, so any delay is automatically visible
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the ward or secure service clinical governance meeting; if effective, adopt the dual time-stamp field trust-wide
evidence: Topic card 'Seclusion practice and review' notes that huddles and weekly meetings reduced average seclusion duration from 30 to 20 hours in one service [3105], showing seclusion duration (including the tail end of an episode) is a measurable and improvable indicator
pitfalls: Staff may record the review decision time and the ending time as the same moment out of habit, masking a real delay: use system time-stamps rather than staff-entered times where possible
A delay may be clinically justified (e.g. arranging safe staffing to support the patient leaving seclusion): capture the reason for any delay rather than treating all delay as a failure
Night shifts with lower staffing may show longer delays: report results by time of day
Ending seclusion for a toilet or food break should not be confused with a genuine end of seclusion: apply the Code of Practice definition (free and unrestricted access) strictly
A patient may be reviewed as 'no longer warranted' by one professional but a second required reviewer disagrees: record how such disagreements are resolved and timed
pearls: Use existing seclusion review audit infrastructure (already common in the library) to add these two extra time fields rather than building a new audit from scratch
Recruit ward nursing staff to identify realistic causes of delay (e.g. arranging support) so the fix addresses real barriers, not just recording
Present the library finding that a huddle model cut average seclusion duration by a third [3105], to support a similar staffing/planning change here
Track the reason for delay over time to see if a particular cause (e.g. staffing) dominates and needs a separate fix
Keep this as a standing indicator on the ward's seclusion dashboard rather than a single-cycle audit
effort: ~10 min per episode from the seclusion record
pass: The time recorded for the end of seclusion is within 30 minutes of the review decision that seclusion is no longer warranted
pass_short: Seclusion ended within 30 minutes of review decision that it is no longer warranted

question: Do people living with dementia prescribed an antipsychotic for behaviour and psychological symptoms of dementia have the medication reassessed at least every 6 weeks, with the decision to continue or stop documented at that review?
why: No audit in the library isolates the specific 6-weekly reassessment interval and continuation decision required by NICE for antipsychotics in dementia; the existing 'Antipsychotic prescribing in dementia (BPSD)' topic in the library is heavily audited for physical health monitoring, but the reassessment interval and stopping decision itself has not been separately measured.

standard.source: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, rec 1.7.6 (2018)
standard.wording: When using antipsychotics: use the lowest effective dose and use them for the shortest possible time reassess the person at least every 6 weeks, to check whether they still need medication.

population: Inclusion: people with dementia currently prescribed an antipsychotic for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, under old age psychiatry follow-up. Exclusion: antipsychotics prescribed for a co-existing psychotic illness diagnosed independently of dementia.
sample: 30 consecutive people with dementia on an antipsychotic for behavioural and psychological symptoms, from the old age psychiatry or memory service caseload
data_source: Old age psychiatry electronic record and medication review notes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 6-weekly review reminder to the electronic record for every patient coded as being on an antipsychotic for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, which must be actioned with a continue/stop decision before it can be dismissed
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the old age psychiatry governance meeting; if effective, embed the automatic reminder permanently
pitfalls: A general medication review note that does not specifically address whether the antipsychotic is still needed should not count as a pass: require an explicit continue/stop statement
Community-dwelling patients seen less frequently than every 6 weeks by a specialist may be reviewed jointly with a GP: check both records for the review
Some patients may be on a long-standing, stable dose with an implicit assumption that stopping is unsafe: this should be recorded as an explicit, reasoned decision to continue, not an omission
This audit should be framed around the reassessment interval and action, not repeat existing physical health monitoring audits, to avoid the library's identified overdone territory
A short administrative gap (e.g. patient in hospital) may extend the interval for a valid reason: record and report these separately from true gaps in follow-up
pearls: Frame this audit explicitly as measuring the reassessment interval and stop/continue decision, not repeating overdone physical health monitoring measures
Recruit the old age psychiatry pharmacist to help identify the current antipsychotic-for-BPSD caseload and build the reminder system
Use the NICE wording directly ('reassess... to check whether they still need medication') as the pass criterion to keep the standard unambiguous
Track the proportion of reviews resulting in an actual dose reduction or stop over successive re-audits, as the ultimate measure of impact
Align the re-audit timing with the service's existing dementia care review cycle to avoid extra data collection burden
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the old age psychiatry record
pass: A documented reassessment, with an explicit decision to continue or stop, is present at an interval of 6 weeks or less throughout the prescribing period
pass_short: Antipsychotic reassessed at least every 6 weeks, with explicit continue or stop decision

question: Do adults with a learning disability prescribed medication for behaviour that challenges receive only a single psychotropic drug at a time, rather than two or more used concurrently for the same target behaviour?
why: The STOMP topic card notes single drug therapy fell from 19% to 34% in one repeated-cycle audit [3268], but no audit in the library specifically measures polypharmacy for behaviour that challenges as its own single, plain question distinct from rationale, review or monitoring audits already covered.

standard.source: NICE NG11 Challenging behaviour and learning disabilities, rec 1.8.3 (2015)
standard.wording: start with a low dose and use the minimum effective dose needed only prescribe a single drug monitor side effects as recommended in the NICE guidelines on psychosis and schizophrenia...

population: Inclusion: adults with a learning disability currently prescribed at least one psychotropic medication for behaviour that challenges. Exclusion: patients with a co-existing diagnosed mental illness requiring its own separate treatment (e.g. an antidepressant for depression alongside an antipsychotic for a separate diagnosed psychotic illness).
sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability on psychotropic medication for behaviour that challenges, from the community learning disability team or STOMP register
data_source: Community learning disability team electronic record and current drug chart/repeat prescription list
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic polypharmacy alert to the electronic prescribing system, triggered when a second psychotropic is added for a patient already coded as being treated for behaviour that challenges, prompting a mandatory documented reason
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the community learning disability team and pharmacy governance meeting; if effective, embed the polypharmacy alert trust-wide
evidence: [3268] Repeated cycles of audit in one intellectual disability team found single drug therapy stayed low, moving from 19% to only 34% despite improvements in metabolic monitoring (0% to 95%) and risk assessment (68% to 100%), showing polypharmacy specifically resists the general improvements seen elsewhere
pitfalls: Distinguishing 'for the same target behaviour' from legitimate separate diagnoses requires careful case-by-case review: use a learning disability psychiatrist to adjudicate ambiguous cases
Historic long-term polypharmacy may be well established and difficult to safely change quickly: record whether a reduction plan exists even where combination therapy continues
PRN (as-needed) medication used occasionally alongside a regular psychotropic should be recorded separately, since NG11 addresses this differently
The library shows this measure resisted improvement even when other measures improved sharply [3268]: expect this to be a harder change and plan a longer improvement timeline

Switching directly from one drug to another (a brief overlap during a cross-taper) should not be wrongly counted as ongoing combination therapy: define a minimum overlap duration before counting as polypharmacy
pearls: Use the STOMP register as the sampling frame, since it should already list current psychotropic prescriptions for this population
Present the library finding that single drug therapy resisted improvement even where other STOMP measures improved sharply [3268], to justify a dedicated focus on this specific measure
Recruit the learning disability pharmacist to review combination cases and support tapering plans where appropriate
Track the number of patients on 2 or more psychotropics for the same behaviour over successive audits as the key outcome measure, not just documentation of a reason
Keep the audit register with the learning disability pharmacist for continuity across trainee rotations
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the STOMP register and prescribing record
pass: Only one psychotropic drug is prescribed for the target behaviour at any one time, or, where more than one is used, a specific documented clinical reason for combination therapy is present
pass_short: Only one psychotropic drug per target behaviour, or documented reason for combination
